A marriage has been arranged and willlake place early in November between the Marquis of Harting- ton and the Dowager Duchess of Manchester. The Duchess will lose the money left her by the late Duke's will, but that is not likely to di- I her.

Alexander Graham Bell, inventor of the telep ne• , , Professor Elihu Thomson, inventor of the ele4rlc welding machine and other electrical devices; and Edward Weston, a leader in electric lighting, are all of British birth, it is said. They are all Americans, however, adds a New York paper, in ingenuity and by adoption.

A marriage between ex-King Milan and Madame Barrios, widow of ex-President Barrios, of Guate- mala, is announced. This ex-president was a half- civilised man, democratic and warlike, a free- thinker, yet believing in education—the very thing he lacked—and he appropriated the national ex- chequer to his own use.

Mr. Beerbohm Tree is very hard upon Lady Dimio. Both these artistes are performing in Edinblrgh just now, and it appears that Lady Dunlo i the greater attraction. Mr. free says that," with! the charms of 'Venus' the dramatic muse cannot tme- tend to vie. The claims of Nature must ever be stronger than those of Art.'' • ~f,O

. nil Mr. Chamberlain has been saying 'big things to American reporters about the Behring Sea fisheries dispute ;but when he speaks as an anibassador from this country he surely must forget that we have an excellent American Minister in Sir Julian Patitnce fote. Mr. Chamberlain's former intervention ngthe fisheries question had the contrary to a conciliatory effect on Americans.

In view of the rumoured transfer of Mr. Jackson, Financial Secretary to the Treasury, to be Chief Secretary for Ireland. (vice brave Balfour, deposed), it is interesting to note that Mr. Jackson left Lon- don for Dublin, Ot2 Saturday last, for a month's tour of political and social observation in various parts of Ireland. It is rumoured that he will devote spe- cial attention to light railways, in which be takes keen interest.

Mr. Jackson is at the head of a large tannery in Leeds, and in addition to representing one division of that town in Parliament, is a railway and ;com- pany director. He has steadily improved his Parlia- mentary position of late, and his recent privy coun- cillorship marks him out as the next man among the Tories for Cabinet rank. One of his sons is the well known Harrow and Cambridge cricketer.

The Pope continues to reside at the Casino of Pius IV., where he daily walks in the gardtins,-taking care of the plants and animals, of which he is very fond. Sometimes he redeives visitors inthe garden at a very early hour. His health is good, for the air there is no longer pernicious as it once was, many, sanitary improvements having been made in the Vatican gardens, and the neighbourhood being no longer waste land, but almost all built upon.

Mr. John Dillon stood up boldly on Sunday against the attack on the Plan of Campaign by Bishop O'Dwyer, and a monster meeting at Lim- erick repudiated the charges of cowardice and dis- honesty levelled at the inventor of the Plan. The people of Ireland know where to draw the line between religion and politics. When a Catholic bishop sides with the landlords, justifies evlction, and condemns a great populai leader, 14 runs against a rock.

Mr. J. H. Blackburne, the well-known chess player, who is so distinguishing himself at the Manchester Chess Tournament this week, is a native of Lancashire. He himself attributes a great deal of his success to his memory, which is indeed a , wonderful one. He has been known to play blind- folded eight games at one and the same time, and defeat all his opponents. A most genial mantis he, and a great favorite with all who know him. 1

The exposition Of Anarchism which Louise Michel gave to a London audience on Wednesday 'night was harmless. She said many absurd things about the Parliamentary thieves and the capitalists who exploit the people, and hinted that , the people would one day rise and kill the governors, bus gave no indication as to how tho revolution was to be brought about. As anarchism implies no organisa- tion, no government, or order in society, any defin- ite programme would be out of question.

The Bishop of Worcester,whose resignation is now placed _beyond doubt, is one of the most gentle and kind-hearted of English prelates, and throughout his diocese he is regarded with affection almost uni- versally by people of most divergent creeds. !Many stories are told of his unostentatious charity. He has more than once been known to present a poor but deserving clergyman to a benefice, and to send I him privately a banknote to cover the expenses of removal, which he knew well his , own resources would be heavily strained to meet.

A good story is going round Middle Temple ;circles I At some recent assizes the judge was rather the worse for wear in the hearing department ; indeed, that seems to be one of the chief qualifications for the judicial .bench now-adays. He ground out a homily to a young lady in the dock on the error of her ways, and finished up by sentencing her to eigh- teen months' hard labour. " Why," returned the fair one." I can do that on my head like an adjec- tived toff." " What's that?" said his lordship, add- ing immediately, " it will be necessary for you to petition the Government on that subject." taker

The tithe war in Wales has in a new form. Landlords have changed their tactics. Instead of recovering the unjust tithe with the assistance of the bailiff and a regiment of soldier's, one landlord at least has taken a more summary method of deal- ing with tenants who refuse to pay. He is J. Marshall Dugdale, Llvvyn Llanfyllin, Mont- gomeryshire—a Tory, of course. He presents his tenants with the alternative of paying the tithe or giving up the farm. If others pursue this high- handed policy the disestablishment movement and the domande for land law reform will go forward together in Wales.

A good story is told anent the sojourn of Henry George in Sydney, during his recent Australian lecturing tour. It was suggested to the secretary of one of the racing clubs by a leading local politi-; cian that it would be a nice and graceful thiug jto send Mr. George a comi limentary ticket to the race meeting that was at hand. "Who is he?" queried the secretary: "I never beard of him befere." "Why, he's a man of world-wide celebrity." "Does be own any horses? "persisted the secretary. "Yes two very fast trotters—Progress and Poverty." "Oh, all right," said the now satisfied secretary; "here's a ticket for him".

The latest royal job. Her Majesty, says "Truth," has appointed one of Lord Strathallan's sons to be a page of honour. He will be a page for six years' and get £l5O a year for being it. Formerly, a page wound up his illustrious career with a free present of a commission in the Guards, with several thous- ands a year, but purchase has done away with that. There are four pages of honour, two nominally in waiting every month. But the page only waits .s,va there is a prawing Room, wearing a very pretty uniforta, and sO titileSS there is one of these functions, he need never even get into his fine clothes. £l5O a year is not bad for that kind of work.

Sir Edward Guinness has promised this employe; that, "in recognition of the excellent service which had been rendered to him in the past, whether as sole owner of the brewery or as chairman of the company," he will shortly arrange with them that a personal gift from himself of one month's salary shall be made to every member of No. 1 and 2 strilf of clerks and of one week's wages to every work- ing man on the Ist August. The promise is made at the end of a letter begging the men very fully to consider the consequence of their action, "if, as is reported, they intend joining a union which has unfortunately been involved of late in disputes with employers."

Boulangism is again the talk of Paris. As a poli- tical factor it is long since dead and buried beyond all resurrection, and now the secrets by which the conspiracy was maintained are being unveiled. In a series of articles on "Behind the scenes of Boulan- gism," the amours and intrigues of the General are exposed. The revelations will be interesting when they reach the financial side of Boulganism. The Royalists must have sunk an enormous amount in the General. The requiem which is being” sung over the remains of the "National Party will insure the safety of the Republic against similar conspiracies, and will be a severe blow to the Orleanist pretenders.

Third-class paseen, „ should remember the Mid- land Railway. This line which was the first to abolish second class, will in future provide third- class carriages with lavatory accommodation. This is-a- convenience which is much needed,-but very grudgingly granted by our railways, even for second' an. d_first class_xtuTiages. We are stills long_ way behind the American railways, where the needs of travellers are attended to;. but we , trust that at least this boon of lavatory accommodation will scion be conceeded by all our railway companies. It is in their interest, too,to look after the despised third class,as on more than one line they are the passengers who make the diiidend. .

Some regret, writes a Paris Correspondent, will be felt abroad as well as in France, on account of a recent decision of the Minister of War which de- prives the cantinieres of their soldier-like uniforms. ' The cantiniere, who by the way must always be a married woman, has, as a rule, a distinct influence for good upon the men of the regiment, and trilly merits her vamp of ",the soldier's sister.' Many i of them have the military medal awarded for deeds of valour on the field, and two or three are members of the Legion of Honour. No reason is alleged for depriying.gientraf their uniform, which was their pride and their best protection, and which created between them And their regiments a strong esprit de corps.•
The illness which has sent Mr. W. S. Gilbert over

to Carlsbad is a touch of the gout. There is quite a Gilbertian situation about the librettist's action against Mr. Carte and Sir Arthur Sullivan. Mr. Gilbert, himself la barrister, has made unlimited capital ounif the lawyers. Hellas never tired of poking fun at susceptible chancellors; he has twitted members of the. profession who have been in the habit of Taking a fee with a grin on their face, When they haven't been there to attend to the case "; and helms hit off that legal celebrity who has attained his briefs and his eminence by" falling in love with amish,4aistaraey's elderly ugly daugh- ter." Now the lawyers are making a bit of capital out of him, and their innings begins to look likes lengthy one.
CUE)

The influenza has re-appeared in Vienna. A cor- respondent there says the doctors speak of many cases in their private practice. At the general hospital several patients have been received, and a great many_ come to the hospital to consult the doctor a there and retucn home. One of the doctors at' the general liceipittl hag been • seized. He has himself desaribed'his illness as influenza. ' The' health of Vienna has not been good during this year, and the principle reason is believed to have been the influenza epidemic, Which had developed lung and Chest diseases in persons of weak constitution who might otherwise have lived. The influenza manifests itself much in the way it did last winter by finer, Chills, and pains in the limbs, but whereas it was attended by- diseases of the throat in the winter months it now appears at the same time as diarrhcea and intestinal compliihts.

To call a distinguished Government official a cove " would sound vulgar and disrespectful, but " Kovana ", is highly deferential. This is the title by which the Administrator of New Guinea is known among the natives. These natives know when discretion is the better part of valour, and have a remarkably frank way of saying so. When the Administrator was bunting the murderers of Cap- tain Ansell the Huhuna tribe were bent upon fight- ' ing. They canto down to the beach with their spears and in their war paint, and the Europeans had to fire to save themselves from slaughter. Three or fed bf the gallant natives were killed and others wounded. Some time later the " Koval= " and his party entered the village of this tribe without re- sistance, the first to salute them being the widow of the chief who had gallantly led the attack and had been the first to fall. The tribe at a formal meet- ing expressed deep regret fortheir folly in attack- ing the " Kovana," and, says Sir William MacGre- gor," excused themselves by saying they did not know how powerful we were."
PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS

A STAG is often obliged to run for deer life. GOES WITHOUT SAYING.—The deaf-and-dumb alphabet. To what rhythm does a saw-mill run I—Log-a- rhythm. THE people who give tone to society seldom give anything else. "IT'S little things that tell," says a philosopher. Yes, doubtless; little brothers and sisters, for in- stance. A FASHIONABLE girl's motto—" Never put off till to-morrow what you can get your mother to do

to-day." SEASONABLE HINT FOR HEADS OF HOUSEHOLDS. —The proper way to provide for warming the house is to keep the cellar coaled. WHAT portions of the body are the best travel- lers 7—The two-wrists. A LUMINOUS QUERY.—Is a lantern-jawed man invariably light-headed? AN oculist may not be an elocutionist, but he is sometimes a first-class re-sighter. WHAT is that which has got feet and nails, but no legs, toes or claws 7—A yard measure. To obtain down from the bosom of a lake, wait till you see a boatman feather his oars. IT is a father's duty to supply food for his children. He should always remember that he is their pap-pa. WHEN you see a sea captain dressed in black, don't ask him if he's gone into mourning for a "dead reckoning." WHAT is the difference between a young lady and her nightcap One is born to wed, and the other is worn to bed. A VAIN and ostentatious ignoramus having unex- pectedly come inte property, sent for a tailor to come and measure him for a coat-of-arms.
Ai r insurance agent refused to take a risk oil the house of a poet, because he was told that the poet was "imbued with the fire of genius." _

you, acuidentally open. I was standing by it close, when, all of a sudden, the other man hit me 3 blow and knocked me down plump. I was stunned

like.' " ' Well,' said his master. Go on,' he says. " ' In a minute, sir, the other man was through the top of the window, and taking out a pistol he held it at me. Then he cleared the silver right off, and handed it to this one; and then, still pointing the pistol—and I was afraid to stir—they got away with the plunder.' "'What was the other manlike asked a gentle.. man. "Well,'"l can't for certain say,' replied the butler, 'but he had a grey coat on, and a black piece of cloth on his face. This fellow had nothing but a cap pulled down over his eyes, and he scuttled away across the park as quick as he could. The other man went off by the wall and up on the hill.' "'Why didn't you give the alarm ? said the gentleman. 'There were plenty of men in the stables and in the grounds.' "'Have you any idea where the plate has been taken to?' asked Sir Walter, with a look in his eyes which the man did not like. " I can't tell, sir,' replied the butler, 'and it's very unpleasant having insinuations made at me. I will go downstairs, if you please. Perhaps the accomplice can tell.' " ' Very likely it's in the bathing box where you and your friend the thief planned the robbery ,last night, I said. Try there, sir! ' "Ye never in all your days saw a man so 'flabbergasted' as the butler was when I said this out among all the'people. "Who are you ? ' he says, pushing his way toward the door. But he was prevented going out by some of the men and the gentlemen of the house. "'You saw me, did you,' I said. 'Well, then, I have witnesses to prove where I was. Now tell the truth, if ye can.' "He was quite knocked up, and when he saw the police officer, who had tracked the robber, but never caught him, only he got the rate back. When he saw the policeman come in, I declare he fell on his knees and confessed it all, crying like a great girl. "It was a very pretty plant,' I can tell ye," con- tinued the signalman, "and I got my ten pounds and more. Many of the ladies and gentlemen sub- scribed money and gave it tome, and I have it safe against a rainy day, hid away in the corner of the signal-box, where no one ever can find it."- "That's right, George; but suppose anything hap- pened to you,. and you wanted it, what would ye, do?" ,"I'd tell someone then, and I don't mind telling you. It's up near the levers. on the left side, buried near the box in the woodwork. What's that noise ?" "What noise?" she said. "I heard nothing." "A creak," he said, anxiously. "1 wouldn't have anyone to know of my hiding-plaaenfor all the money." "It's nothing, George" she replied, looking out and returning briskly. "But you didn't finish your story. How did you know that the man who took the plate was Sandy Sam ? " "Partly by his voice,. whiich I can swear to, and partly because I picked up something belonging to him which matches with something he has new. If ever I get the proof it will be bad for him. Ho has- done me an ill. turn, more than once, and' I'll even) "Well, George,. I must go down to, the 'village: Thank ye for your story..l willkeep yourseeret quite, eafe." "And I must be getting, ready fore my turn to. night," said the man. "Good-bye, Lucy. All that. there money and things will be yoursimy girl, when 1 die—never fear." ".Don't talk like that, George; Fire sure I don't, want them. But Pia glad you've confidence kerne. I think I will take Bridget% cottage,, and. save you my company." " Yes ; I thinkye had better, Lucy.. We can't live• here together. If ye want anything.,l will let) ye. have it if I cane but never mind me—good-bye; I'll be out all night."' " I'll call to-morrow. and tell yen) my plans.. 1 may remain here to-night, I suppose, withthochild P" "0' course; o”courser was the:answer; ." you'll have it alPto yourself." She went away inthe)direction otthe village. The- signalman went for his coat and. lamp, and busied. himself about tea and• Sandy Sanancrepttunder the hedge from the 'window where he had been listening,. and with stealthy steps and a murderous expression in his face, took his-way unseen along, thee railway cutting..

CHATTER XVIII: FACE TO FACAtt NIGHT lias • fallen upon the neighbourhood;,ancl save, for the occasional barking of a dog, and—nearor the town—the never-ceasing hum, of movement con- nected .with the canal and the railway, we may say- that Landstone- is silent. But:unseen andemheard a great struggle'is.geing: on, notenly inthe,town in the hearts oftnen„but an the workshops, which are almost silent toe. " Sandy " Sam, .a lazy, idle good-fior-nothing fellow,,whonever did any work that he could help, and: yet who had brainaufficient to do the right thing at the right time, and who alto pe.ssessellthe art of commanding men—making them. work-- "Sandy." Sam was busy. Very busy—as well emplbyed as:the devil is said to be in a gait of 'wind. lie hact been idle, long eneag,h,.and now his evil genius prompted him ta turn upon his em ployer,. for be- had long been waiting an opportuuity; to. "spite "' Sir Walter, and to obtain. rev enge for the, disappeintanent he had eexperienced at thes weddir.g. of Lady Watson's sister.. But he had ntiscalculated his influence. What. over may have been the chairman's faults of temper and manner, he WOG just and straightforward, honest, and tam; to his mew He only employed those who- riighstly carried out his orders, and more than once- "sandy " Sam bad got "hauled over the coals" for intittention or self-will when the chair- man came- ipokin g his long nose into the shops," as .Mn. Sam .chose to phrase it. There- are some natures which will, when re- proved, in= gine themselves slighted and ill-treated; they canoe t brook reproof, and so sulk, not dazing to rebel,. bat with all the will and intention to be reveweil. Sandy Sam' who had gained his title from hia, pale, freckled face and sandy hair, was a most map leasant customer to deal with. He stored up every little slight, and by degrees built up his mole lxi,/ is into quite a formidable range of mountains csL offs ce. The last difficulty had caused him to set the. new lc ,comotive along the sails; and when this dia- bolies 1 act had been nearly traced to him, and. with it hit 3 supposed complicity in the presence on it of yens ig Edward Watson, who might have thereby lost his life. I kg acting foreman, Sam knew quite well that the en gine had steam in her. He knew or guessed that ye eine-6 Edward had intended to sleep in the shops, so as to be ready early in the morning, as he had done /adore. He knew all these things, and had put him on the engine. It was deliberate and intended murder, 'but "Sandy" Sam kept his own counsel, and was only dismissed without ceremony. Unfortunately all this tended to make his revenge the more deliberate and sure. There were thus some slight resemblances between him and Lucy Layton, but she had acted from a feeling that she had been deceived, and became thereby em- bittered. Sandy Sam was wicked, and delighted in mischief for its own sake. The "shops" were silent; the men had gone home. A few cleaners and other assistants were employed in the engine "stables" and sheds, but many men had left that evening with the avowed deteimination not to go to work again in the immediate future. A strike was imminent, and " Sandy" Sam had been

undermining the men. Meanwhile George Collier had left his cottage, and locking it up, had put the key where Lucy could find it if she had not been successful in finding lodgings for herself and child. The signalman soon reached his box, and after a few minutes' conversa- tion, he took over the _.duties from the man in charge. He was rather uneasy in his mind still concerning the confidence he had placed in Lucy concerning his hidden treasure, and knowing that about mid- night he would, in all probability, have some moments to spare from the signals, he made up his mind to transfer his hoarded wealth to an equally safe but not so easily an available hiding place. When the mail and fast goods had both gone by, he would make the change. There they go. Both trains 'passed rapidly, all safe and well,but at the same time a desperate man was advancing cautiously along the embankment to take the signalman by surprise, and seize upon his little store. All is quiet. George Collier advances to the well known hiding-place near the heavy lever, worked with a spring-catch, and pulled off with much difficulty, for the wire to the signal post extended some hundreds of yards, and was not easy to move, while the rebound was tremendous when the signal was lot go. The signal was pulled back, and George Collier went upon his hands and knees to see whether the little hoarded wealth was still untouched. Yes, there it was quite safe. div.head: OFFICIAL RAILWAY GUIDES.
div.p: OFFICIAL RAILWAY GUIDES.

People who are on the iottk out for "fresh woods and pastures new" as a Means of pleasantly spend- ing their holiday hours could not do better, if they have visited well-known resorts, than procure a number of the-official guides Di the leading railways of the country. After perusing them, it is not too • much to say they would be astonished at the num- ber of attractive places which will bold out to them temptations for a visit. We have received from Messrs Cassell and Co., four of these official guides, I relative to the Midland, the London and South- - .

Western, the South-Eastern, and the London Brigh-, ton and the South Coast railways. The Midland, it is hardly necessary to say, is a very extensive sys- tem. The 'list section of the Midland guide is devoted to the great main line that reaches from St. Pancras to the far-off highlands; the second shows the celebrated. Manchester and Liverpool ex- press route, which proceeds through the pictureque peak district of Derbyishiiel the third comprises the famed Yorkshire service, via Nottingham and Sheffield to Leeds and Bradford, whilst one of the most important communications of the system is that which runs between the North-Eastern coun- ties of Northumberland, Durham, and Yorkshire,to the west of England and Wales, which is dealt with in the 4th, sth, and 6th sections. It will thus be seen that the traveller may journey from Edinburgh or Glasgow, by Liverpool and Manchester, on through Derby by Leicester and Lyndon, or through Gloucester and Bristol by the South Coast. Altogether there are over 3,000 miles of well-laid permanent way, running through the most interesting parts of the kingdom. The guide includes four panoramic bird's-eye view maps printed in colours, besides ten route maps delineating some of the notable objects adjacent to the line. In addition to these maps, there are admirably executed illustrations on almost every other page. The London and South-Western Railway enables the traveller to journey from the metropolis, by Windsor, Reading, and Salisbury, as far north as Bath, and on to Exeter and Ilfracombe, or south and west to Plymouth and Bodmin. The Company has an authorised capital of 33 millions, and possess 840 miles of permanent way. Its iron track covers the counties of Surrey, Hampshire, Middlesex, Berkshire, Sussex Wiltshire, Dorsetshire, Somersetshire, Devonshire, and Cornwall, and it has working communications with the London and North- Western, and Midland, and the Great Northern Railways. The guide is embellished, not only with an official and suburban map, but with continental maps, besides pano- ramic views, six route maps, seven engraved plans, and imerous capital illustrations of the notable places along tte line. The South-Eastern system with London as its centre, runs westward as far as Reading, southward to East- bourne, Hastings, Hythe, and Folkestone, and eastward to Sheerness, Whitstable, Margate, Ramsgate, Sandwich, and Dover. The Company has a capital of over 27 mil- lions ; it controls, over 400 miles of permanent way, and { during 1888 carried over 27 million passengers. In ad- dition to its extensive railway cennections at home, it is in *eking union in France with the " Chemin de Fer de Nord." It is thus in direct communication with Paris and the Royal, mail route to India and the Colonies. rhe guide • contains no lass than three official maps, two coloured panoramic maps, four route maps, and eight specially engraved plans of cities and towns, besides about 100 engravings. The London, Brighton, and South Coast railway has its centre, of course, in the metropolis, and embraces Guild- ford, Midhurst, Chichester, and goes westward on the south coast as far as Portsmouth and the Isle of Wight, while along the coast the route includes Littlehampton, Worthing, Shoreham, Brighton, Newhaven, Seaford; Eastbourne, St. Leonards, and Hastings. The capital of the company may be set down at 25 millions, while the permanent way comprises a distance of some 500 miles. There is direct communication with the London and North-Western Great Eastern, Great Western, Midland, and Great Northern railways, besides the Western of FratiCal railway, with resulting Continental services via Newhaven to Dieppe to Rouen and Paris. The work is supplied with official maps, including outlines of the direct express routes to the leading Continental capitals, two panoramic and four route maps, togetherwith seven well drawn plans and over 100 illustrations. All of these official guides furnish a careful and brightly written account of the principal places through which the lines pass, and, as they are in all cases accom- panied with excellent engravings, it will be seen that each work is alike picturesque and interesting, and in- valuable for purposes of reference. Messrs. Cassell and Company are to be complimented upon the admirable way in which the guides have been produced. The shilling which is charged for each work cannot possibly cover the expenses, the balance being met, we suppose, by each of the railway companies.

_ "How beautifully your wife always dresses I" said one gentleman to another. "Yes," sighed the husband; "I only wish she'd dress my dinner half as well." WANTED—A cover for bare suspicion, a veil for the face of nature, buttons for breaches of privilege, binding for a volume of smoke, cement for broken engagements. THERE is said to be a biting dog in Boston that never had the least sign of hydrophobia, and yet it is affirmed that he never bites a man without making him mad. "Is it possible, Miss, that you don't know the names of some of your best friends 7" "Certainly I I do not even know what my own may be in a year from this time." "THAT friend of yours is rather a dkagreeable person, isn't he 2" asked a gentleman of a humorist, who replied: "Well, I must say that he is usually as disagreeable as the circumstances will permit." A WEATHER prophet, on being asked how he accouated for the cold snaps in March and April, said "the winter had been so open that lots of cold weather naturally got in, some of which, of coarse, held on rather late.' A QUESTION agitating New York just now is, "Which is the worst enemy of society—the family that keeps a parrot, or the one whose son is learning to play the bugle?" "IT kinder strikes me, Minnie," said the old gentle- man as he peered over his glasses," that if you'd had that dress cut much lower you would have to go into the cellar to put it on." IF your laugh is loud it is low. But if it is low it isn't loud. The English language is a fine struc- ture, but when we have to talk straight logic we generally use Greek ourselves. A LITTLE girl came home from school the first day, and when asked how she liked the school, said, "There ain't but one Yankee in the whole school; that one is John Jones, and he is an Irish- man." SUBURBAN ROSCIUS—"Ah, I saw you were at our 'theatricals' the other night. How did you like my assumption of Hamlet?" Candid Friend—" My dear f'llar, great'st piece of assumption I ever saw m' life I" The papers say that "wine is disappearing from the table.' Mrs. Haische' who keeps a boarding- house, says she has noticed the same peculiarity in bread, butter, beef, potatoes, and other eatables. One of the famous divorce lawyers of New York, in his advertisements in the city papers, says, "Hymeneal incompatibilities as a speciality delicately adjusted. 'Tis slavery to detain the hand after the heart bath fled." "SPEAKING about journalistic courage," remarked the snake editor, "I can name a paper which has more grit than any other, and one which you would hardly think of, either." "What paper is that ?" asked the horse editor. " Sand paper.' " Wiix do you wink at me, sir 7" said a beautiful! young lady, angrily, to a stranger, at a party an evening or two sinoe. "I beg your pardon, madam," replied the wit; "I wink as men do when looking at the sun—your splendour dazzled my eyes." ALGERNON (to his betrothed)—" Belinda, my darling, nothing shall ever part us!" Belinda (who has just been reading accounts of divorce trials)— "Ah I my love, and is it so 1 Shall nothing part us —not even marriage T" MISLAID.--" Why didn't you get some eggs from the hens' nests this morning 2" asked a farmer of his son, who answered: "Because there weren't any. If the hens laid any they mislaid 'em, so't they can't be found." MAGISTRATE (to MTS. Con Kelly) : "You claim, Mrs. Kelly, that Mrs. 0"loolihan gave you that brui.,ed and blackened lace?" Mrs. Con Kelly: "She did, yer honour, or I'm not Irish born." Magistrate : "And what you want is damages ?" Mrs. Kelly: " Naw sir; I want satisfaction. I have damages enough." A WRITER in Macmillan records a remark made by S. T. Coleridge to a schoolmaster, with whom he was making the trip to Margate by the old Mar- gate hey. Coleridge watched his friendis efforts over the side, and at length said, "Why,. Robin- son, I did not expect this from you •, I thought you brought up nothing but young gentlemen." A WELL-KNOWN Bostonian was trying a horse one day in company with the owner, a professional jockey. Having driven him a mile or two,,the gen- tleman, who noticed that he pulled pretty hard, requiring constant watching and a steady rein, said: "Do you think that is just the horse for a lady to drive T" "Well, sir," answered the jockeys "I must say I shouldn't want to marry the woman that could drive that horse." A WELL-KNOWN lawyer was lately concerned in the case of a contested will, where the question involved was as to the mental conditibn of the testatrix. The witness under examination, herself an aged lady, had testified to finding her friend (the testatrix) failing and childish, and that; when she told her something she looked as though she did not understand. Counsel, cross-examining, tried to get her to describe this look, but she did not suc- ceed very well in doing so. At last, getting a little impatient, he asked: "Well, bow did she look? Did she look at yours I am looking at you now, for g instance?" The witness, very demumly, replied: 4 Well, yes—kind of vacant-like." ' CALLER—"I am so glad, my dear, to, see you looking so well and happy! Your wedding-tour was not of long duration, I notice. Very sensible, very sensible." Brido—"My husband was per- fectly willing to prolong the tour ; but I knew that his presence was requiaed at his place of business." Caller—" Very few brides are so considerate as that." Bride—"Oh, hut I ceased to be a bride very early I In less than a week I became. a wife Caller—" Ido not understand." Bride—z 4 We had not been married a week before he asked me to sew on a button." A roruwat physician was mach pleased with a certain aerated water, and by his assidlous recona- mendations procured for it a colebrity it justly de- served. The doctor acted solely in the interests of humanity generally, and expected no retarn. 'To his surprise, there came, one morning, an effusive letter from the company, saying that his recom- mendations had done theta so ranch good that they "ventured to send him a hundred—" Here the page came to an end. "This will never do," said the doctor; "it is very kind, but I could not thing of accepting anything." Then he turned the page, and found the sentence ran—"oftour circulars for distribution." • HE—" My views on social reform are quoted in full." She—" Wasn't it a very long speech you made?" why, no in ; I wasn't aware of saying very much." She—" N-o, you didn't say very much. I was referring to the length of the semen," "MT dear," said a wife to her husband, at the breakfast-table, as she looked up from her news- paper, "what are preferred creditors I" "The ones who never present their bills, my love." JONES—" So, Smith, you speculate in Wall. street, do you? Did you ever lose anything there 2" Smith—" I was married in Trinity, you know, and I lost many illusions." WREN Jones came in the room unexpectedly, Mrs, Jones gave a scream and exclaimed: "You frightened me half to death." "Did I 7" was the unfeeling reply. "Suppose I try it over again."

CHAPTER XVIL GEORGE COLLIER'S STORY. "IT isn't so very long ago," said Collier, "that me and Sandy Sam met under rather peculiar circumstances. Mind l'm not saying as he is a desp'rate character by any means (here the speaker glanced nervously over his shoulder), but it's as well to mind what you are about with S. S. "You won't remember Miss Ayrton's wedding, for the reason as you were in India on your own hook—" "Oh, George, say no more about me," interrupted the woman. "If I have wronged you I humbly beg your pardon; and go on with your story if you want me to remain here." "Very well," said Collier. "It was the evening before Miss Ayrton's wedding day, for she was to be married from Sir Walter Watson's the very next morning, when I was off duty and had strolled with my pipe along the beach yonder, was where people be bathing in summer time." "I know it," said Lucy. "Near fthe Puffin Hock." "Aye, that's it. Well, the' night was dark as a wolf's mouth, and I daresay darker, and there was a curious dull, heavy feeling like thunder, though the sky was not heavy-looking enough for that, and the boats were all hauled upon the beach, ready for the waves that were expected. "All of a sudden it began to rain, and so thought I to myself, I'll just take the first shelter, and in I popped into a bathing machine which had been hauled up high and dry ready for the young ladies next morning. " It was comfortable enough inthe machine, and I sat down and smoked my pipe, and wished for something stronger then the smell of sea-water and sand. Then I began to think, and from thinking I took to dozing, and so right off to sleep in as regular a suc- cession of changes as a man on horseback in the circus-tent." "I've seen him," remarked' 'Lucy, by way of hinting that the signalman's simile had been under- stood and appreciated. "'Well, then," continued Collier, "there I lay all the time—at least I don't know how long—until I was awakened by a murmuring sound, and when I stirred myself to listen—for I was curious, I can toll ye—l made out one of the voices was " "Sandy Sam's," interrupted Lucy, hastily and injudiciously. Trust a woman for rushing to a conclusion. The voice, I know, was the tones of the butler at the 'Towers '—Sir Walter's place, ye know— and ho was speaking in a very quiet voice to somebody beside him. And this is what he said: "'I tell ye how to manage it, mate.' He said mate,' because I noticed it as queer a respec- table butler would stoop to such word's with strangers." "It mightn't have been strange: to the man," hazarded Lucy. "No ; but Il think so all the same. Well, any- how, he said, tell. ye how to manage it. Do you just come to the pantry window at eleven o'clock to-morrow, and they'll all be going to church. Then all you've to do is to just walk sip stairs and collar the lot. But mind, I'm not in it.' " ' Certainly not. Have ye got the fifty pounds safe P Very well,. that's all right. The presents and all is there, isn't there?' said the man I couldn't see. ," 'Right as ninepence,' said the butler; and then, after some more conversation, all of which I could not catch, he said, 'Well, I'll be off now.; mind, eleven o'clock, and no larks about it.' "So they said good-night, and when the sound of their boots on the gravel had quite died away, I' came out of the old bathing-box, feeling as if I had been dipped by Mother Jones at high water." "No wonder, George," said his companion. " am surprised you kept your presence of mind." "There wasn't much to keep," replied the signal- man, with unconscious truthfulness. "There weren't so much mind as action about it. The thing was what was to be done. There was no time to lose, and delays is, asiwe know, dangerous, on the railway more especially. "So, I says to myself, I'll go and 'tell the family. That the family was likely fast asleep in bed, and no use. Besides, what could I prove? I couldn't swear to the men, and voices are not always truthful—not in many ways," he added, bitterly. If Lucy penetrated the meaning of this back stroke, she took no notice of it. She only said as Collier paused— " And what did you do, George ? " "Well, I went to work and made up my mind go go and see Sir. Walter the very first thing in ,the morning, and inquire about the plate and finery for the bride and the young man who had, perhaps, left a, change of things there for the breakfast. "Next morning, about nine o'clock, I was off duty, having gone on at midnight, and I went up to the 'Towers,' and asked to see the mast.r of the house. A woman opened the door to me, and, as the butler was net just then in the way, she took my message into the library. "He came into the halL'and inquired raybusiness. told him as well as I could what I suspected, and likewise that the robbery would take place bysthe pantry window. "'sow do I know that you are not in this plan yourself, and want to put me off the scent., rwill ask Marsden.' "Marsden was the butler, and would, of course,, deny everything, so I said— " Better, wait, sir. You may depend upon it it's meant. I heard , c-yes,,and perhaps intend to share in the job,' says the old gentleman. Old birds are not caught with chaff,' he says. "'Not when they've plenty of corn,' I says, impu- dent Me, 'but there's no "chaff," sir. Heep ma here if ye like,but mind the plate. Illnwear it'a. all straight.! I'll believe you,' he says, 'but I'll:, leek ye up till after the ceremony, will that do? If you arc wrong I'lLoommit ye. If ye are right 111 give pa £lO.. Ts it a bargain?' "Done twith you, sir,' Lsays. Lock me where, ye like, only remember, Pm on duty atrfour on,tho railway.' ""Very well,' he says, you shall have the monei and your dinner before that. But mind if them's- any deception--' ""There ain't, sir,' I says. 'I dee/are I,have told you the truth!' "He, staid no more, them but touched a bell,. and. up came his men. ".' Take care of this man for me until after thawed- ding party returns from the church. Don't de. him any harm but let him. earn his dinner in the stables and,, Eabert —I can depend upon,you—deeyou. look I after him, and say not a wordgo,anyone. Do. you understand me?' "I touched my cap, and the gentleman =Aided and went upstairs. "Mr. Robert, wits was a great big fellow, call( xl me out and handedsme into theicare of the stab'le- mem some of whom I knew. "Come for a jib and a bit. George?" sais tl fey. 'Well, come along; there's plenty to, do. We'll look after him, Mr. Robert.' "The big servant was glad to get away„ and after whispering to one or two that I was to be tubs ded, at which my,frierals alllaughed, for I was truf dy , I hope, the great servant in stockings went insida 'and told his master I was in good hands. "Well, there I remained all right, and turned my hand to anything, and it came near eleven o'clock. I was getting very nervous and, excited.„ for all ths family had gone to church, and. I couldn't tell what the gentleman had done. But there was no alarm, and the married couple came back from church. "The men who had been left to watch declared they had heard nothing,and shen the party had come home—for I saw them coming up the avenue—l went, down to the house, expecting; my ten pounds and, my share of the good, thing, as according te promise. "As soon as over I had appeared in tin back pre. raises the butler runs out at ma or yin' out as loud at bo could— "'Here's one of them; this is thO man wliu tried the window at first.' "In a minute I was surrounded and caught like an escaped lunatic, and hurried upstairs, where all the ladies and gentlemen, in white waistcoats and grand dresses were waiting for their food after the churching—" "Wedding, George," said Lucy, by way of paren- thesis and correction. "Well, they went to church,Pdn't they? How- somdever," continued the signalman, I was dragged up,'and Sir Walter:he came up,and said— "'So be 's one of them, is he?' "'Yes, Sir Walter,' replied the butler, steady as you please; yes, sir. I was just finishing putting out the plate when I noticed this man and another coming pp to the window,_ which was, as I told

div.p: nollowed out to make room for it. ‘, A piece of-a gilt: button, a common ornament enougn, lay hidden with • the money. "That piece of metal had belonged-to the man who had committed the robbery, and for whose appre- hension Sir Walter had offered a handsome, reward —that is, a handsome reward, when we consider, as he did, that every man in the neighbourhood was - more or less dependent upon him, and that it was extremely generous of him to offer any reward at all under the circumstances to men who only did their duty." George Collier gazed at the token. become aware that this link in the chain of evidence would, if properly used, forge the fetters- of Sandy Sam, who had made unkind remarks, and who had done many bad things, and stirred up strife in the district. That Sam deserved hanging Collier never doubted—the difficulty was to prove the facts. "Well, this is all right; but I think I'll put the - stuff a little higher up. There's a capital place behindi the instrument out of everybody's way, and I can have it under my eye. Nobody would ever dream of looking for, money in a cabin like this. , So here we are." In a short time he had cut away a- small space behind the telegraph instrument, and carefully obliterated all traces of the shavings and pieces of wood he had taken away. Then be took the little bag from its hiding place near the levers, and measured the spaces. The " plug "he intended to put into the neatly-made aperture was ready to his hand, and he was about to finish the job when the ringing of the electric bell aroused him,- and he rose to attend to the levers and instrument. While he was thus engaged the door was noise- lessly pushed back, and a man, entering suddenly and silently, crouched down in the most shaded part behind the arm-chair, and near a locker in .the corner, where a beam threw a shado:v assisted by the gas. Again Collier was about to make the transfer* . when something attracted his attention. .He looked . round cautiously, and said half aloud— "I may as well fasten the door though." Ile proceeded to do so, and was turning to resume his occupation when his gaze fell upon the figure ,- crouched in the shadow. He stared intently—the , firm did not move. Then, as he advanced, the man rose up* and George • Collier found himself face to face with his enemy— sandy Sam. (To be continued.);

TEIR SUPERIN7',ENDENT'S 'REPORT. Superintendent Largesubmitted his annual report with reference to the conduct of the licensed victuallers and beer retailers in 'the 'division during the year ended 31st .ffuly, 1890. There were 23 licensed victuallers, ,two beersellers and foui,others who-sold off the premises, totSl 29 ; which, gave an average of 288 of the population to eAch license. ' One licensed victualler had been proceeded agranst during theyear and not convicted, as compared with three pro- ceeded against and three convicted in the preceding year. • One,beerseller had been proceeded against and not con- victed. div.head: 'NOVEL INVENTION FOR HILL ,CLIMBING.
div.p: 'NOVEL INVENTION FOR HILL ,CLIMBING.

Signm Abramotf, the popular prime basso of the Carl Rosa Company, invited a party of friends to I.Bray the other day to witness the first trial in Ire- land of a new invention of his own for the ascent and descent of steep inclines. Half a dozen gentle- men responded to the signor's rriendly overtures, and travcilled to Bray by an afternoon train, some, lit must be added, being rather saeptical as to the promised result of the experiment. The party made at once for the head, and having crossed the with, in defiance of the proclamation against so,do- ing,Signor Abrarnoff was asked to try the invention I by walking up the steep slope towards the peak—a test sufficiently severe, one would any. The sigscr, however, astonished his guests by , scoffing at the I proposal and stating that a much steeper acclivity should be sought. There was some (faculty in find- ing a suitable place, but at last a dangerously pre- cipitous'blulloverlookincNaylor's bathing place was selected, and this, after a brief preparation, Signor' Abramoff walked up and walked (lowa Safely and easily, smiling pleasantly at the SUCCOGS of his ven- ture A few words now about the invention. It is very simple corsisting, ccrasisting of a pair of boots so shaped that the support for the feet remains hori- zontal, even when the sole is on an incline of fifty degrees. A-row of spikes prevents slipping. The boots look sligWy cumbersome, but are in reality very light, and at the same time strong. 'The effi- ciency•of the appliance wasrecognised not.only by the parties invited but by a large crowd of ,curious onlookers. The invention is patented, and Signor Ateramoff believes its utility will be quickly recog- nised.

div.head: ." POOR JACK SCRIVNER."
div.p: ." POOR JACK SCRIVNER."
MS FAREWELL LETTER.

A black felt hat and several articles of clothing w•(!re discovered on Sunday afternoon on the banks of the Thames, near Isleworth, together with the following letter, written in pencil in a good boldhand : "Good-bye to friends and enemies.. I have come to the end of my journey at last, and life has no further charms for me. Before I go let me give one word of warning, especially • to young men. Avoid betting and the racecourse as you would avoid Poison. Four years ago I was a rich man, possessed of something like £20,000 from one source alone. My fortune reverted to me suddenly, and I lost my head over so much gold, and immediately launched into a fast life. The company of bad women (how horribly bad some of them are !) and low and illiterate men was my delight almost as soon as I set foot in London, coming straight from the peaceful village of Upwav, in Dorsetshire, where I had resided for years amid good surroundings. My gay companions quickly introduced me to the gambling table and the turf. Intoxicated with pleasure, I did not consider for one moment whither they were leading me. Every race meeting I attended, and seldom won as the result of my friends' (?) advice. There are thousands of low, cunning blackguards frequenting the racecourse who live upon the stupidity of men like myself. They live to lie and cheat and blaspheme, utterly regardless of a hereafter. I have lunched with princes, dukes, and lords, and have assisted to swell their ill-gotten gains. The racecourse is a veritable hell upon earth, and betting is England's curse and, will ruin her in the end. I am about to do as scores of others in their desperation have done before me. Poverty and starvation have taken the place of affluence and comfort. My friends have for- saken me, and life is no longer worth living. Please com- municate with Burden-st., Bristol. He knows all. When lam picked up, perhaps— and his pals (here the name of a well-known sporting man is mentioned) will subscribe towards giving poor Jack Scrivner a decent burial. Farewell."
THE RAVAGES OF .PLEITRO- PNEUMONIA HEAVY PUBLIC EXPENDITURE.

At the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guar- dians, on Wednesday, the Clerk (Mr. J. C. Sutton, CC.) said he had been favoured by the Clerk of the County Council with a return of pleuro-pneu- monia in the West Derby Hundred, for the quarter ,1 ending 28th July, 1890. Of the 61 persons resident in that Hundred alone to whom compensation had been allowed, he regretted to say that the bulk were from his own and the adjacent divisions. The suf- ferer, for such at the best they were, could only be com- pensated according to the judgment and discretion of the Committee,and that:in future:unfortunate persons having affected cattle might understand their position, he might say there had not been perfect accordance with the deci- sions arrived at, as regarded the compensation awarded. It as most essential that on the first appearance of pleuro symptoms the owner should communicate with the proper authority. It was a hard thing to lose a valuable herd because of contact with one that was af- fected, vet serious consequences might follow conceal- ment of- the fact. Personally, he had to deplore the des- truction,withi n the three months, and within the districts referred to, of 365 head of cattle, 50 only of which were found to be actually affected. The value of the destroyed animals was £8.594 7s. 6d. ; the compensation awarded was £8,212 03.7 d, ; the proceeds of the sale of sound carca.ses was £3,640 15s. 10d.—the difference between the last named sums falling on the County Council rates. This loss to the county was exclusive of the loss to the county by the slaughter of the large and valuable herd at the Rainhill Asylum, one of which proved to be affected. —The chairman asked how it was that there was such a difference baween the compensation given, and the sell- ing value of the careases.—The Clerk said he supposed that most of the animals would have a selling value as live animals which they had not as dead meat.—Mr. Hood-Wright said it was a great shame that animals which had to be slaughtered because they had been in ' contact with deceased animals should be allowed to be driven along the roads and to railway stations. He had timself written to the Home Secretary on the subject.— Mr, W. Houghton : It is the way to spread the disease. —The Clerk said that since that matter had beenbrought under the notice of the County Council Committee they had stopped it, and all animals had now to be slaughtered on the premises, no matter what additional cost it was to the county authorities.—The subject then dropped.

They also recommended that when any suspicious case occurred at the workhouse the Master should at once report to the police. The Deputy-Coroner said he quite agreed with the verdict. IDJOI7RNED INQUEST AND VERDICT.

- - The adjourned inquest as to the death of Alice Ann Dashwooct, an Earlestown woman, took place at Warrington Workhouse on Monday morning, before the deputy coroner, Mr. W. T. Husband. The woman was admitted to the Workhouse hospital on the 17th June and died there some days after giv- ing birth to a child. Her bcrdy was considerably I bruised, but as she was in •an imbecile state of mind she could give no account of how she got the bruises. Her husband appeared to have deserted her a few days before her admission to the Work- house, and allegations had been made that he had been in the habit of abusing her. The Deputy Coronor, having read the evidence given at the opening of the inquest, Mary Jane White (sister of the deceased) corroborated the evidence given by her on the previous occasion ; but added that the deceased had not been subject to epileptic fits. She had had several strokes. Witness had never-seen Dashwood assault his wife. Dr. Spinks, medical officer for the Workhouse, in answer to the Deputy-Coroner, said he could not say whether or not there was anybody at the confinement of the deceased. He did not remember 'telling the police that there had been no one-present. It was the nurse's duty to be present not his. Re had madea post-mortem examination, and found that death was due to chronic meningitis. Meningitis was very often produced by violence, but it might come on naturally. He was not able to say whether itowas due in this instance to natural causes or to blows. .A long-course of ill-treatment would cause this meningitis if deceased had been hit on the head. The body otherwise appeared perfectly healthy.— The Deputy-Coroner: How long have you been doctor at the Workhouse ?—Dr. Spiriks : Thirty-five years.—The Deputy-Coroner: Who-has been in thehabit of reporting these cases to the peliceP—Dr. Spinks: -Generally the master.—The Deputy-Coroner-said he should like to know why that case had not been reported to the•police. In answer to Inspector Spinks, Dr. Spinks said that -repeated falls to the floor might causethe various wounds he saw on the deceased. Sergeant Longworttr: Do you iemember stating to a policeman that deceased was of unsound mind, that she -might to have been in an asylum, 'that she was all covered with bruises, -that you were not aware of her being pregnant, and that the first intimation of it was when the child was found in bed ?—Dr. -Spinks: I did not tell the policeman 1 did not know she was pregnant. —Did you tell him that no one was with her when she I was confined P-1 do not remember telling him so, but I ' may have told him.—How did you come to the conclusion that these bruises were caused lay ,kicks ?—I was told so 'by one of the nurses. The Coroner: Would inattention at the time of con- finement in any way hasten death?—)r. .Spinks: It- would not. 3essie Rose Davidson, nurse at the Workhouse, said she knew deceased was pregnant on the day she was admitted. The other nurse was present-at.- the time of confinement. Dr. Overton, assistant to Dr. -Watkin, of Newton, spoke to having attended the deceased on several occa- sions. On one occasion he made an order for.her to be removed to the Workhouse because she was an imbecile and not able to look after herself, while her husband's wages were not sufficient to hire a -nurse. That order was not carried out because the Guardians said the husband was in work and they did not conekler the Workhouse was a hospital. That was in March. The Guardians at Newton practically ignored the order.— The Deputy Coroner: They knew better than ,you, I , suppose.—Dr. Overton: Yes.—The Deputy Coroner : In March of this year would you have been surprisedif she I had died'?—Dr. Overton: No.

div.head: THEATRICALS IN TROUBLE AT EA.RLESTOWN. SMART CAPTURE BY AN EARLESTOWN
div.p: THEATRICALS IN TROUBLE AT EA.RLESTOWN. SMART CAPTURE BY AN EARLESTOWN
POLICEMAN.

On Monday information was given to the Earles- town police that an actor named Arthur Armfield, and his wife, Lilly Armfield, an actress of no fixed address, had stolen a box, containing a dolman, cape, and several articles of wearing apparel, of the value of .E 7 Bs. 2d., the pronetty of Mildred Cohen, an actress. The parties, it appeared, lodged toge- ther at the house of Mrs. Waddilove, 10, Booth-at., Earlestown. The Armfields had been engaged in a Com- pany which occupied the boards of the Earlestown theatre last week. On the conclusion of the engagement, Cohen came to Earlestown to take up another engage- ment this week, and went to Liverpool on Saturday night, asking Mrs. Waddilove's daughter,before she left, to take care of her box until she returned. On Monday the two Armfields left, taking the box in question with them, and telling Mrs. Waddilove that when Cohen re- turned she was to tell her to write to the General Post Office at Beetle. They then left the house, and pro- ceeded to Earlestown Station, calling on the way at the pawnshop of Mr. Jones, Market-st., where they pledged the dolman for 12s. Ed. When Cohen returned on Mon- day from LiverpooLshe foundher box gone,and ascertain- ing from Mrs. Waddilove what had become of it, she at cnce gave information to the police. P.C. Bowes was ' detailed to trace the thieves, and, pursuing his inquiries with some acuteness, he succeeded in tracing them to Manchester, where he lost the trail. After spending I I some time in visiting the various theatres, he .ultimately succeeded in running them to earth at St. James's Theatre, where he espied his quarry seated in the upper circle. He arrested them, and conveyed them to the Town Hall, where, after being charged,they were locked up. On Tuesday morning he conveyed them to Earles- town, together, with the box and stolen articles, and they were brought up before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, at Newton Town Hall, on Tuesday afternoon, on the charge of stealing the articlesinquestion. Mildred Cohen, an actress, living at 44, Thomason-st., Liverpool, said the box, and all the articles produced, were her property,and valued at 17 Bs.2d. She last saw them safe on Saturday, the 23rd inst., at the Earlestown Station, when she gave them to Margaret Waddilove to take to her mother's, at 'No. 10, Boot h-st., Earlestown, to keep until she canes back. She had an engagement at the Earlestown theatre during the same week, and the two prisoners, who were theatricals, also had an engage- ment there, and lodged at No. 10, Booth-st., where wit- ness also lodged. After leaving on the Saturday, she did not return until about-one o'clock on Monday after- noon, the 25th inst.„ when her box and contents were gone. She did not give the prisoners permission to take the box, nor tell them to look after it while she was away.—Other evidence having been given, the female prisoner, in answer to the charge, said there was but one skirt in the box, and one prosecutor lent her; the other things she gave her to take care of.—The male prisoner said he knew nothing about them.—Both pri- soners were then remanded until Saturday.

RE-OPENING OF NEWTON LAKE.

We are this week able to publish an item of news which will be hailed with delight by the inhabit- ants of Newton and Earlestown. We are authorised to announce the fact that Newton lake which, since the death of Mr. John Lane, has been closed to the public, will be re-opened in the course of a week or two. The closing of the lake caused great dissatisfaction , to the people of Newton, and a petition was drawn up, and presented to Mr. Legh, imp g the co nce of the privilege so long enjoyed. The matter has been under consideration for some time, and it has now been finally decided to restore the fine sheet of water to the public use. Mr. Barrow, son of the late keeper of Dean dam, has been appointed keeper of the lake, and will have under his charge four of the old pleasure boats which have been purchased by Mr. Legh, from the re- presentatives of the late Mr. Lane, and these will be let on hire to the people of Earlestown and Newton, as be- fore, at a fixed charge. There are, however, certain re- strictions connected with the privilege, one being that only the approaches to the lake, and the lake itself, will I be open for use to the people residing in the districts of Earlestown and Newton. Picnics will not be allowed, as the owners of land surrounding the lake object to the wholesale trespassing upon their grounds which formerly took place. • •

7,T •, RUNCORN WATERWORKS COMPANY. The annual meeting of the shareholders of this Company was held at the Public Hall, on Monday afternoon. Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P., chairman of direc- tors, presided, and there were present Messrs. T. Banks, W. Whittaker, W.'Hayes, E. Timmins, James Collier, R. Foulkes, and W. F. Salked (secretary.) The directors report stated that the revenue account showed a balance of £Bl5 17s. id.. including £167 12s. 9d. brought from the previous half year. The direc- tors recommended a dividend to be declared of £4 ss. Od. per cent, per annum free from income tax •, this would absorb £635 10s. Od., leaving a balance of £l7B 7s. id. to be carried forward. The statement of accounts was taken as read.—The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report, expressed the pleasure the directors had in presenting to the shareholders a more favourable re- port this year than in the past. There had been a great demand for water which had been amply met by the resources of the well both as regarded the quantity and quality ; and the result had been a much larger balance to the credit of the Company than had been the case hitherto. During the year there had been an increase of 110 houses to which they had to supply water, which of course helped to improve their revenue. During the half-year ending June 1889, the amount received for water sold by meter was £340; last half-year the amount was £579 13s. 6c1., showing an increase of £240. This was highly satisfactory to the directors and to those who had to receive anything in the shape of dividend. They hoped this good fortune might continue, and that they would be able to present as good a report in the future. The repairs to the engine "Weston" had been carried out, and both engines were now in thorough ; working order. They had been working 20 years, and they might expect that in that time they would need extra repairs. As regarded the works everything was in good working order, and the directors trusted that the balance next half-year would be still further improved. The demand for water was very great both from the Chemical Works, the Ship Canal Company, and the contractor to the Ship Canal Company, and they were kept very busy, and Mr. Salkeld, as an employe, was only too glad that their exer- tions had resulted in such a satisfactory balance.—Mr. Banks seconded the motion.—Mr. Timmins referred to the admirable manner in which the supply of water was continued during the repairs to the engine, and said the future of the Company looked very bright indeed.—The motion was carried.—The retiring directors, the Chair- man, and Mr. Whittaker, were re-elected. Mr. James Collier, the retiring auditor, was re-appointed.—On the proposition of Mr. James Collier (who paid a high compliment to the secretary for the manner in which the books were kept), seconded by Mr. Foulkes, a vote of thanks was accorded to the directors for their services.

An alarming fire occurred on Thursday morning at the beam and scale factory of Messrs. Anderson Bros., Stockwell-st., Glasgow. Twelve horses were extricated with difficulty from the adjoining stables. The loss of property amounts to several thousands of pounds.

FARM PREMISES DESTROYED BY FIRE. A WOMAN BURNT TO DEATH. A dreadful discovery was made on Thursday at Bob- bing, near Sittingbourne. Shortly before midnight en Wednesday a large barn was struck by lightning. The :thatch ignited, and the building was soon in flames. liienry Jarvis, aged 29, of Chatham, and Ann Taylor, aged 32, employed as harvesters, had been sleeping there. Aroused by the flames they, endeavoured to escape. Jarvis was successful, but the woman was btarnt to a cinder, her charred remains being found amongst the daris on Thursday morning.

div.head: TRIAL OF IitULME AT STOCKPORT.
div.p: TRIAL OF IitULME AT STOCKPORT.

Trs trial commenced at Stockport., on Thursday, of Elizaheth Hulme, aged 56, for the murder of Sarah Gresty„ aged 25. The evidence showed deceased called on the prisoner twice in July. Deceased was subse- quently confined of still-born twins, which prisoner buried secretly. Deceased died on July 2Tth, and Use doctor, who had disappeared, certified that death was from hemorrhage of the lungs. The doctor subsequently made a post-mortem examination, and found that death in all probability resulted from an illegal operation. The prisoner was committed for trial on the capital charge.

TANNERIES AND STREAM POLLUTION. _ MR. EARP'S REPLY.

GOVERNMENT INSPECTION REQUESTED. Alfted D. Adrian, assistant secretary to the Local Government Board, forwarded a communication, which the Board had received from Mr. W. R. Earp with refer- ence to the pollution of the Kekewick Brook by the re- fuse from the tannery at Preston o'th' Hill. The Board directed him to inquire, having regard to the representa- tions contained in Mr. Earp's letter, whether the Rural Sanitary Authority contemplate formulating complaints against the owners of any other tanneries, so that such complaints might be investigated at the same inquiry in the event of one being directed. The enclosure was as follows :—" Pollution of Kekewick Brook, Preston Brook, August 2nd, 1890. My Lords and Gentlemen, I have the honour to reply to your communication respect- ing the alleged pollution of Kekewick Brook, and beg to call your attention to the following facts. 1. That the brook in question empties itself into the River Mersey, and is the only outlet for liquid refuse from my tannery and that rights of user must extend back for more than one hundred years. The date on my house is 1762, and portions of the tannery appear some hundreds of years old. 2. That the brook in question has also been the only outlet for the refuse of other tanneries founded many years ago, but that now the leather sheds are used as farm buildings and the liquor pits have been filled up, and that my tannery is now the only tannery in work. 3. That I can bring evidence to prove that the Kekewick Brook is not in any worse condition now than it always has been whenever the tannery has been working, and I believe that I can I also bring evidence to show that the brook is in a better Istate than it has been. 4. That there are three other tan- neries within the Runcorn Rural Sanitary district each of which send their liquid refuse down similar brooks runt fling into the river Mersey and that the refuse from thee tanneries is some hundreds of times greater than the refuse from my tannery. That the names of these tan- neries are Messrs. F. W. Reynolds and Sons, Astmoor Tannery; Messrs. Ockleston and Sons, lialtsn-road Tannery; and the Highfield Tanning Co., Runcorn. 5. That one of these tanneries, namely, F. W.Reynolds and Sons, belongs to Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., and that I understand that it is his agent who has complained about the refuse from my tannery, and I wish to draw your attention to this inconsistency,that whilst he complains, his own tenant is discharging twenty times the amount of refuse down a similar brook running through pasture fields for over a mile into the ever Mersey. 6. That I am quite prepared to do whatever any other tanner will or can do to obviate pollution as much as is possible, but that I cannot undertake to make the brook drinkable under all kinds of circumstances, and I am not aware that anyone else can, and that if there is really any danger attaching to cattle drinking the water the only way is to rail the brook off. 7. That the brook is already ' railed off over a portion of its length and over a still greater portion the brook is some four or five feet below the ground level, having vertical sides so that cattle can- not get at it, 8. That there is no necessity for the brook as a water supply for cattle, since it runs down a valley or marsh with a large number of pits in most of the fields adjoining the brook, and further that it never can have been relied on as a water supply except in wet weather or winter, as in dry weather there is very little going down the brook except what I put down. 9. That this is owing to the fact that the Bridgewater Canal takes the water from one feeder, and the other feeder which should come past my tannery has been diverted ever since the railway through Runcorn over Runcorn Bridge has been cut. 10. That in consequence of this, as well as from our having to draw our supply of water from a deep well and this water giving over 130 grains of solid matter in solution to the gallon to start with—the water iu the brook is always sure to show a large total of solid matter to the gallon. 11. That the samples submitted for analysis have been taken after a term of dry weather, when there was no water in the brook except what I put down, and that the Inspector stated that there was no water at all in the brook above the tannery so that he could not take a sample of that. 12. That what the Inspector stated was true but that there was a quantity of sewage lying in the brook above the tannery which comes from three or four farm yards, and that when a flood of top water does come it will wash the sewage into the Brook below the tannery and so increase the pollu- tion in that part where samples are taken from. 13. That from the above circumstances you will discover that the samples submitted for analysis were simply our waste liquors undiluted with any other water, and that as such we considered them many times better than what usually run from tanneries. 14. That the writer is a patentee for a fluid to unhair hides without lime, and that the use of this obviates the passing of some tons of lime down the Brook weekly, in the shape of dirty thick lime water, and that the good results mentioned are chiefly owing to the use of this. 15. That tan liquors hold the matter in solution and not in suspension so that filtering the liquors would be useless. 16. That some portion, and I think it must be a good portion, of any pollution caused from the tannery is from the rain falling on old pit holes that have been filled up with spent bark, &c., and then draining into the Brook. It also arises in part from therein in wet weather falling on a large heap of spent tan (one hundred tons or more) which is outside my yard, but I have already gone to a great expense in putting down special furnaces and apparatus for consuming this heap at a great rate. The furnace will be in work some time next week, and before the year is out this source of pol- lution will be entirely done away with. That lam ex- pert in tanning matters and receive frog' tanners single fees as high as £2oo—for advice on the management of their yards with the greatest economy and the least pos- sible loss and nuisance—so that the singling of me out and endeavouring to take action against me for manag- ing a tannery badly (for that is really what the complaint means, if it means anything legitmate at all that is) seems to me a trifle absurd.—l have the honour to remain, my Lords and Gentleman, your obedient servant, William R. Earp."—Mr. Aaron asked what had that Authority to do with Occleatou'a tannery; it was not in the Authority's district.—The Clerk ; Teither is Highfield tannery.---:In reply to the Chairman, Mr. ii rington said there was the same pollution Of water in the brook at Reynold's tannery as there was at Preston Brook, but at the latter place the stream was largely used as a drinking place. He should think that at times the stream below Reynolds' would be used for cattle drinking.—The Deputy Clerk: There has been no com- plaint about that In this:case we have direct complaint from the agent of the property.—Mr: Aaron said they had nothing to do,with the 1 other tanneries. Mr. Earn stated his tannery had been in existence for a hundred yeto ; it did not matter if it bad been there three him -1 dred years, he had no right to turn into the stream poi- sonous chemicals which killed the cattle that drank the water. It was a great hardship to the farmers. He moved that the Clerk write to the Local Government Board and ask them to send down an inspector to inspect the brook, pointing out that two of the tanneries men- tioned by Mr. Earp were not in the Authority's district and there was no complaint of the third.—Mr. Lewis asked did not Reynold's make the same kind of stuff.— Mr. Aaron: They don't use the same kind of materials. —Mr. Lewis: It is rather awkward for Sir Richard Brooke's agent, to complain of Preston Brook Tannery when there was a tannery on the Norton Estate.—Mr. Aaron said he had no animosity whatever against Mr. Earp, but he did not think it right that a man should rent a farm and his cattle die.—Mr. Lewis; But I think we should serve all alike—Mt. Farrington suggested that he should make an inspection of the brook at Reynold's tannery, and then he should be prepared with information for the Government inspector.—Mr. Aaron: We have no complaint from there and I think it is time enough to do that when we have a complaint.—The Chairman seconded Mr. Aaron's motion which was carried without dissent. div.p: THE EXA.MINER,
SATURDAY. AUGUST 30', 1890.

THE A nnnal Sessions- for the renewal, Brewster refusal, or; granting of additional Sessions. licenses have been held in various &wad-4ring the past week'; amongst others at Daresbury, Eddisbury, Rimeorn,.aiad Warrington. Atßtincorn, Superintendent Large had a favour- :able report to make, and'there was a renewal of all the licenses, except that of, the Castle Hotel, which ,was-referred to the adjourned Sessions to be held on the•2.thld September. . At ,Warrington the pro- ceedings. were of a more important character. It will be remembered that last.year• a special com- mittee of magistrates madean inspection of licensed houses,.and took objection to ten of them. The, 'consideration of these particular cases was ref( to the adjourned sessionsi but the objections, it was found, could not be sustained in consequence cf 6 irregularity, or oversight, in giving notice to , holdersof licenses. It washopedi that this year the magistrates would againobject,,taking care to put( themselves properly before the .Ceurt ; but, as they,- took.nemaction at all, it-was decided that objection, should be taken to six of the licenses by represen, tatims of the Warrington Temperance Federation.. Thisw.as done in open Court,.on. Tuesday, and, in addition, objection was takento)the holder of the- license of the Royal Exchange,Market Place. The, grounds of opposition to the renewal of these- licenses are, in the main, that they are not required for:the necessities of the -neighbourhood, and that,. structurally, they are notadapted for the purposes of a.license. These were the conclusions comets) last year by the Magistrates Committee; anditis the belief that them conclusions were soundmnd just which warrants the Temperance party in bringing the matter-to an, issue in the interests of the public. The Licensing Magistrates, onalires- day,,saw the reasonableness of the course taken, for they raised no difficulty whatever as to ,at pro- posed adjournmentof the Court in order that due notice of objection might be given. Indeed;, as it iranspired, two other licenses were held over; so that the renewal:or, refus,al of nine licenses is de- 'pendent upon the decision at the adjourned Ses- sions, which will.be heleL on the 22nd of, Septem- ber. There can-be no.quostion that the rnagrstrates have absolute discretion to refuse a renewal on the ground that a, house is not needed in any par- ticular neighbourhood,, apart from anyether con- sideration. The contention that either the publi- can or the brewer has a vested interest in the licence which the court is bound to recognise has been blown to the winds. It is to be hoped that the magistrates will therefore act without fear or, favour, and show themselves equal bathe occasion,. In Liverpool there has been considerable weeding out during the peat tan years. Why should thane.; not be a similar weeding out in Warrington?
