Turning to another phase of the proceedings,it was alike interesting and amusing to witness,the renewed efforts of rival brewers to occupy now territory. The great Powers, of Europe We not more eager to extend "the sphere of influence " in Africa than are big brewers and little brewers to extend their "sphere of influence" in Warrington. To judge from the plans, of palatial buildings which these brewers submitted to the court, and which, they professed, they were anxious to erect, it would appear that they are overflowing with philanthropic regard for the earthly happiness of the neglected people who live in the neighbourhood of Battershy-lano and Bewsey-road. Indeed, if they were only permitted to dominate these districts and monoplize them in the way of drink supply, they were prepared to give up various other licenses which were, it is whispered, of little or no value to them. It does not seem to have

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

The new scheme which " General" Booth is per- fecting points to a Labour Bureau; Industrial houses—not workhouses—where the unemployed may find work, food, and shelter; training in agricultural districts; and finally emigration and colonisation. It is premature to express any Opinion upon the scheme; but this much can be said that almost any experiment is better than doing nothing at s.ll.

Mr. Balfour is Irish Secretary, but he spends _very little of his time in Ireland. Perhaps it would be inconvenient for his theories if he spent sufficient time there to learn the truth of things. " Punch" nas a hit at him this week for golfing, at Berwick, Whilst the Irish are bordering on famine. There W 53 one Nero who fiddled whilst Rome burned ; keeping. like Balfour, he had no character worth -Keeping.

Liberal Unionists do not seem disposed to encourage liberality in thought and action. Mr. Caldwell, one of the members for Glasgow, who Showed some independance during the late sitting of. Parliament, has had notice to quit from the bissentient Liberal Association of Glasgow. He is told that he has been "indifferent to the Unionist !nliance." So it is "the Unionist alliance" that is in danger! Thank Heaven it is no longer "the raPire."

-- The numerous boating disasters of the past fort- night emphasise the need of greater care on the Part of those who go down to the sea and take Pleasure in deep waters. It is characteristic of holiday people to incur a considerable amount of risk by way of spicing the enjoyment; but it is always as well to have in mind that, while a spill ,no land may mean no more than a bruise or a broken limb, a spill in the sea frequently means loss of life.

A London contemporary says :—" Miss Fortescue, Ivilo is playing at Scarborough with a first-rate Company, has been quite invalided from the strength o.f the air." Just so; Scarborough air is strong, or was not the writer of "Touch and Go" in- l'alided by it ? "Ah me !" and likewise "Oh dear I" If a man were to make his way to the ;!erth pole, and sit on the top of it, it would act like Scarborough upon him—he would be "quite ini,alided from the strength of the air."

Mr. Gladstone seems to have received a large number of letters with reference to his speech on rabbit farming, &c. There is something just a trifle disagreeable associated with the idea of breeding tame rabbits for slaughter and food • but that is because we are not used to it. We think tothing of killing and eating tame cows, tame •sheep, tame pigs, and tame poultry. In the sweet bye-and-bye, it will be a matter of course to get toothsome rare-bits from tame rabbits.

-- The Young Men's Christian Society of Penketh ulight have been worse, and they might certainly 'have been better, employed than in listening to an ?say on "Musketry." Our literature and life is (03 much saturated as it is with the " glory " of things military. Hence as one of our poet's has it--
-- The child, Ere he can lisp his mother's sacred name, 'ells with the unnatural pride of crime, and lifts }Ls baby-sword even in a hero's mood.

The Sultan has at last" screwed his courage to tile sticking place," and has banished Mousse Bey, Flo greatest scoundrel yet unhanged. He has sent yam to Mecca—in the hope, perhaps, as he dare not give him his deserts, that he may be carried off by the cholera. The Armenians are at present Oil the borders of revolt—so terribly have they suffered from ruffians of the Mousse Bey type. If the Sultan does not do something for them, they may do something for themselves, and in the end Turkey will have lost wing.

--- The Empress of Austria is an admirer of Heine, and .the other day, whilst in Paris, she paid a visit t 9 his grave at Pere Lachase. Heine, however, had little regard for Emperors and Empresses. In his "Reisbilder he says :—" For thou, my people, art the true Emperor, the true lord of the land thy will is sovereign and more legitimate than that purple Telest notre plaisir, which grounds it- self upon divine right, without any better guaran- tee than the quackery of shaven jugglers—thy my people, is the only righteous source of P 0 War."

But it will be rather as the poet that the Em- press admires Heine; and truly Heine—the ten- der, the bold, the satirical—is always himself and not another, whether he writes in prose or verse. tlere is a clever and characteristic bit :- -

Upon my darling's beaming eyes I plied my rhyming trade; Upon my darling's cheery lips An epigram I made. Hy darling has a blooming cheek, I penned a song upon it, And if she had but had a heart, Her heart had had a sonnet.

English readers are as a rule but little acquainted With the works of this marvellous German Jew who lived most of his life in Paris, and, like most poets, learnt in suffering what he taught in song. He was born at Dusseldorf in December, 1799, and died in Paris in • February, 1856. His was a nimble wit, and Englishmen would do well to follow it in order to sharpen their own. Mr. Walter , Scott has made the way easy by publishing a shilling volume of his poems, and another shilling ' volume of selections from his prose writings. Differences arising out of caste prejudices are just now exciting attention in Surat, which is the spot in India "in which the British power first took root 283 years ago." But Surat was noted during the time of the American civil war for its miserably poor cotton. William Billington, a Lan- cashire poet, thus described the attempt to weave it It's just like rowling stooans up broo, Or twistin rooaps o' sand; Yo piece yo'r twist, i'd comes f two, Like cobwebs i' yor hand. Aw've work'd and woven like a foo ! Till aw'm as weak as a cat, Yet after o' as aw could do, Aw'm konkurd wi Surat!

The latest inquiry into the doings of the Cheshire Police proved highly interesting. Superintendent 'Egerton's letters to ex-Inspector O'Donnell are as good as a play. He has a racy style, and he is a hard hitter; but he lets the cat out of the bag When he says the Tories who appreciated 0 Donnell's "good work" would be disgusted if they found he had "submitted his case to Brunner and Co." A nice admission truly; but it confirms , the previous impression, namely, that O'Donnell's Liberalism stood in his way. We shall have Ss of this truckling to Tory landlords when the Police are put, as they should be, under the sole "eontrol of the County Council.

The Rev. Dr. Preston, speaking at the annual jollification in connection with the Daresbury Primrose League, said, if the Liberation programme Were carried out, "our churches would be taken Irnin us and sold by auction to the highest bidder, and the endowments, by means of which so much good had been done, would be lost to them; God's eervice would suffer ; the working-men would suffer; 11-le poor would suffer as well as the country at arge." It would be interesting to know where the Tv• gentleman gets his authority for these absur- mites. Can it be that, after the members had been 43,!Igaged in ascertaining, by a competition, who was 'ao quickest at swallowing a bottle of lemonade a bun, Dr. Preston came to the conclusion that 'neY would be prepared to swallow anything?

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

A WOMAN STABBED AT WIDNES. Before Mr. Timmis, at Widnes Police Court, James Miskeler, a labourer, 18 years of age, of 34, Barn-st., was charged with unlawfully wounding Mary Jane Riley, by stabbing her on the back. The parties had al quarrel in Sankey-st., and were afterwards seen in an entry there, where it is believed the prisoner stabbed the woman. Dr. MacLennan had examined the woman and had sent her tl the Hospital. She was suffering from fa wound at the lower angle of the shoulder blade ; the wound must have been caused by a knife. When appre- hended the prisoner told P.C. Thompson he had struck the woman, but he did not stab her.—Prisoner was re- manded for a week. CRITCHLEY. High Class Tailor. Bold-st.,Warrington.—Advt. SHOCKING FATALITY AT W IDNES. , William Stokes aged 26, of 2, Chatham-st. Widnes, met with a shocking death at the British Alkali Works, on Wednesday night. Stokes was employed as a breaks- man, and at 9 p.m. he was engaged in shunting wagons to various parts of the works. The engine was backing a number of wagons to some other wagons, and Stokes jumped from the engine and ran to couple them. As the driver received no signal he shouted, and n t receiving an answer he went to see what was the matter and found Stokes jammed between the buffers of two wagons. He was quickly released, but life was quite extinct. His chest was terribly crushed. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—. 7. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. DROwNING MYSTERY AT RUNCORN. On Saturday evening, Ann Maher, aged 38 years, wife of John Maher, farmer, of Church Willaston, near Neston, was found dead in a pit on Runcorn Common. Mrs. Maher,who had been in ill-health for some time,was on a visit to her brother-in-law,Mr. John Wilson,of Greenway- road, and had been in Runcorn for several days. About two hours before her body was found, a man named George Edge saw her sitting on the edge of the pit. The relatives thought she had had a fit and fallen into the water. An inquest was held on the body on Tuesday, and as there was no evidence to show how she met her death, a verdict of " found dead" was returned. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. Is W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st.. Warrington.—.Advt.

div.head: – TiE RAILWAY COMPANY AND DIVING FROM RUNCORN – _ _
div.p: - TiE RAILWAY COMPANY AND DIVING FROM RUNCORN - _ _

- _ BRIDGE. During the past week, a notice has been placed at each end of Runcorn Bridge, with the object of deterring those foolhardy persons who have recently dived and dropped from that structure, from repeating their performances. The notice at Runcorn approach threatens to invoke the penalties of the law on any person who climbs upon "any part of the gangway," but the Widnes notice is more explicit and runs as follows:—" London and North- Western Railway Company. Any person climbing on the parapet, lattice work, or other part of the bridge will be prosecuted. By order." The company intend to strictly enforce this order, and it is to be hoped the desired effect will be obtained, and that Burns and his imitators will desist from their dangerous displays. Now OPEN FOR THE SEASON. --Smart and Co.'s private Writing and Commercial Academy for ladies and gentlemen, at Mr. Chantry's. 13 Sankey-et., Warrington. Open every Friday from 3 to 9 p.m. Writing : Gentlemen are taught a fine, bold, rapid business hand, and ladies an elegant and Sowing style. Terms for the complete course, One Guinea. Book-keeping : Pupils are taught how to open. keep, balance, and close a complete set of books by double entry ; and our certificate for proficency is given to each pupil. Arithmetic and mental calculation taught practically. Shorthand. Pit- man's system. Pupils will be received on Friday next, at any hour from 3to 9 p.m. No classes, the instruction is individual. Card of terms and full particulars may be had at Mr. Chantry's 13, Sankey-st., Warrington, or post free from our Head Academy, 2, Brewn-St.. the Market, Man- chester.—Adrt.

----- -- FEROCIOUS ASSAULT WITH A GLASS AT WIDNES. Michael Donlan, of 31, Charlotte-st., was brought be- I fore Mr. Tiinmis. at the Widnes Police Court, on Mon- day, charged with having, on the 16th inst., unlawfully wounded Miles Darsy, of Suttons-lane. The men had a dispute about their work, while drinking in the Crown Vaults, and came to blows. A labourer named Bartholo- mew Sheridan separated them, and the prisoner threatened to "settle accounts" before he left the house. A few minutes afterwards the prisoner picked up a pint glass and threw it with much violence at Darsy. The glass smashed on Darsy's right cheek, and caused a fearful gash, a portion of flesh hanging loose from the bone. Darsy fell to the ground unconscious, and had since been under the care of Dr. O'Beeffe. The prisoner was committed to the Assizes for trial, bail being allowed. Man CARTs for children.—Garland, Ironmonger, Warring- ton and Earlestown.—Advt. DEATH OF AN OLD RUNCORNIAN. Our readers will learn with regret of the death of Mr. Robert Evans, who died at his residence in Blantyre-st., on Wednesday, at the age of 73 years. For the long period of 48 years Mr.; Evans was in the employ of the Bridgewater Navigation Company, the greater por- tion of which time he spent at Runcorn: He was the manager of the import and export department of the docks, and was not only respected by the numerous per- sons. under his control, but was generally respected by the inhabitants of the town. When he severed his con- nection with the company some years ago, he set up a business as general carrier on his own account. For the last twelve months he had suffered from a painful illness. He was a member of the Order of Freemasons, and was connected with the Ellesmere Lodge and with the Bridge- water Chapter. ELECTRO PLATED GOODS.—Garland's oldest 'established Ironmonger, Warrington.—Advt. WANTON MISCHIEF AT RUNCORN MARKET. A youth named William Jones was summoned to Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, to answer a charge of wilfully damaging a stall in the Market by cutting it , with a knife.—Mr. Lake prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Commissioners, and said there were a number of btalls on the Market ground, which youths like defend- ant used as a kind of playground or gymnasium by swinging on the cross bars and other performances, the consequence being the stalls were continually damaged. The case against the defendant was rather worse than that. On Friday last he was seen to deliberately cut pieces ef wood from a stall with a knife, and the Board asked the Bench to inflict such a :penalty as would be a warning to others.—Superintendent Large said the police were continually driving boys away from the Market.— The Chairman, who described the defendant's conduct as wanton mischief, imposed a fine of ss. andcosts Bs. 6d. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. a W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st...Warrington.—Advt. LIFE AMONGST NAVVIES ON FRODSHAM MARSH. At Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Hamlington,orHamblin, of Three Huts, Frodsham Marsh, was summoned by William Griffiths, of the same place, for assaulting him on the 11th inst. Defendant was also summoned for threatening him on the 15th inst.—Mr. Fletcher appeared for complainant. He stated that the defendant lodged in a hut belonging to the complainant, and because he was given notice to quit, bad feeling was engendered. He came into the room where Griffiths was Seated, and struck him a most violent blow in the mouth, bursting his lip and doing considerable injury to him. Complainant next day went to the police, and took out a summons against him. Immediately defendant aot it. he renewed the attack upon him. He struck at Grif- fiths, who, however warded off the blow. Defendant was a dangerous man, and got very violent; and the complainant was in fear of violence from him.—Defend- ant denied the assault, and said the prosecution was out of spite.—A fine of ss. and costs was inflicted for the assault, and he was bound over to be of good behaviour for six months in his own recognizance of £5, and in a surety of the same amount. EMIORATION,—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the " Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Guion, American, and other lines.— John Walker, agent, "Examiner' Office, BeWSey-st., Warrington.—Advt.

A POLISH QUARREL AT WIDNES.—DRBADFUL INJURIES. At the Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. J. Brock, a Pole named Dominaki Dovitsk was charged with wounding Silvester Oustra on the previous night in a house in Watson-St. The evidence was given through an interpreter. From the evidence of a married woman named Rose Ann Kevitch, in whose house the row occurred, it appears that Dovitsk quarrelled with Oustra, and in the fight which ensued the latter was knocked about in a slicking manner. The witness alleged that nothing but a brush was used while she was there, but she did not see the whole of the occurrence She was unable to say what caused the blood to flow. Dr. Hud- son, assistant to Dr. Hutchinson, said that he dressed the wounds of the injured man. He was very seriously cut about the head and face, and some of he wounds weie very deep. On the left side of the head there was a wound three inches long and half an inch deep; near it was another one three inches long and three inches deep; on the top of the head was a wound nearly two inches long, and another an inch long. Behind the ear was a cut an inch long, and on the left cheek a wound nearly two inches in length. The left thumb was sprained and near it was a clean cut wound, while the whole of the left arm bore evidence of having received many blows. So serious was the condition of the injured man that wit- ness at once ordered him to be removed to the hospital. The sharp piece of iron (produced) would be just the thing to cause such wounds, and the stains upon it were, he believed, blood stains. Prisoner was remanded for

eight days.' UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. &W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. THE ROYAL VISIT TO LLANDUDNO. The place selected for the Queen of lloumania's stay at Llandudno, is the Marine Hotel, the whole ground floor of which has been taken for her Majesty during her stay at this popular seaside resort. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. &W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Ach.l. THE LAND OF THE WARRINGTON BLUE COAT SCHOOL. The Liberals of Mosley Common have decided to build a new club on a piece of land near the recrea- tion ground, Mosley Common, Tyldesley. The ground belongs to the trustees of the Warrington Blue Coat School, and Mr. J. H. Macdonald, the pre- sident of the club, has been negotiating for its pur- chase. The cost of the building will be between

£2OO and £3OO. STEAMER " ST. TUDNO." Visitors to North Wales will be glad to see from the advertisement in our advertising columns, that the New North Wales S.S. Co.'s popular steamer, "St. Tudno," will, on and after Ist September, leave Garth Ferry, Beaumaris, and Llandudno in the afternoon half an hour earlier than hitherto, arriv- ing back in Liverpool at 6 o'clock instead of 6.30 p.m.; and now that the days are shortening this will be found a very great advantage. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. NEWTON PARLIAMENTARY REVISION. The Revision Court will be held in Newton Town Ilan on Wednesday. September 17th, Mr. J. T. Foard sitting as revising barrister for the revision of the voter's lists for Newton-in-Makerfield, Burtonwood, Houghton and Middleton with Arbury, Southworth with Croft, and Winwick with Hulme. The Liberal party have made about 228 objections and about GO claims for the division. The objections on the Conservative side number nearly 200, with 177 occupiers' and 156 ownership claims and re-claims. A WRONGFUL CONVICTION RECTIFIED. Information has been received in Altrincham of the liberation from Stafford Goal of Samuel Reit and James Aldcroft, who were sentenced at the Chester Assizes to seven years' penal servitude for highway robbery at Broadheath, in October last. Owing to circumstances coming to light after the conviction, an influential representation was made by the visiting justices at Knutsford to the Home Secretary. Further inquiries were insti- tuted by the Cheshire police, with the result stated above.

_ SUBSIDENCE IN THE CHESHIRE SALT DISTRICT. At a meeting of the Winsford Local Board, on Thursday afternoon, the clerk read a resolution passed by property-owners and ratepayers at North- wich urgently requesting Mr. Brunner, M.P., to introduce next session a bill providing a remedy for the heavy losses sustained in the salt districts owing to subsidences. Mr. Hulse moved, Mr. Atherton seconded, and it was carried, with one dissentient, that the Winsford ,Local Board should also memorialise Mr. Brunner to take immediate steps to remedy the grievance. Mr. Ritchie hav- ing refused a Royal Commission to inquire into the matter.

NEWTON DIVISION LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. Under the auspices of the above, a meeting was held at the Budge Inn, Burtonwood, on Monday night. Mr. P. M. Campbell presided, and there was a fair attendance of Liberals. Mr. Campbell, in the course of a lengthy speech, explained the position of the Association in the division, dwelling particu- larly upon its financial aspect, and urging upon all good Liberals the importance of giving their earnest and practical support to the cause. Some discussion afterwards took place upon the advisabil- ity of organising a club for the resort of the Liberals of Buttonwood. Mr. Campbell, however, pointed out that it would be far better for them to meeZ, together once a week for the discussion of political topics, rather than to establish a club, and run the risk of probable failure, a course which would not redound to their credit. A resolution was after- wards proposed that a club be instituted, which, on being seconded, was unanimously adopted. CRITCHLEVO Tailoring meal 4110 times.—Advt. LOCAL FoOTRALLERS AT SWINTON. A nine-aside contest took place on Saturday at Swinton, under Rugby Union rules. The following result was arrived at :—First round: St. Helens Recreation beat Swinton Hornets, Clifton beat Rochdale Hornets, Warrington (in the absence of the Werneth team) walked over, and Swinton, Tyldesley (Berry's team), Tyldesley (Sutcliffe's team), Wigan, and Walkden drew byes. Second round: Swinton beat Wigan by one try to nothing. Tyldesley (Berry's team), walked over. Walkden beat Warrington by one goal to a dropped goal, and St. Helens Recreation beat Clifton by one goal, one try, and one minor point to one try. Third round: Tyldesley (Berry's team) beat Walkden by one goal, one try, and one minor point to one try and three minor points, and Swinton beat St. Helens Recrea- tion by two goals to one goal. Final round: Swinton and Tyldesley were left to compete in the final struggle for the premier position. They proved to be well matched. A minor point to Tyldesley was the only point scored in the first half, whilst in the second portion of the round Tyldesley gained a goal to Swinton a minor point, Tyldesley (Berry's team) winning by a goal and a minor point to a minor point. The Recreation team won the third prize. BATHS, all kinds.--J. S. Garlands, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge Street, Warrington, Branch—Earlestown.—Advt.

LIBERALISM AT BURTONWOOD. A meeting of the Liberals of Buttonwood was held in Anders' Inn, Burtonwood, on Saturday night. There was a fair attendance and Mr. P. M. Camp- bell, the Liberal registration agent for the Newton Division attended and was asked to preside. Mr. Campbell, in the course of an address, reviewed the position of the party throughout the township and referred particularly to the township and parish of Buttonwood. He strongly advised them not to embark upon anything that would necessitate any considerable outlay, but rather to hire a suitable room where they could meet in order to discuss the position of affairs in their own parish. He pointed out from his experience how needful it was that they should work up their own parish thoroughly, and said that now so many new houses had been built the political complexion of the parish was greatly altered. Beforetimes but few Liberals could be found, but now they were in the majority in the parish, and since the parish had been made into a separate polling district it would be much -easier for them to work the district satisfactorily. He urged upon them the necessity of maintaining their organ- isation in view of the election that seemed so near. After an experience of 40 years in the dis- trict and more than half of that time a practical, working politician, he could bold out to them a reasonable hope of carrying the parish with them as it had never been carried before. He gave detailed statistics as to the position of politi- cal parties in the division, and showed that at least one-third of the electors on the present register had not voted for the Newton Division. Among them would have to be found the majority of the Liberals, and whether the majority was 350, 850, or 700 time alone would tell. Having visited every house (12 000) in the division he was in a position to give them the comforting assurance that they were in a fair way for carrying the division if they had any- thing like a good candidate. They must have a man who would endorse labour questions and go in for Home Rule, for there was no reasonable doubt* that politics, and politics alone, would form the piece ele resistance of the next general election. (Applause.) A discussion followed Mr. Campbell's , address, and hearty thanks were tendered to that gentleman on the motion of Mr. M. Gaffney, I seconded by Mr. Thomas O'Brien and supported by Mr. Bellfield, ecc. As a result of the gathering, arrangements will be made for the hiring of a , suitable meeting room, to be used for club purposes.

THE WALKun ,Ani GALLERY. The 20th autumn exhibition of pictures at the Walker Art Gallery, Liverpool, will be commenced next Monday, and there will be a private view to- day (Saturday), open to season ticket holders. C AITCHLEY. Practical Tailor. Bold-at.. Warrington.—Advt.

TEE HOME IRON TRADE. There is a decided improvement in the English iron market, and prospects are ever so much better than they were a short time back. Prices are strong, and higher. The rise in values has been participated in both by pig-iron and finished iron and steel. A large trade has been done in Scotch warrants at fairly steady prices. Scotch makers' iron, which meets with a better demand, has risen from 6d. to is. 6d. a ton, while Middlesbrough iron has gained is. 3d. per ton on the week. Elsewhere prices are strong, and in an upward ten- dency. In the north-west, Bessemer has declined 6d. per ton since last week, but trade is much better. Finished iron is higher by 7s. 6d. to 10s. per ton since a fortnight ago in the north of England, and Scotch bars have advanced ss. since last week. Welsh bars are quoted ss. more. In the north-west steel is quiet and lower, but in Scotland, the north of England, and Lancashire higher prices are ob- tained. The tide appears to be turning at last in favour of shipbuilders, who are booking more work. Engineers are fairly active.—lron.

RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. TUESDAY.—Before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes. CLAIM FOR DEMURRAGE.—George Thornton, master mariner, and Porter's Shipping Company, Limited, of Fleetwood, sued John Duckworth, Nursery Works, Rad- cliffe, near Manches er, for £lO demurrage by reason of the defendant refusing or neglecting to unload a cargo of a vessel at Runcorn within the time specified by the Charter party.—The defendant did not appear, and lodg- ment was entered for the plaintiff. THE FRODSHAM LABOURER AND HIS FURNITURE.— Mendel Blank, furniture dealer, Bridge-st., Runcorn, sued Henry Grice, labourer, Main-st., Frodsbam, for £2 15s. Od' . value of a chest of drawers supplied. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys appeared for the plaintiff—The plaintiff gave evidence as to receiving the order person- ally from the defendant, and the drawers were delivered. Subsequently he applied for payment but the defendant said he should neither pay for them nor raturn them.— Walter Gerrard, clerk to Mr. Humphreys, said the de- fendant told him that rather than the plaintiff should have the drawers he would chop them for firewood.—The de- fendant told the Judge that he had never ordered the drawers, but he had them in his house in the place where the plaintiff left them. He had had a previous transac- tion with the plaintiff, who had pressed goods upon him without an order. He supposed he wanted to do simi- larly with the drawers.—Mr. Humphries: You consider Mr. Blank made you a present of the drawers ?—Defend- ant: Yes, certainly.—The Judge said he was disposed to believe the man's story that the things were unduly pressed upon him. He asked the defendant why he did not give the things back if he did not want them.—De- fendant: I never give anything back after its given me. I shall want something for my trouble.—The Judge told the defendant to return the things, and entered judgment for the defendant without costs.—Mr. Humphreys asked his Honour to make it part of the order that the goods should be returned.—His Honour: I cannot do that.
Board

untrained assistant master rose from LW to £BO and of an uncertificated assistant from £5O to £eo. The max- imums for assistant mistresses were respectively £BO, £65, and £45. The increases are dependent upon a favourable report from the School Management Commit- tee. The salaries of male pupil teachers were fixed at £1.5 for the first year rising to £2ll. for the fourth year. Female teachers commence at .£l3 and rise to £22. Dean Finegan said this matter had been forced on the Committee, who had made no change whatever in the salaries except in one case, and that was in favour of the teacher. Several members expressed an objection to bonuses, but the schedule was accepted in its entirety.

TECHNICAL EDUCAI lON. A circular letter from the Science and Art Department with regard to manual instruction was read. It stated that with a view to assist and encourage the formation of classes for manual instruction, grants would be made by the Department towards the maintenance of such classes in connection with elementary schools teaching drawing. The instruction must be (a) in the use of the ordinary tools used in handicrafts in wood and iron; (b) given out of school hours in a properly fitted workshop; and (c) connected with the instruction in drawing, that is to say, the work must be from drawings to scale pre- viously made by the students. The teacher if not suffi- ciently qualified, must be assisted by a skilled artisan.— The Chairman asked if this would not overlap what the Local Board were going to do.—Mr. Deacon: No sir; what the Local Board are going to do excludes elemen- tary school children.—Dr. O'Keeffe said he had suggested that a joint Committee of the Local Board and School Board should be formed to carry out the Technical Edu- cation Act.—The Chairman said it was for the Local Board to take the initiative.—The letter was referred to the School Management Committee. THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c. BY AN "OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT." The annual election of Runcorn Commissioners takes place on Thursday next : but the system of election is so antiquated and clumsy that no accurate forecast of the candidates can be made. There is no system of nomination, and each elector is at liberty to vote for any ratepayer he chooses, provided his choice has the necessary property qualification. The voting, too, is of a very open description, and the ratepayer cannot conceal in which direction his sympathies lie. It is time the ballot box was introduced. In former years "The List " meant the five nominees of the " Works " party, who were dominant in the town, and the pressureexerted usually led to the success of their candidates. "The Works" as such have now ceased to interfere in these elections. There will be a list presented for the , ratepayers' acceptance next Thursday, but there will be no interference with their free will, and the claims of the candidates will be based upon a desire to serve the best interests of the town and the ability to do so. The list will be composed of the following names :—Mr. Samuel Taylor (Chairman of the Board), Mr. William Whittaker, Mr. William Fisher, Mr. Walter Timmins, and Mr. Thomas Handley. For about the fifth time, Mr. S. Yarwood will offer his services to his fellow townsmen, and perhaps on the present occasion his perseverance will be rewarded with the coveted seat. Mr. Peter Smith, one of the retiring members, will probably seek re- election, and the name of Mr. Wynne llumphreys has been mentioned as a likely candidate, but there is a doubt as to his "coming out." Mr. Richard Abel, it is said,will endeavour to wipe out the defeat he sustained at the poll twelve months ago, and there may possibly be other candidates. The elec- tion will as usual be non-political. Providence has just blessed the wife of ex-In- spector O'Donnell with a daughter, and the little stranger arriving during the time of the extraordin- ary inquiry which her paternal parent has set in motion, Mr. O'Donnell apparently intends her to re- mind him of the event by the name he has bestowed upon her. There is a eioe where a man burdened his boy with the names of 14 Russian generals, of whom he was an admirer, but Mr. O'Donnell has not been so extravagant. Annie Slater Hamersley O'Donnell, bears the name of her father's champion, ' and, it is presumed, of his'opponent, the Chief Con- stable, and had not the Catholic Church placed re- strictions on more than three names, the chairman of the tribunal, Horatio Lloyd, might with advan- tage have been added. Considering that the Chief Constable invited Mr. Slater Lewis to " come out": in sanguinary fashion, how will he appreciate this close conjunction of their names? The prospects of the Chemical Union being formed do not, from latest accounts, appear so bright, and the people of Widnes, the tradesmen especially, rejoice thereat. The opinion is strongly held that the union would not be to the advantage of the town, and those local manufacturers who have been pre-eminent in attempting to form the syndicate are not spoken of in at all flattering terms. The paper makers still continue their stren- ous opposition.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY TRAGEDY AT BURTON WOOD. SUICIDE OF TWO GIRLS.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY TRAGEDY AT BURTON WOOD. SUICIDE OF TWO GIRLS.

An event unparalleled in the history of Burton-, wood, and the district, which has caused a most painful sensation in the neighbourhood, took place in Burtonwood on Tuesday evening. The actors in the dreadful affair were two little gills named Elizabeth Farimond, 10 years ;of age, daughter of Thomas Farimond, collier, Green John's-lane, Burtonwood, and Margaret Andrew, 11 years of age, daughter of Jonathan Andrews, collier, of Tan House-lane, Burtonwood. So far the affair is shrouded in mystery. It appears,however, that the two girls attended the Catholic day, school at Burtonwood, and were present on Tuesday as usual. After school hours, shortly after four o'clock in the afternoon, the girls were together, and Andrews, taking off her clogs, gave them to her younger brother, telling him to take them home, as she was going to drown herself, at the same time shaking hands with him, and bidding him good-bye. The girls then proceeded in the direction of Gipsey-lane, which leads down to the Sankey Canal, and is fully a mile and a half away from the school. About five o'clock they were seen by a lad named Joseph Hewitt, who lives at Red Bank Farm, running, along the canal bank, and this was the last that was seen of them. The boy Andrews, after parting with his sister, went home, and told his father what his sister had said. The father,hardly realising that the girl contemplated destroying herself,thought, it better to look after her, and accordingly he went in search of his daughter. Ile pursued the same direction as that taken by the girls, and about half- past five reached the canal bank. After walking along it some short distance, he espied two hats floating on the water, onebf which he recognised as that worn by his daughter. The sight so unnerved him that he fainted, and on recovering found a man named James Smith standing by to whom he com- municated his fears. They obtained rakes, and were shortly afterwards joined by another man named Pomfrett. Together they commenced a search for the bodies of the children, and very soon recovered one, the other being brought to the surface shortly afterwards. The bodies were taken to their homes, the police were informed of the affair, and the Coroner was notified. Mrs. Farimond and her husband received a ter- rible shock when intelligence of the death of their daughter was conveyed to them. The mother states that she cannot in any way account for such a rash act on the part of her girl, and can only surmise that she has been persuaded to it by the girl An- drews. When her daughter left home after dinner to go to school, she told her to be quick home, and she would make a cake for her, and the girl pro- mised to do so. When she did not come home at the proper time, the mother became anxious, and on inquiring from a boy who attends the same school as to the whereabouts of her daughter, she was told that she had gone with a little boy to Newton Com- mon. As the Farimond's had previously lived at the Common the mother displayed no further anxiety, and the next tidings she had was the sad news that the child was dead. The girl Andrews had no mother, and lived with her father, and he is perfectly bewildered. So far as he knew the child had no trouble, and no aetion of his would tend to make her tired of her life. It appears, however, that she had twice previously en- deavoured to destroy herself, and no later than Tuesday morning she said she had tried one pit, but it was not deep enough. The mistress at the school can throw no light on the affair, and it is not thought that any harsh treatment on her part has anything to do with it, as all the children speak very highly of her. An inquest will be held in due course. INQUEST YESTERDAY.

Yesterday morning Mr. Brighouse held an inquest into the death of twolittle girls who were drowned in Sankey Canal, near Eariestown, on Tuesday evening. The event has cast quite a gloom over the neighbourhood of Burton- wood, where the girls' parents were well known and respected. The inquest was held at the Chapel House Inn, Burtonwood. Jonathan Anders, a widower, with five children, said his daughter Margaret was eleven years of age. Re left

- for his work at 4.40 on Tuesday morning. Margaret got up, and when cloSingthe door behind him said " Father, the fire is out :good morning." He had not the slightest suspicion of his daughter's intention when he left home. On his return, Margaret was at school, and soon after his son Henry came in and said "Father, our Margaret is drowned." Henty said she had gone to the canal with Elizabeth Farimond, and gave him her clogs for him. Witness set off towards the canal, and met two little boys, and asked them if they had seen anything of the girls. The boys said they had not, but had seen two hats in the water. He went as directed by them, and on seeing the hats exclaimed, "Lord help me." The bodies were shortly afterwards recovered. Mrs. Farimond, wife of Thomas Farimond, 10, Green John-brow, said her daughter went to school in the morning, and came back at 12.30 for dinner. She went back after one. When she got to the garden gate she asked witness if she might stay at home to clean the floor, to which witness said no. The girl, when she catne home at dinner time,said, "Mother, what do you think ? Anders' girl has been to drown herself." Witness said she saw no mere of her daughte:. She had a dread of water. Alice Anders, aged fourteen, the eldest sister of the de- ceased, Margaret Anders, said she kept the house for her father. She remembered Tuesday morning last, when she got her brother ready for school. Margaret left for school at a quarter to nine. She did nottake any break- fast, neither would she take her dinner with her. There was some word about a piece of cheese being missing at the table, and as Margaret was leaving she said to wit- ness, "You will not see my face again unless you see it dead." The last time witness saw their father chastise Margaret was about two months ago, when she went to a flower show against his express orders. Henry Anders, nine years of age, said his sister Mar- garet went with him to school. On Tuesday morning she took no breakfast. She was angry about some cheese, and witness told her that he would tell their father she had been playing truant. About 200 yards from the house she took off her clogs, and went into a brook, but said that was not deep enough. She did not go to school that forenoon, but came at the afternoon. After four o'clock she went to the boarded barns, saying they were going t drown themselves. The girl Fari- mond was with her crying. Witness thought they were in fun,and followed them. His sister gave him herclogs. In answer to Sergeant Devlin, witness said that en Tuesday morning his sister said she wished God would strike her dead. On passing Cooper's Pit she said if that pit were not near a house she would drown herself in it. She said to witness and his brother Jonas "Come and drown yourselves with us." Jonas cried, and wantesl to go,but witness kept him back. Witness had no idea why his sister wanted to die. Eliza Anders, wife of John Anders, collier,said she was no relation to the girl Anders. About half-past ten on Tuesday morning Margaret came to her house with clogs in her hands, and wearing a pair of old boots. She waited there with her feat at the fire until half-past one, when she heard the bell ring. She said she did not want any dinner, and left for school at that hour. She chuck- ed the clogs under the bed, and after school hours re- turned with the girl Farimond. She was very quiet that day. She stayed in witness's house Monday after- noon. There was nothing peculiar about her then. Mary Jane Lloyd, wife of Samuel Lloyd, Bent's Cottages, observed the two girls walking arm-in-arm towards the canal. Anders told witness's little girl that I "You won't see us any more after to-night you little b —" Witness saw nothing more of them until she saw the dead bodies. The place where they were drowned was about half a mile from witness's, house. Joseph Hewitt, son of James 11ew94. Red House Farm. Burtonwood, also saw the two girl s going towards the canal, and afterwards saw them running up and down the bank. After passing a haystack he could see nothing more of the girls, but soon afterwards saw their hats in the water, just where they were seen running. Sergeant Devlin and Constable Grundy said that the result of their inquiries showed that the parents of the children treated them kindly, and that neither child com- plained against the teachers. The schoolmistress said they were both good children, and prepared their lessons well. A juryman stated that an aunt of the girl Anders was rather imbecile and subject to fits. The jury, after a short deliberation, returned a verdict that Anders committed suicide in a temporary fit of insanity, and as to Farimond, that she was found drowned.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse, on Thursday afternoon. Mr. J. W. Wareing presided, and there were also present the Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, Rev. Dean Fine- gan, Messrs. C. B. Johnson, W. Lowe, W. Middlehurst,J. Marsh, G. Davies, J. Peover, J. Ranson, James Burchall, J. Buckley, J. Kenwright, J. Birchall, J. Mercer, J. Griffiths, W. Borrows, P. Longton, W. Daine, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). RELIEF.—The Workhouse'Master reported there were 507 inmates this week, 486 last week, and 496 in the cor- responding week last year. 'I he number of vagrants relieved had been 48, against 52 in the same week last

year. AGED PERSONS IN RECEIPT OF RELIEF.—The Clerk re- ported the receipt of a communication from the Local Government Board, asking for a return of the persons over 80 years of age who were in receipt of relief on the Ist August last. The information, the Clerk added, would be forwarded. GIFTS.—The Rev. B. A. W. Norris (chaplain) acknow- ledged the receipt of useful parcels of books and periodi- cals for the use of the inmates from Mrs. Willox (Huy- ton), Mrs. Huntington (Huyton), Mrs. Mather (Rainhill), and Mrs. T. Dennett (Prescot). Rirscarkriow or A NURSE—Miss Probert, at present an inmate of the Royal Southern Hospital, Liverpool, wrote resigning her appointment as night nurse at the Work- house. The resignation was accepted, and the Clerk was instructed to advertise for a successor. COUNTY PRECEPT.—The Clerk stated that he had received from the Clerk to the County Council a precept requiring the Guardians to pay £4,265 18s. ld. on the 15th September. That was ,considerably less than the precept issued for the corresponding period of last year when the amount was £6,013 9s. 9d. Ile added that he (the clerk) had reduced his estimate of the probable expenditure of the Guardians accordingly. THE ESTIMATE OF EXPENDITURE.—The Clerk sub- mitted his estimate of the probable expenditure of the Guardians during the half year ending March next. It I amounted to a total of £22,756, while the actual expen- diture during the same period last year was £25,316. To the estimate was added 10 per cent, for contingencies, making a total of £25,031.—0n the proposcion of the Rev. Dean Finegan, seconded by Mr. Peover, the estimate was approved. HOLlDAYS.—Relieving Officers Stuart and Treacey were granted a week's leave of absence. RE-APPOINTMENTS.—On the proposition of the Rev. Dean Finegan, seconded by Mr. Davies, Dr. Cooper was re-appointed medical officer for the lower Widnes dis- trict at a salary of £7O per annum. Mr. R. G. Water- man was also re-appointed assistant relieving officer for the Woolton division at a salary of £l5 per annum. This was the principal business.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday. Pre- sent Mr. T. S. Timmis (chairman), Rev. Dean Fine- gan, Rev. J. Clarke, Dr. O'Keeffe, Major Wareing, Messrs. Deacon, Brown, Barlow, and Danby (clerk).
'CENSUS OF THE _TOWN.

The District Education Committee reported that dur- ing the holidays the Attendance Officers were employed in taking a census of the children of the district, and the results were given in tabular form. Table one showed that there are 5,221 houses, of which 5,139 were in- habited, 82 empty, and 40 in course of erection. The total accommodation at the schools in the district was 6,992, whereas the number of children between 3 and 13 is 7,647, and allowing the usual deductions, there were 5,572 school-going children. There was thus an excess of school accommodation of 1,420. The total number of children who ought to be on the rolls was 6,544, and the total number on the rolls is 6,382, leaving 162 children over five years who ought to be on the rolls, but are not. There are 121 children attending school who did not live in the town. In taking the census, the officers had appa- rently omitted 47 children. The proportion of school- going children to populatson (estimating the population at 30,000) was 1 to 5.38.—Mr. Deacon, in presenting the report, said the census was taken every two years, and a remarkable feature of the present occasion was a de- crease of 98 in the number of houses, while the number of inhabited houses had increased by 84. The number of empty houses was less by 92.—The Chairman said the decrease in the number of houses was partly accounted for by the extension of the works of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co ,andMessrs.Bolton and Sons. Mr. Deacon went on to say that the number of children between 3 and 13 had only increased by 2, and this was not creditable. The number of school-going children was only two differ- ent from last census,and the number of children attend- ing private schools had increased by 21. The number attending no school had decreased by 142. They now came to some remarkable figures, the number of child- ren between 3 and 4 having decreased by 139. The only way in which the officers could explain this was that in previous years some children just under 3 years must have been counted as over 3. It wasperfectly incredible to think that the number of inhabited houses should have increased and the number of children decreased. The number of children between 13 and 14 years, who ought to be on the rolls but are not had decreased by 46. There was an increase of 44 children attending school, who did not live in the town, and these were mostly from Ditton. The number of children on the rolls had increased by 87. The proportion of scholars to population had not altered, but he was informed by the clerk to the Board, that the population was estimated at 31,000 and this would make a slight difference.—Dr. O'Beeffe said considering the number of lodgers in the town, he believed the present population was 35,000.—Dean Finegan said that figure was excessive. It was usual to estimate that each house contained 5 persons, but taking the number at six to allow for lodgers, they would only get a total of 30,000. Dr. 07/Keeffe said he had Personal knowledge of many houses with only accommodation for five persons, which contained 13.—Mr. Deacon said there was much less over-crowding than in previous years and there were few houses which contained more than one family.— Dean Finegan said that was his information toe. He could scarcely name two houses in his district where there were two families living. Tax SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE submitted for approval a schedule of salaries of head teachers, in place of one now in force. Head master of a school ,with an average attendance of 200 or more,com- menced the first year with £l3B, rising by increases of £3 and £3 per year to £l9O. In a school with an aver- age attendance under 200, the master rose from £133 to £175 ; and in a school of under 140 scholars the salary rose from £12.3 to £l5O. In the senior girls department, the head mistresses rose to a maximum of £l3O, £ll9, and £lO5 respectively ; in the junior girls to £125, £ll4 and £lOO respectively. In the infant department the I maximum salaries were £125, £ll4, and £95. div.head: ALLEGED ABDUCTION.
div.p: THE ALLEGED ABDUCTION.

There has been a good dual of talk during the past week about the case of alleged abduction of two girls from Warrington, particulars of which were given in our last issue. We understand that the parents, whilst naturally concerned at 'what had happened, have shown themselves reluctant to take proceedings, in view of the unpleasant publicity that would necessarily ensue. There has been some communication with the police, but it is not now thought that legal proceedings will be taken.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO THE REV. WILLIAM BROOKES.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO THE REV. WILLIAM BROOKES.

On Sunday the Rev. W. Brookes preached his fare- well sermon in Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapel. There was a large congregation. The discourse was founded upon the words: "Finally, brethren, fare- well, Be perfect, be of good comfort, be of one mind, live in peace; and the God of love and peace shall be with you" (2 Cor. xiii. 11). In closing, he expressed a hope that the congregation would receive his successor (Rev. Alfred Freeman, Liverpool), as kindly as they received him when he first cams amongst them. At the conclusion of the service several members of the congre- gation assembled in one of the vestries, when the rev. gentleman was presented with a pocket sacramental service for use in the sick room. It was enclosed in a leather case, on the outside of which was the inscrip- tion :—" Presented to the Rev. William Brookes, on the occasion of his leaving Warrington, by the officials and friends of Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapel, August 24, 1890." Mr. Elijah Place, in opening the proceedings, said Mr. Brookes was highly respected by them all, and they determined he should not be allowed to leave War- rington without something being given to him to remind him of his friends in his old circuit. The matter was only mentioned last Sunday, but more than sufficient money was obtained to meet the purchase, and it was then decided to make a presentation to Mrs. Brookes. Mr. John Bennett made the presentation to Mr. Br ,okes, and the rev. gentleman, in reply, said it was always a joy to labour among those who appreciated one's efforts, and there was no greater reward for a minister than to live in theaffections and memories of his people after he had left them. He thanked them very sincerely for their kindness. Councillor Beaman, Mr. John Haywood, Mr. Isaac Haywood, and Mr. J. Bailey and others spoke, after which Mrs. John Bennett presented a handsome satchel to Mrs. Brookes, who said that much as she would prize the present, she should still more highly prize the kind and loving things which had been said about her husband. After a speech from Mrs. Lloyd, the proceed- ings were brought to a conclusion.

div.head: ODDFELLOWS' MEETING AT WAR RINGTON. THE ORIGIN OF THE ORDER.
div.p: ODDFELLOWS' MEETING AT WAR RINGTON. THE ORIGIN OF THE ORDER.

-- The sixtieth anniversary of the Loyal Britain's Glory Lodge, Grand United Order of Oddfellows, was celebrated on Saturday evening, at the Lodge House, the Waggon and Horses Inn, Buttermarket- st., when about 70 members and friends sat down to dinner, which was admirably served by Host Jones, and gave great satisfaction. After dinner a meeting. of the members took place, P.G.M.P. Morris in the chair, and P.N.F. Wadsworth in the vice-chair. The Chairman, in an interesting speech, described the origin of the Order, which is of very an- cient date, being established by the Roman soldiers in camp after the Order of the Israelites during the reign of Nero, the Roman Emperor, A.D. 55, at which time they were called "Fellow-Citizens." The name of Odd- fellows was given to this Order of men, A.D. 79, by Titus Cesar, Emperor of Rome, from their singularity of notions, from their knowing each other by night as well as by day,and for their fidelity to him and theircountry. It was very probable that the first Odd-fellows made their appearance in North Wales about that time, under the command of Agricola one of Titus Ccesar's generals, and shortly after on the island of Mona. The first ac- eount we had of the Order spreading into other countries was in the fifth century, when it was established in the Spanish dominions under the Roman dispensation, and in the sixth century by King Henry in Portegal, and in the twelfth century it was established M France, and afterwards in England, by John de Neville, attended by five Knights from France, who formed a Loyal Grand r Lodge M London, which Order remained until the reign of Gearge 111, when a part of them formed themselves into a union. On this account the lodges,. which are very numerous throughout the world, call themselves the Grand United Order of Odd-fellows, being a portion of the original Order, and they use now the signs and emblems as granted by Titus Csar. The secre- tary (Mr. Morris) stated the lodge was in a flourish- ing condition, there having been twenty new mem- bers initiated during the past year, whilst the juvenile branch of the order, which was established in 1568, had now a capital of nearly £2,000, whilst it had paid in benefits during that time £l,OOO. The proceed- ings were enlivened by songs, recitations, dm., given by ' Bros. Welsby, Morris, Griffiths, and others. After the meetin., the room was cleared for dancing, which was indulged in until nearly 12 o'clock, the music being provided by Bro. Wright. Great credit is due to the Committee, and the host and hostess, for the way in which the affair was carried out.

SUDDEN DEATH AT BANK QUAY STATION.

Yesterday afternoon Thomas Metcalf, about 60 years of age, expired suddenly at Bank Quay Station. Warrington. He had gone to see a niece and two children off to Bradford by the 3.16 p.m. train. They got into a wrong carriage, which was de- tached from the Manchester train, and were taken to Arpley Station. Mr. Metcalf missed his niece, and asked Inspector Tanner where the carriage had been taken to. On being told it was at Arpley, he hurried there, and found his niece in the train. They all hurried back to Bank Quay to catch the next train. Mr. Metcalf went into the waiting-room for a few moments, and afterwards took a seat on the platform. Ile was observed by William Brad- shaw to fall on one side. Bradshaw and Dr. Bow- den, of the Warrington Infirmary, rendered assist- ance, but Mr. Metcalf died almost immediately. He was a native of Bradford. Yorkshire, but was on a visit to Mrs. Jones, 2, Moss-brow, Moore, near War- rington.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL
The monthly meeting of this Council will be held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening next, when amongst other business the following will be dealt with.

THE WATCH COMMITTEE AND THE POLICE. The Watch Committee's minutes contain the following resolution :—That Mr. Councillor Percival be elected a member of this Committee ; that Francis Jones be ap- pointed Sergeant at 31s. per week, in the room of Sergeant Shaw,resigned ; that on the recommendation of the Chief Constable, the following alterations in the .Regulations of the Force be made :-1. That the Chief Constable be authorised to allow at his discretion an equivalent in time to the men employed on Court duty. 2. That duty in the Park, Markets and Cemetery, be reckoned as regards time as ordinary duty. 3. That an annual leave of absence be allowed as follows :—Con- stables not exceeding 14 days; sergeants and inspectors, 21 days. The Committee after considering information received from other towns cannot agree to make any alteration in the time lists, which must remain as at present. The Chief Constable was instructed to bring under the notice of the Committee, any special case of sickness, or any case of sickness of more than six weeks duration.

STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE. This Committee proposes that Councillor Henry Roberts be appointed a member of it. THE SANITARY COMMITTEE. This Committee recommends that the premises of Mr. John Ford, as described in declaration of the Inspector, be declared infected with pleuro-pneumonia, and that in the opinion of this Committee, it is desirable that the sanitary provisions of the Public Health Acts,Amendment Acts, 1890, be adopted by the Council. THE PRESENTATION TO THE ART GALLERY. The minutes of the Museum, Library and Arts men- tioned the fact that the Chairman of the Committee (Mr. R. Davies) had presented to the Art Gallery, the marble Agure of "Rachel," by J. Warrington Wood, which had been purchased by Mr. Chorley, at a sale in London. The Committee accepted with gz eat pleasure the hand- some donation and conveyed to Mr. Davies their unanimous and hearty thanks for the same. The Com- mittee also tendered their best thanks to Mr. Chorley for the great interest he had shown, and the trouble he had had in connection with the acquisition of the above work of art. THE TOWN HALL, PARK AND BATHS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this Committee contain the following items :—That Mr. Alderman Wright be appointed a mem- ber of this Committee ; that the tender of Messrs. Patte- son, of Manchester, to prepare and lay Roman marble mosaic pavement in the vestibule of the Town Hall, be accepted, subject to certain alterations in the designs; that 12 dozen towels be provided for the use of bathers in the second class plunge bath, on a charge of id. per towel, and that six large roller towels be provided for the free use of bathers; that a suitable washing tub be provided in each plunge bath for the free use of bathers; that soap be provided for use in the private slipper baths; that an additional £5 be voted to the bands for playing in the park on Sundays during the remainder of the season.

GESER&L PIIRPOSES COMMITTEE. This Committee recommends :—That the common Seal of the Borough be affixed to the agreement made between the Corporation, and the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, Limited, the Whitecross Com- pany, Limited, and Rylands Bros., Limited, relating to the water supply, of those companies; that the Town Clerk be instructed to take the necessary steps for the adoption by the Council of the Public Health Acts Amendment Act, 1890, and that a print of the Act be supplied to each member of the Council; and, that, in compliance with the requirements of the Local Govern- ment Board, the application for the sanction of that Board to the grant of the plot of land to the Trustees of the Warrington Infirmary be made by memorial, and that the common Seal of the Borough be affixed thereto."

div.head: RE-ARRANGEMENT OF THE WARDS IN
div.p: RE-ARRANGEMENT OF THE WARDS IN

WARRINGTON. As we have already explained, Warrington is to be divided under the new Act of Parliament into nine wards instead of five as at present. The Act pro- vides that a Commissioner shall be appointed within three weeks of the 14th August, when the Royal assent was given to the Act. That being the case, the Town Clerk expects to receive a notification of the appointment of the Commissioner within the next few days. The Commissioner is required to proceed with all practicable despatch and so as to complete his scheme before the 30th day of Septem- ber. Clause 23 of the new Act says the Commis- sioner shall by his scheme.—" 1. Apportion all the existing councillors among the wards of the borough as altered, so as to provide as far as practicable for such councillors continuing to represent as large a number as possible of his former constituents, and every such councillor shall hold his office in the ward to which he shall be so assigned for the same period as he would have held such office if the wards existing had remained unaltered. 2. State for which of the wards of the borough as altered the five aldermen, assigned by the Council as returning officers on the 9th day of November, 1889, shall act, and shall also name aldermen to act as returning officer to each of the remaining new wards." With a view to assisting the Commissioner, and, facilitating the despatch of the work, the Town Clerk and Borough Surveyor prepared a provisional plan which is at present under the consideration of the Parliamentary Committee of the Corporation, and it will, if approved, be laid before the Commis- sioner on his visit to Warrington. The plan which has been prepared divides the North-west ward into I three new wards, and the North-east ward is also. divided into three wards. The South-west ward it is proposed to leave as it stands, with the exception that it would have three representatives instead of six as at present ; and the same practically applies to the South-east ward,, the only difference being that there would be a slight addition to the ward under the borough extension. This, however, is not material at present from the voting point of view, as it adds one elector only to the voting list. Latchford would not be touched in any way. It already returns three representatives, and may be taken therefore to be the model ward of the new scheme. Taking the new wards as divided, we rmderstand that the nambers of electors would be as follows : Latchford, 8%; South-east, as before, 1,.60; South- west, as before 539. With regard to the North-west ward when divided into three wards, the first of the three, which would take the district in the neigh- bourhood of Sankey-st. and the Town Hall, would have 989 electors; St. Barnabas district, £3&; and the Longford Works district, 788. When the North- east ward, is divided into three wards, the first ward, that is the Winvriek-road district, would con- tain 633 voters ; the barracks district, 904 ; and the North Church-st. district, 1,214. It will, of course, be for the Commissioner to finally determine what shall be the boundaries ot each ward ; and every elector will, we presume. have the opportunity of going.bef ore him and offering such suggestions as he may think frt. To take a case in point, it would be possible to rectify the great disparity in numbers between the south-west ward and south- east ward by adding to the south-west ward the- electors between Academy-st. and Bridge-st., which are at present inthe south-east ward. With regard to the transference of councillors, the south-west and south-east wards will each lose three councillors in November next. Two of these three will by effinxion of time hare ceased to, repre- sent theirconstituents, and it will be for them, if they like, to seek re-election in one or other of the new wards, but there will still be one representa- tive too many for both the south-West and south- east wards, and in this case it will be for the Com- missioner to allocate these representatives to one or other of the new wards. There will be no addition, to the number of town councillors or the number of aldermen. rm wards,en and Iti s ianquestion n purely the allocation of of a new division existing councillors.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

BODELLA KNOCETON'S GAOL EXPERIENCES. Bodelia Knockton, whose appearances at the Warring- ton Borough Police Court are frequent, was on Monday charged with being drunk and disorderly in sank-st. on the 16th August., The Mayor observed that this made her 40th appearance. Out of seven years she had served five, all but a few days, in prison. It was a difficult matter to know what to do in such a case. As the prisoner was under the influence of drink when in the dock, she was remanded until Tuesday, when she was discharged. A WIFE BEATER PUNISHED. Yesterday morning' at the Warrington Police Court, a wire-worker named Michael Corless was Lrought up in Custody on a charge of having assaulted his wife. The , case having been proved ,Mrs. Corless asked for a separa- tion order, stating that her husband had frequently ill. I treated her, and had been convicted before of assaulting I her. She had forgiven him many times. She had, she said, a family of eight. The magistrates fined prisoner 20s. and costs, and granted a separation order, prisoner to pay 15s. a week towards the support of his wife and family. A WARRINGTON FOUNDLING IN COURT. The lad,;John Warrington, who was brought up as a foundling in Warrington workhouse, and whose name has oftened appeared in the newspapers in connection with strange freaks, was on Saturday before the Warring- ton magistrates on a charge of having been found loiter- ing in the Cheshire Lines Wagon Works, Battersby-lane, about midnight. The company's official who found the lad thought he was out of his mind, and brought him to the police station. Alderman Burgess, who presided, said it was a difficult case to deal with, but the Bench would send Warrington to gaol for seven days without hard labour, and the officials of the gaol would have an opportunity of ascertaining whether he ought to be in an asylum or not. DISGRACEFUL CONDUCT IN BOSTOCE-ST. At the Warrington Police Court, yesterday morning, a rather complicated case was heard by Alderman Harri- son and Dr. Gornall. Lassie Jackson, an elderly woman, was summoned for having, on the 23rd Inst., assaulted Mary Dutton, and George Jackson, son of Mrs. Jack- son, was summoned for having used threats to his mother. Mr. Percy Davies appeared for Mrs. Dutton. It appeared that George Jackson is" keeping company" with Mrs. Dutton's daughter, and went to her house in Bostock-st. on Saturday afternoon. His mother followed him, and, having used bad language, struck Mrs. Dutton a blow on the head, knocking her down. On her part, Mrs. Jackson alleged that her son used threatening language to her, and called her daughter, who said that no assault was committed. The magistrates fined Mrs. Jackson £1 and costs, and dismissed the case as against George Jackson. Alderman Harrison, in giving the decision of the Bench, said that he could not resist the opportunity of saying to Mrs. Jackson that a more atrocious case he never heard in his life. He believed that she had committed wilful and deliberate perjury, and if ever a woman de- served to be punished for it she was the woman. Both he and his colleague, Dr. Gornall, utterly disbelieved what she had stated. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT THE BRIDBWELL.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday morning, Thomas Miskell, a well-known character, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bank-st. on Saturday night; also with assaulting P.C. Jones, Thomas Jowett, Thomas Marlow, and Thomas Lamb, and further with wilfully damaging a rug, whilst in custody. Prisoner accosted P.C. Jones. When ordered to go away he struck the officer, and was taken into custody. He then became very violent, and six men were required to con- vey him to the lock-up in the fashion known as the "frog's march." He behaved very noisily when in the cell, and the officer on reserve had to visit him frequ- ently. On going in for about the tenth time the officer found the prisoner attempting to hang, or strangle, himself with his rug, which he had torn into strips. He asked the constable to give him a knife to stab himself with. He said he would go to the gallows for a police- man. Prisoner had stripped himself naked, so the officer put him as he was into an empty cell for a time. The Mayor remarked that the prisoner now made his 50th appearance before the magistrates. Replying to the Chief Constable, prisoner said he had spent three months in Rainhill some time ago. He came out of gaol only on Thursday, after serving three months. If the magis- trates would give him a chance he would sign the pledge and go to work. The Mayor said the Bench would dis- charge him on condition that he would go to the Work- house fora few weeks. Prisoner gave the promise, and was discharged.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Francomb), and
Alderman Harrison.

BAD CONDUCT.—iii;:g;iiii-;;;;Wjd Ss- and costs for having been guilty of indecent conduct in Buttermarket- st., on Saturday night, and Alice Thomas, for a similar offence committed at Arpley, was sent to prison for a week. CIIIIENET o FlRE.—Michael Mannion was ordered to pay Bs., the costs, for haying allowed the chimney of his house to be on fire. ALLEGED STONE THROWING.—John Kelley and William Cunningham were summoned for throwing stones, on the 17th inst., to the danger of passengers. The magistrates thought there was no case, and dismissed the defendants. THE Boas' ORDE2.—Thomas Hewitt Dutton was sum- moned for allowing a dog to be at large, unmuzzled, on the 18th inst. It appeared from the evidence that the dog had bitten a girl in two parts of the leg, although the defendant said that at the time it was wearing a muzzle. The magistrates held that the animal could not have been sufficiently muzzled, and ordered defendant to pay 14s. costs. DisrunntNn THE Paecia.—Two men named Longshaw and Hopkins were bound over for committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Market-place, and another I couple named Flannery and.Garritty were similarly dealt with for a like offence. DI2I7NKENNESS.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence: Joseph Downes. in Sankey-st., on 1 Saturday night, fined 55., including costs; Mark nea- ley, in Buttermarket-at., on the 17th inst., fined 55., in- cluding costs ; and Elizabeth Duffy, in the Old-road, on the 18th inst. fined ss. and costs. TIIESDAT.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Francomb), and Mr. R. Garnett. DRUNICErNESB.—For this offence John Rowlands, Dominick Knockton, and James McHugh were each fined 55., including costs.—Joseph Simc,ock, for having been drunk and disorderly in Rigby-st., and for having done damage to a door of a house occupied by John Beaker- vine, was fined 10s. and costs, and ordered to pay for the damage, ss.—William Wilson was fined ss. and costs for drunkenness, and for having assaulted Constable Wade, whilst that officer was in the execution of his duty. Wanwasnar.—Before Alderman Holmes, and Mr. John Fairclough. Scsroor, ATTENDANCE CAsns.—A number of parents . .

were summoned for neglecting to regularly send their, children to school, Mr. George Riley, the school attend- ance officer, proving the cases. Fines of 2s. ed. each and ss. each were imposed in the majority of the cases, and the magistrates resolved to request the Workhouse autho- rities tAii shelter one boy who was suffering from soma complaint requiring medical attendance. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison, Dr. Gornall, and Dr. White. MiscELLANnors.—Margaret Fallon was fined Ss., for neglecting to send her child to school regularly.—Wm. Stratford, Arthur Stratford, C. Fawkes, and R. Lee, were each ordered to contribute towards the support of

their parents. CHARGES OF AssAULTS.—Bridget Sheer was summoned for having assaulted Mary Ward. The case was oismiss- ed on payment of costs.—J. Buckley, a youth, was sum- moiled for assaulting a woman named Margaret Ken- wright, and her baby, Beatrice Kenwnght. It was alleged that he hit Mrs. Kenwright on the forehead with a stone, and that he threw some dirt at the child. De- fendant said Mrs. Kenwright threw at him first. Tha magistrates ordered him to pay costs.—Mary Donoghue was summoned for assaulting Ellen Bradshaw, and a cross-summons charged Bradshaw with assaulting Donoghue. Both cases were dismissed.

WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. J. Tinsley. DIUTSZEIINESS.—A man named James Mullen was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Rixton, 011 Saturday, and wastfmed ss, and costs. P.C. Schofield fICIrc4 UV case.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. O. L. Wigg. A CHILDREN'S SQUABBLE.—MatiIda Temple, a girl, was summoned for assaulting Mary Emily Faulkner, nine years of age, daughter of Peter Faulkner, of Parker-st. Mr. Lake prosecuted. It was alleged that the defendant, without any provocation, had dragged the complainant into her parents' yard, and there thumped and kicked her, causing black bruises on the girls leg. The defend- ant denied the assault, and said the complainant walked into the yard and pulled faces at the window, and when running away fell off the step into a hole. The Bench considered the case proved, and fined defendant 2s. 6d. and costs, us. 6d. ASSAULT.—John Boden, farm labourer, pleaded guilty to assaulting another farm labourer, named John Cellary, and he was fined 6d., and costs, 9s. 6d. DRITNIC.—John Basnett and Thomas Stretch were each fined Ss. and costs for this offence.

THEFT OF A HAlL—Richard Condon, a stranger, was brought up on remand, charged with stealing a ham worth Bs., the property of George Wharton, grocer, Church-st. He was sentenced to fourteen days. hard labour.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THIIRSDAY.—Before Lieut.-Colonel Gaskell and Mr. F.

Stapleton Bretherton. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Thomas Breen, Catherine Grady, and James Campbell, were each fined ss. and costs tor being drunk.—Amelia Standish, Mary Foleand, Thomas Connor, Thos. Bell, and Catherine Bryson, were each bound over to be of good behaviour for three months, for creating breaches of the peace. COMPULSORY EDUCATION.—A number of parents were summoned by the School Board for not sending their children regularly to school and the usual fine of ss. was imposed in each case. THEFT.—Ann Callon, Chapel-street, was sentenced to seven days hard labour for stealing a tablecloth worth 2s. 6d., the property of James Lomax. WASTING WATHR.—William Pali' n grocer, Ann-street, was summoned by the Local Board for illegallly wasting water at his shop on the 30th ult. Mr. J. T. Allen pro-. secuted. The defendant was allowing water to run over some bacon. The defendant, who said it was a mistake the tap was left open, was fined ss. and costs. ROAD OBSTRUCTION.—WiIIiam Almond, farmer, Cron- ton, was fined ss, and costs for allowing his cart to stand in Liverpool-rd., forty minutes.

PLEuno-PrisumontA DtsrnicTs.—John Weir, farmer, , was sumnkoned for having moved a calf into a pleuro- pneumonia area at Stockton Heath, without a license, on the 18th August. It appeared that the defendant had sent the calf in a cart from Lower Walton to Stockton Reath, and there called at Sergeant Booth's for a license, instead of getting the license prior to moving the animal at all. He said he had been under the misapprehension that this was sufficient. A line of is and costs was imposed.

FRODSRAM RF.CRRATION T. CAIRO-ST. UNITY (2nd).— This match was played on the Unitarian ground, and after a well contested game resulted in a win for the home team by 14 runs. Score :—Frodsham 30, Unity 44.

WARRINGTON T. WIGAN.—The return fixture, as above, was played at Wigan on Saturday, and resulted in a win for the home team. Warrington won the toss, and at half past two S. M. and J. J. Crosfield began batting, in a very bad light. J. J. was caught fourth hall of IstlcCauley's first over, and Clarke was easily taken next ball, two wickets being down for none. Lawton scored four, when he was out the same way as Clarke-3 for 5. A stand was made by Crosfield and Armstrong, 20 runs being put on before S. M. was caught. Jolley quickly scored a couple of twos, when lie retired-5 for 30. Armstrong and Yonge put on 17, and then the former retired with 15 to his credit. Some hard hitting was seen during the time Yonge and Voisey were at the wickets, the former scoring 12, which included two hairs, and the latter 9, which also included a couple of fours. The innings quickly closed for 64. The home team sent in W. Wall and Rennick to face the deliveries of Jolley and Bell. The latter with his first ball clean bowled W. Wall —1 for 3. McCauley joined Rennick, but at 15, the amateur was caught. Halliwell joined the pro. and a stand was made, but at 32 the pro. was out to a very fine catch. Murphy did not stay long, being run out at 38. Italliwell's was the next wicket to fall. His 15 included seven twos and a single, and was a decidedly lucky innings. Knowles was out lbw after scoring 1; and Jackson hit up five before being caught-7 for 60. A. Shaw and Taylor were now together, and quickly put the result out of all doubt, and were not parted until the score had reached 79. Armstrong and Worsley gave very little trouble, the innings closing for 86. The visitors were not as smart in the field as usual, and all their bowlers had hard lines, they: beating the batsmen time after time, but getting no wicket. WIGAN.
