THE CHARGES AGAINST THE CHESHIRE POLICE. EXTR &ORDINARY LETTERS FROM EX-SUPER- INTENDENT EGERTON. The final stage of the inquiry into the allegations made against the Cheshire police by Mr. Slater Lewis was entered upon on Monday at the Chester Castle, before Sir Horatio Lloyd and the other mem- bers of the special committee. A great mass of correspondence was read by the Clerk of the Peace, the first letters being from ex-Chief-Super- intendent Egerton, of Birkenhead, to ex-Inspector O'Donnell, upon which Mr. Slater Lewis said he based his case. In the first letter Superintendent Egerton stated that O'Donnell's case had been treated by the Joint Committee just as he anticipated, and proceeded, "I think vou were unwise in mixing up with the Radical side. You know all the Home Rulers and their supporters hate the police as they do poison—(laughter)—and would be but a rotten stick to lean on from old Gladstone down to the mad lunatic O'Brien—(laughter)—and at present they are greatly in the minority. Perhaps in the long years to come, when neither I liar even yourself inhabit the sublunary globe things may have been changed. We may be then living again, but the mischief is we shan't remember what has oc- curred in this decade. At any rate, you must allow that men like Corbett, Bushell, and Graham—all men who know you and appreciate the good work you have done, and who doubtless would be glad to help you if they could—would be disgusted when they found you had submitted your case to Brunner and Co., who are styled , mischievous rascals, and most assuredly will injure any man they try to befriend, unless indeed they open their purse and do it individually. Any man who has sym- pathy with the police must in these days be a Tory and Unionist, which is the same thing. (Laughter.) As to Large, his clerk, Gosling and Co., you must bear in mind that according to holy writ since our Saviour left this world and returned to heaven , miracles ceased, except in the minds of silly women and superstitious men, and those of the Church who invent and get them up so as to impress the ignorant portion of their flocks, and keep them under their priestly domina- tion—so the worthies you have named must bide their time. And you may possibly live to see your desire on your enemies. You may be sure that Large has been in- fluenced by Hollingsworth again, and I am inclined to think that some one else has not thanked you for bring- ing this man's conduct so prominently before him. , . . . The C.C. has known Hollingsworth's course of life years ago, and has had his own little reason for keeping his eyes shut. You know the old adage, Don't show your grandmother how to suck eggs.' (Laughter.) You know my opinion as to Home Rule. By all means give it, I said so years ago, but first settle with the insane moonlighters now in Parliament : and when they are hung or destroyed by the electric spark try another lot. (Laughter.) I would suggest they should be men selected by the Pontiff ; he, I think, is a sensible man, although a Pope." (Great laughter.) In the course of another letter dated 18th March, 1890, Superintendent Egerton says :—" As regards the strikers no words in my vocabulary could half convey my detes- tation of the hounds. I trust they will get shot down if they begin rioting, as they richly deserve. (Laughter.) The paid delegates who are fattening on the misery they cause don't deserve such an honourable fate. Cuning- hame Graham, Burns, &c., &c., down to the lowest, , agitator in the scale, I would hang along with the Irish members, and Lord Randolph Churchill should be the , executioner. (Great laughter.) That office would suit his tastes, as he is always ready to stab his best friends. (Renewed laughter.) . . . As to Lewis, they have t given him a sop to keep him quiet. (Laughter.) You know when a man becomes troublesome and mischiev- ' ous at St. Stephens, if he possesses talent sufficient to make him dangerous, he always gets a sop such as Foreign Secretary or the governorship of an island. (Laughter.) They have frequently offered old Glad- stone a peerage, and now that his head has commenced to grow—(laughter)—he may probably accept a duke- dom, as if he keeps on he will be too big for his present position. . . . You may have paid attention to my advice, but not heeded it, otherwise you would have now been superintendent of police." Writing under date 29th March, 1890, Egerton says : " I know it is of little use disputing or arguing with you on theological subjects, or trying to convince you how absurd it is to conceive for a moment that the Almighty will trouble about Superintendent Large while he in- habits this world, or his family, or, in fact, any of the children of men. When he is disposed with here God will doubtless find a way of dealing with him according to his deserts, and with all of us when the time comes; but you may depend that every man, so far as the world goes, is the arbiter of his own fate. . . . I certainly feel disappointed at .the way you left the force, and pro- voked at your telling me you had paid attention to my advice. If you had done so you would never have seen a superintendent when he was drunk—simply confined yourself to the detection of crime, in which you had no competition to fear, as very few, if any, could surpass you as to pubs." (Laughter.) In another letter dated sth May, 1890, Superintendent Egerton, after remarking that lie had no idea that the Chief Constable had told O'Donnell that he was a failure as an inspector, and that it was certainly strange that a man who had made so good a sergeant should make so bad an inspector, says :—"You must be aware that if% the Chief Constable is in a position that he has issued general orders, &c., for duties to be performed in accordance with the law of the land, and has always taken measures to carry out what is right to the best of his powers, the charges as against him must of necessity fall to the ground. Of course there are always individuals who do wrong, bobbies who go night working with keepers, accept tips from justices who are game preservers, &c. This class of men—l should say a few of them—will probably be ruined by the immaculate Mr. Lewis—(laughter)—if he has good reliable evidence, but it could not injure Col. Hamersley I therefore feel certain that the Chief-constable will sail clear, and perhaps some fellows who never did or thought you an injury will be ruined. . • . I think you ought to feel pleased that lam not able to attend Chester, not that I could in any way injure your case, but because I am sure I should contra- dict your friends, and I may tell you that lam of opinion , that for councils to get the management of police ' establishments would seal their ruin. A good chief- constable, with sole and entire power, and no appeal,&c., a well-raid force, would prove a good one." Another epistle of the superintendent's contained the following :—" I repeat that assembling men on roads to watch for poachers, otherwise thieves, is a most import- ant duty, but never to consort with keepers, who are the greatest of all poachers themselves, and are frequently in league with poachers. As regards receipts for chief- constables and general inspection, what you name will always occur so long as ill-raid clerks are made out of old soldiers, who if not incompetent and thieves, turn out drinkers. As to the -malpractices at Macclesfield or elsewhere I know nothing, but I do know that no fund was in existence sanctioned at headquarters for rewarding police for the capture of poachers. I have no doubt when constables made good catches on' roads of these thievish fowl- stealers, might or did reward constables for their vigil- ance, and if they still continue the practice I see nothing wrong. I never heard you object to this kind of thing before, any more than to the pounds, shillings,and pence at Christmas. (Laughter.) If all these charges don't dissolve into thin air on close investigation I shall be much surprised, and I think in the end you will regret that you did not take my despised advice. You will also find that your witnesses will deceive you. Men have an objection to cut their own coats when they come to the point, and deny former statements or put different colour on those given perhaps under the influence of whisky toddy and Aympathy, which dies away on reflec- tion afterwards." (Laughter.) After denying that he had prompted O'Donnell on his present action, the super- intendent proceeds—" It has always a shady appearance to wait until you are injured before you complain of malpractices in carrying out the law. I don't mean it is requisite to see those of higher rank if they happen to , get t ight ; this would be certain to make enemies all round. . . . I trust your friends will not drag pre- sent members of the force who have done you no wrong into this inquiry—l mean worthy, straightforward men, such as Costello. If they do, I need not tell you what that means. I merely make this remark from the fact of your eloquent friend—(laughter)—courting privacy rather than publicity, as one would have supposed under the circumstances." Writing at a later stage to O'Donnell, Superintendent Egerton says—" As regards the allegations made as to the shortcomings of the police, referred to so freely in the public press, I can emphatically say that so far as my experience goes these statements are untrue." Inspector O'Donnell, writing to Superintendent Eger- ton on the 7th June, 1890, says :—" I can only express my very great regret at the way you have all along tried to hamper me in the matter, and you now wish if you can to crush me out of any chance I may have of prov- ing to the world the injustice of my treatment at the hands of scamps whose sole object was to get the chief to ruin me, because they thought I would do my duty. How many men might be dismissed the force if all the times they swore, &c., were paraded before the chief for the years they were in the service. I had no intention of making any use of your letters, but having showed ' them to Mr. Lewis he stuck to them, but he assures me 1 he has no intention of using them, but hopes your 1 health will be in such a state as to be able to be present next meeting of the commiteee." Replying to this on the following day, Superintendent , Egerton informs O'Donnell that the correspondence must close, and says:—" I may tell you that may opinion is not altered one iota, and I see but little in your favour from proceeding before the last committee meeting, some decidedly adverse ; as regards drunkenness of individuals who appear to have been already punished, that does not weigh the balance in your case. That is purely a matter of discipline, as I told you, brought on fig- uratively to speak, by running your head against- stone walls. It would have been just as sensible on my part to have kicked up a row when I only got two thirds .of my pay as pension, when I ought to have got the whole for life. . • . As regards the numerous allegations made as to police administration, if asked on my oath

my answer would be, to the best of my personal know- ledge, they were utterly untrue. Another of Superintendent Egerton's letters to O'Don- nell contained the following characteristic observations: —" I have not much faith in the Secretary of State, or, in fact, any ot them. (Laughter.) All men of high or low office are simply placemen, whether they be Whigs, Tories, Radicals, or 'even your favourites, the Home- rulers. (Laughter.) The tatter might possibly be the most honest, if they were not composed greatly of lunatics or assassins. (Great laughter.) I refer to the heads of the party. In your case I trust I may be mistaken. As regards the County Council, until a special act is passed rescind- ing the County police acts in general, and the old Cheshire , constabulary act in particular for this county, they have no power to interfere with the police in any matter of discipline or order, the Chief-constable for the time being, whoever he may be, being supreme, and as long as he is one of the right sort I maintain it is thebest system for the men. A nice state of things would be the result if every pettifogging fellow like our friend were a master. In my opinion it would be worse than being the inhabitant of a small hell—(laughter)—with this difference, there you are supposed to be stationery, but in the police a man can get leave to quit." (Renewed laughter.) The last letter of Superintendent Egerton was written to Mr. Reginald Potts, clerk of the peace for the county. He states his belief that O'Donnell had made a great mis- take in the course he was pursuing, that he was acting unwisely in allowing Mr. Lewis to influence him, that if he could have anticipated that O'Donnell would have been dishonourable enough to commit a gross breach of good faith by showing his private letters to others he should not have corresponded with hint, or taken any in- terest in his affair, and that his only object throughout had been to prevent O'Donnell from making a fool of himself. Concluding, he says, "As regards my political opinions, lam not ashamed of them. If lam a disap- pointed policeman I have no intention of parading my disappointment before the Cheshire County Council. As to charges, I have made none, except perhaps against Mr. Lewis, who I believe inspired O'Donnell's letters, except the last, for the purpose of fishing. lam at a loss to understand what Mr. Lewis found in my letters on which to base his appeal to the Secretary of State." k In reply to Mr. Lewis, Col. Hamersley said he did not think the Government Inspector would object to the en- tries in the officer's journals to the effect that the men had been watching for suspicious persons. He thought iat this stage of the proceedings he should read a letter he had received from the Government Inspector. By the consent of the committee, Col. Hamersley read the letter, which was as follows : Longstone Lodge, Bakewell, 9th August, 1890 Dear Colonel Hamersley,—With reference to the state- ments that have been made during the inquiry into the conduct of the Cheshire police by some ex-members of the force that they had been in the habit of entering in their journals that they were engaged "watching for suspicious characters" when they were really looking after poachers, in order to "deceive the Government inspector," I have to say that I should not have been in the least deceived by such an entry, knowing perfectly 'well that a poacher is usually a" suspicious character," not particular as to what he keeps himself to, and that should the police of any county suspect that such per- sons were out at night it would be their duty to watch for them, and so prevent fowl robberies and other offences for the prevention of which and the general pro- tection of life and property the police are maintained. If any constable so far broke the regulations of the police as to go on land and act as a gamekeeper, and then made a false entry in his diary, I should not believe him on his oath, but my experience of seventeen years' police work precludes my believing that such a practice can be carried on, or that any but the very smallest number of constables and a still smaller proportion of officers could be capable of so acting, or would run the risk of the instant dismissal from their force which would assuredly follow a discovery of such disgraceful conduct by thei chief constables.—Believe me. yours sincerely, C. J. LEGGE, H.M. Indpector of Constabulary. The Chairman (to Mr. Lewis) : You will not hereafter complain that O'Donnell's letters are-not put in. Mr. Lewis: Certainly not. At the same time I should not like the committee to have the idea that there is any- thing in O'Donnell's letters that I am keeping hack. Mr. Beckett : O'Donnell s letters are.not given to the other side. Some discussion here ensued respecting the game fund, whereupon Mr. Graham remarked 'that he was under the impression that the fund had been;discontinu- ed some years ago. Mr. Lewis : Oh, no. Mr. Graham : Certainly that was our impression. Mr. Beckett was of the same opinion, but if there was a treasurer in existence up to Jannary of this year, it altered the whole thing. Mr. Lewis : I stated in my letters that the fund had existed, and Col. Hamersley has admitted in the letter to the Home Secretary that that fund did exist, and has been stopped as soon as I called attention to it. The Chairman: My impression from the evidence of Constable Breeze, who said it was closed for some years, was that it had been closed for some time. Mr. Fletcher mentioned that that impression arose from the fact that all the constables from Macclesfield said they had not received; anything from the fund for three or four years. Mr. Lister : Can we have a return of the'fund Col, Hamersley : I know nothing of the fund. Mr. Beckett : It is of the essence of this inquiry that this fund should be searched out. Ex-Inspector, O'Donnell, recalled,said he never reported a reward to the present Chief-Constable, but he did to a Chief-constable—the late Captain Smith. Mr. Fletcher : That is very ancient. O'Donnell said he received a reward from the late Mr. Shaw for capturing poachers in Wirral. He reported the reward, and got permission to accept it, minus the 10 per cent. deduction. In answer to Mr. Lewis, Col. Hamersley said he had not written to the Government inspector, and the letter was not sent to him at his request. The Chief-constable added that so great depredations had been caused by poachers in the county during the night that on two occasions he had received letters drawing his attention to the matter from Sir William Harcourt and Mr. Matthews, Home Secretaries, based on complaints as to " nocturnal depredations," made by Lord Stanley of Alderley and farmers in the district. Supt. Walker was next called, and denied having written to anybody saying that he dare not move in the inquiry. Police Constable Boyle WAS called. Examined by Mr. Lewis, he said he remembered meeting him one night and having conversation with him. He did not remember whether it was after one of Mr. Lewis's political meetings. Mr. Lewis: Did not you say to me that you had been watching for poachers for 27 consecutive nights ? Witness: I said nothing of the kind to you. Mr. Lewis : You gol Get out of the court at once ; you are a liar, sir ! Witness : When I speak, I tell the truth. Mr. Lewis: I am sorry I lost my temper, but I feel it very strongly indeed. This man told see so with his own lips, and I told Mr. Jeffs, of Helsby, the same night. That is a very good instance of police witness, that's all. I am very sorry that this little thing should have caused this incident at this minute. Mr. Slater Lewis then summed up his case, and in the course of a speech of five hours' duration he entered minutely into the details of the evidence, and generally contended that his charges against the police of drunken- ness and irregularities at Runcorn, and of assisting gamekeepers in watching for poachers to the neglect of their own duties, had been substantiated. Mr. Fletcher proposed to address the committee with reference to what had been alleged against Superinten- dent Hollingworth, but the Committee ruled that it was unnecessary, as Hollingworth was merely an individual member of the force. The inquiry then terminated, and some time must of course elapse before the committee's decision will be made known.
MURDER AND SUICIDE AT BRADFORD.

Late on Saturday particulars of a dreadful tragedy at Lingbob Wilsden, a small village near Bingley, in the West Riding of Yorkshire, became known. The victim was the wife of a man name Hezekiah Sutcliffe, quarry- man, and after the deed Sutcliffe went and committed suicide by drowning in a mill dam near his home. The details to hand show that the couple have only resided in Wilsden for some nine months, previously having resided at Egypt. in Thornton, near Bradford. On Friday night the couple went shopping to Thornton Heights, and seemed on friendly terms; but at 11-30 o'clock on the same evening the children went to bed i leaving their parents quarrelling. When the children awakened next morning, shortly after eight o'clock, they gave information to the neigh- bours that their mother was dead in bed. About half ,an hour previous some men had noticed a body in the mill dam, at Birk's Head. The dam is four feet deep with water, and the man's head was firmly embedded in the mud at the bottom, with his legs sticking out of the water. On being recovered it was identified as that of Sutcliffe. The woman appears to have been strangled, ' there being marks on the throat of a thumb and fingers. They leave six children, two of the eldest residing away from home. The woman is given an excellent character by the people in the district. At the inquest, on Monday, on the body of Hezekiah Sutcliffe, the jury found that Sutcliffe murdered his wife and afterwards committed suicide whilst of unsound mind.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

The sensation of last Saturday was the defeat of Sur- rey by Yorkshire. It was a thoroughly well-deserved victory, earned against formidable opponents, and under circumstances which at one time seemed to preclude all hope of success. They had to go in a second time against a deficit of 15 8 runs, and yet played so well , that Surrey were p in to get runs—and failed. It was the greatest failure of the season, and the Yorkshire executive will, perhaps, recognise the soundness of Lord Hawke's judgment in preferring Harrison to the "fledgling "Mr. Jackson. The ground exactly suited Harri- son after the rain, and he really won the match for his county. George Ulyett played a grand innings; and the performance of the Tykes in this match was quite worthy of the traditions of the, county.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

The Blackburn Rovers- tean-illo—r as many of them as have been got together up to date—are busy practising on the Hole-P-th -Wall Ground, once the quarters of the now defunct Olympic team. Lowe, of Denton, has signed as goal-keeper, and it is expected that ,when the season proper opens the team will include more than one new player.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

Not content with having secured all the safety bicycle championships, and lowered all the old records, R. J. Macredy, the great Irish rider, must needs conquer him- self. After winning the half mile safety handicap at the Bristol Bicycle Club meeting from scratch, in lmin. 12 1-ssec., he turned out at the close of the sports to attempt to again lower his own two mile safety record. In spite of a heavy track, consequent on a storm which had taken place a few hours before, he actually suc- ceeded in getting inside his recently established record by 2 2-ssec., riding the full distance in smin. 12 4-ssec. The performance is a magnificent one, and one wonders what the pneumatic tyred machines will eventually do, as someone is almost sure to be found in the future with capabilities fully equal, and possibly superior, to those of Macredy.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

_ A lot of people will be sorry to hear that R. Pilling,the Lancashir,; wicket-keeper, is till far from well, and we understa:id it is his intention to have a voyage to Aus- tralia, In the hope that it may recruit his health. We sincerely trust it will,

It may be news that thegreatest of all great cricketers, W. G. Grace, was in his youth a, capital runner and jumper, and it would seem as though the athletic mantle of the father has descended on the son, for at the Bristol meeting W. G. Grace, junior, won the 220 yards handicap very easily, and ran second in the mile, the winner being J. Mealyer, of Bath.

A writer in the "Athletic News" says "When in I London last week I came across Mr. Ayton, who, it will be remembered, was treasurer to the Maori football team when the latter were in England. He has just returned from New Zealand, aad he tells me that a lot of trouble was caused by one or two of the team before the men got home, Keogh being the principal offender. Two of the team, Webster and Kauraria, died soon after their return to New Zealand. Mr. Ayton says that no money was I made out of the trip."

The great event at Witton Football Sports on Saturday was the 120 yards scratch race for the Fielden Challenge Cup. This trophy was originally presented in 1888, and was then won by Wilcock after a great struggle with Staveacre and Southworth. Last year Southworth was successful, but he has this season been very unfortunate, and seems to have lost every vestige of his old form. On Saturday the competitors were Sergeant Hartley, of St. Helens, H. M. Warner, Salford Harriers, and Craven, of Bradford. A perfectly even start was made, and Warner and Hartley raced right away, a neck and neck struggle ending in a most popular victory for the "champion of the British Army," Warner being about six inches behind, whilst Craven was beaten off.

div.head: STRUCK DOWN IN BITRMAH.
div.p: STRUCK DOWN IN BITRMAH.

Beethoven composed music he was too deaf to hear, and the fastest steam craft in the world was built (both hull and machinery) by an American who has been per- fectly blind for many years. Nevertheless, the one would have been the better for his hearing, and the other for his sight. A soldier may be a model of patriotism and courage, but of what use is he in an army if he can- not carry a musket? Allow us to illustrate the point by a short story. Mr. John Hodson, now thirty-two years of age, was born at Warboys, in Huntingdonshire. When he was twenty- five years old he took work as a navvy under the great railway contractors, Messrs. Lucas, Aird, Sons, and Co., of Westminster, and remained under them seven years. He then enlisted in her Majesty's 51st Regiment, and went with it to India in 1883. He assisted in the Bur- mah Expedition in 1885-6, and was at Mandalay when King Theebaw surrendered. With this explanation we will now let Mr. Hodson tell his own tale. He says : After reaching Shorebo I began to feel badly. I had a sinking sensation at the pit of the stomach, and was so drowsy I could scarcely hold my head up. I had pain in my right side and under the shoulder blades, lost my spirits, and took a gloomy view of everything. I could neither eat nor sleep. I lay in bed awake night after night. My liver was perfectly torpid, skin and eyes yellow, tongue badly coated, heart irregular, no appe- tite, cold extremities, sickness, vomiting, and an inces- sant diarrhcea ; with these symptoms I was in bed four months in the year 1887. In the Hospital I was treated by the Regimental physi- cian, and was visited by Dr. Bell, of the Indian Govern- ment, who said I was suffering from dysentery. I became so weak I could hardly stand, and passed nothing but slime from the bowels. No treatment availed to stop the diarrhcea. Finally I was sent home, and arrived :at Gosport in Dec., 1888, and was transferred ;to the hos- pital there until Feb., 1889, when I was discharged as incurable and placed in the Army Reserve. I returned to Warboys, and, feeling a trifle better, tried to work. But I soon had to give up. I became so thin that people who had known me for years did not recognise me. My old friends and mates said," Hodson, you needn't trouble to buy any more clothes to wear in this world. The next wit you'll want will be made of wood." Still I ate something, of course, but it gave me no strength. After eating I was often .obliged to leave the table hurriedly,so severe were the griping, gnawing pains that seized me. My father and mother were alarmed at

my condition. I consulted a physician at Warboys, who gave me some medicine, which, however, made no im- pression upon my complaint. • I then went to Mr. Nicholl, the chemist, of Warboys, (now of Croydon), whc said, " You had better try Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup." I got a bDttle and took it, but it seemed to have no effect. Mr. Nieholl said, "Try it again, I have such confidence in it that I will give you the second bottle free of charge." He did so, and before I hut taken the half of the second bottle I began to feel better. I got a third bottle, and before I had finished it I had so much im- proved that I was asked to go back to my work. But I was afraid, and said, No, wait until lb ave used three bottles more ; for this wonderful medicine is doing what nothing else in India or England has been able to do—it healing me feorn the very depths where I was ill and dying. I kept on with Mother Seigel, and indeed a Mother she truly is to the suffering. The fifth bottle was gone at last, and I presented myself to the astonished people of Warboys as robust, strong, and well as ever I was in all my life. I returned to my work, and my comrades looked upon me as one risen from the dead. "What has done this for you ?" they asked, with wondering eyes. " owe my life and health to Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup," I answered, "and lam willing all the world should hear me say so." ' I have never lost an hour's work since, and will gladly reply to any letters of inquiry addressed to John Hodson, Warboys, Huntingdonshire. To the above true and faithful account of Mr. Hod- son's experience it is only necessary to add a word of , explanation. His real disease was indigestion and dyspepsia, brought on by change of climate, habits, and . food. The diarrhea, of which he speaks, is (strange as it may seem) an effect and symptom of prolonged and prevailing constipation. It is nature's last efforts to free the bowels of their terrible and poisonous load. In
this crisis Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup came to the rescue, and not a day too soon.

div.head: SANITARY CONGRESS.
div.p: SANITARY CONGRESS.

At the Sanitary Congress at Brighton on Tuesday, Dr. Poore delivered a very interesting address on "The liv- ing earth." Mr. James Turton reads paper on " Some points in relation to septic and infectious diseases," and one on the sanitary advance of Brighton was read by Dr. Ewart. On the motion of Mr. Henriques, a resolu- tion was adopted recommending the Council to aid in promoting a Bill in Parliament for the purpose of making landlords liable for all sanitary improvements on their property. A large number of members of the Sanitary Congress on Thursday inspected the Corporation Water- works at Brighton, and more were present at a brilliant soirée given by the Mayor in the Royal Pavilhon. Medi- cal officers of health met in conference and among other matters, the importance of education in hygiene among the young and the increase of .diptheria. Section 2of the Congress heard papers on the "Treat- rent of Sewage" and on "Industrial Dwellings."

ALLEGED SERIOUS WOUNDING CASE.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Wednesday morning, a widow named Annie, or Frances Savory, who lives at 7 Buckley's-yard, Haydock-st., was brought up in custody on a charge of unlawfully wounding Ellen Titchett, wife of John Titchett, • flogger and slater, also living in ilaydock-st. Mr. Hunt (the chief constable) said that on Tuesday morning Mrs. Titchet asked prisoner to pledge something, in order to get drink. The prisoner was an- noyed at the suggestion at first, but ultimately a pair of , child's boots were pledged, and the two set to drinking. r At about 4.30 in the afternoon the women were seen to ' go into the house in Buckley's-yard, and shortly after- wards Mrs. Titchett was seen to run out with blood flowing from a wound on the cheek. From what he (Mr. H.int) could gather, she had been hit by prisoner with a jug. Complainant was taken to the Infirmary. • and as she was unable to appear he asked for a remand- -Dr. J. T. Smith, from the Infirmary, said that there was a wound on Mrs. Titchett's right cheek, about inches long, extending from the middle of the cheek to, ' the edge of the jaw. The wound was deep, and a good deal of violence had been used. It went down to the bone, and divided one of the arteries of the face. Such an injury might have been caused by a jug.—Other formal evidence was given, and prisoner was then re- manded, the magistrates intimating that they werepre- pared to accept bail—two sureties in £lO each. Yesterday morning Savory surrendered to her bail, and was now charged with an aggravated assault. Mr- ' Percy Davies represented her, and, on her behalf, pleaded not guilty. The complainant, who was said to be now' out of danger, gave evidence to the effect that on the • afternoon in question Mrs. Savory accused her of having taken some coppers belonging to her, and then struck her on the face with a quart jug. When doing so, she said "I never strike without I draw blood. That's John Bull." In answer to Mr. Davies, complainant denied that she was drunk on the occasion in question. In defence Mr. Davies contended that the two women had been drinking together very freely, and that the complainant injured herself by falling over a chair, the wound being caused by contact with a rocker.—After the magistrates had consulted together, Alderman Harrison, who presided. said that in his opinion there never was an assault more clearly proved in this world. That was his opinion decidedly. He was sorry to say that the two gentlemen who sat with him did not agree with him, and thought that the case should be dismissed. Having expressed-hie opinion, he had no alternative but to say that the case would be dismissed.—Dr. Gornall said that after what had fallen from Mr. Harrison he should like to give his opinion why he could not support a conviction. It was because there had not been proper medical evidence brought before the Bench. He should always decline to take the evidence of police officers on questions of that kind. When medical evidence could not be obtained, then they must take the evidence of officers. He thought this was a proper case for medical evidence to have been called.—Mr. Davies There has really been no evidence at all as to what took place.—The Chief Constable said he thought it right to say that Dr. Smith held himself in readiness in case Ihe. was asked to come. If the magistrates had thought 11; essential, he would have sent for him.—Mr. Davies: am very pleased he is not here.—The case was then dis. missed.

div.head: WARRINGTON BREWSTER SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BREWSTER SESSIONS.

• THE FRESH APPLICATIONS REFUSED. RENEWALS OBJECTED TO. The annual meeting of the Licensing Committee for the borough of Warrington was held on iTues- " day morning, in the Irlarn-st. Sessions-room, which ' was crowded with persona who take an active in- terest in the matters brought forward at the Brewster Sessions. Amongst thoSe in Court were the Revs. J.J.Langham, John Yonge, J. Warnock, *-John Gunnell, and J. W. Varley, Councillors H. Robert Mr. John Walker, Mr. W. Diggle, Mr. W. Roberts, Councillor Joseph Taylor (president of the Licensed Victuallers' Association), and several pub- licans and representatives of Wilderspool brewery. The Licensing Committee consisted of the Mayor (Alderman Francomb). Alderman Holmes, Alderman Burgess, Alderman Chandley, Councillor Monks. Captain Ridgway, and Mr. John Fairclough, all of ' whom were present. ▪ THE RENEWAL OF EXISTING LICENSES—OBJECTIONS. • At the commencement of the proceedings,on the Clerk asking if there were any objections to the renewal of ale- house licences, Mr. Arthur Browne said he appeared on behalf of the Rev. John Yonge, Mr. John Walker, and Mr. Richard Storey to object to the renewal of a number of existing licenses. The Committee would re- member that at the last licensing meeting a number of licenses were objected to by a Committee appointed by the justices, and the question was adjourned for the pur- pose of the grounds of opposition being gone into. Ow- ing, however, to some technical error, the grounds of ob- jection could not be gone into, and it was ruledthat the objections could not be sustained. The Temperance Federation, felt that, such proceedings having taken place last year, again this year the same procedure would be carried out, but they found that notice of objection had not been given. Their only duty now was to - object to the renewal of some of the old licenses that were objected to last time, on account of non-suita- bility of' the houses, non-requirement, because they ' were not structurally adapted for the purpose, and I also on account of betting and the meeting of bad characters. He should ask the Committee to adjourn the renewal of the licenses he was about to name -till the 23rd September, when he should be prepared to go into the matter. He objected to the renewal of the following licenses :—Eliza Ruske% Shakespeare Inn ; John Allen, the Pelican, Buttermarket-st. ; Chas. Roddy, Bull's Flead,Bridge-st.; Hy.Gittens,Swan inn, Bridge-st. ; :Wm. Jones, Curriers' Arms, Buttermarket-St.; and Eliza- beth Earl, Fox Inn, Butterrnarket-St. Objection was Made to there houses last year, and they now felt also bound to object to the renewal of the license of Edward Bullock, of the Royal Exchange, Golden-grove. In the case of Ruske% the license was not required for the necessities of the neighbourhood, the premises were not Structurally adapted for the business, and the house was frequented by low and bad characters. In Mr. Allen's case the license was not required , and the premises were not structurally adapted for the purposes of a license. 'The same applied in the case of Mr. Roddy. The license of the Swan Inn was not required, the premises were unfit for a public-house, and were used for betting pur- l:loses, and the house being up a private entry, away from the main street, the police had not sufficient supervision over it. In the case of Jones, the license was not re- quired, and the premises were not suitable. The same applied to the Fox Inn. In the case of the Royal Ex- change, the objections were that the license was not required, the premises were not structurally adapted for the purpose, Sic., and that the premises were used for the purposes of betting. The Rev. John Yonge and Mr. John Walker having formally objected on oath to the renewal of the licenses named, the Committee adjourned the consideration of them until th 3 23rd Sept. All the other existing licenses were then renewed. THE NEW APPLICATIONS. THE PROPOSED NEW HOTEL FOR BATTERSBY- LANE. Mr. Swift, barrister, Liverpool (instructed by Messrs. Robert Davies, Sharp, Kirkconnel, and Co.), applied on behalf of Mr. John Sampson for a new victualler's Provisional license for an hotel proposed to be built in Battersby-laste, and Mr. Browne opposed the application OR behalf of Messrs. Furness, Siddall, Joseph Titchett, Councillor Garner, and others. Mr. Swift asked the Committee to agree to the removal of the license of the Green Dragon in Bridge-st., to the hotel it was proposed to build in Battersby-lane. The Green Dragon was an Old-established inn, and was the property of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., Limited, and the land in, Battersby-lane, upon which the house would be erected,l belonged to them. If this application was granted it I was proposed to build an hotel in place of the.Grees Dragon; and in doing so the company desired to carry I out what appeared to be generally regarded as desirable,l namely, tO find new houses for new districts, I and to remove licenses from districts which had already a considerable number of licenses. The company would also allow to lapse a beer-house called the White Bear, in Buttermarket-st. Thus the number of licenses would be reduced by one,- . as the Battersby-lane license would exist in place of the Green Dragon and the White Bear. His next application would b. a similar one with regard to other premises, and in that case Messrs. Greenall and Company proposed to give up one licensed house, the Fox Inn, and two off- beer licenses, so that if both applications were granted the number of licenses would be reduced by three. The firm would hold two licenses instead of five. The off- licenses related to premises in Hoyle-st., off Bewsey- road. In regard to the application of Mr. John Sampson, Mr. Swift said that when the hotel was built stabling Would be provided for three horses, and the cost of the hotel would be about £2,500. The neighbourhood was already populous, and the population was still increasing. There were only one or two empty houses in the district. Warrington was not over-stocked with public-houses in prdportion to the number which existed in other cities and boroughs in Lancashire and Cheshire. The number In Warrington, according to a return made in the House of Commons during the_present year, was 3.2 per 1,000, and that was below the average of Lancashire and Cheshire. There were many places where the proportion Was greater. An objection which might be raised in the Case of Warrington was Pat the public-houses were clus- tered together more closely than was absolutely dasirable„ and the proposal the company now made was to relieve' the centre of the town from any possible plethora in that respect. It should be understood that the figures 3-2 in- cluded both the beersellers and the licensed victuallers. The number of beersellers was unusually large in Warring- ton, as therewere 70 beerhouses to 80 full-licensed houses. At common law any person might sell liquors, but for the good of the general community the law restrained the universal sale. It was, however, never intended to deprive the public of a reasonable supply of drink for their requirements. He wished the Bench to take a liberal view of the situation, and of the intention of the Legislature, and to satlsfy every public requirement.— Mr. Browne took a technical objection. Mr. Swift was applying for a removal. There could be no removal to a place which had not been built. The only way to get a license for premises which had not been erected was by applying for a provisional grant.--The been argued, and the Clerk havino, ruled against having Mr. Browne, Mr. Down, managing director for Messrs. Green- s% Whitley, and Co., was called. In aswer to ques- tions, he said the White Bear paid, and he should also I say the Green Dragon was doing so. The renewal of the license of the Pox Inn was objected to by the magis- trates last year, and thetwo houses in Hoyle-street had out-door licenses. These were tied houses. Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. had no interest in the retailing of spirits.—Formal evidence having been given, the next application was proceeded with. MESSRS, OREENALL'S CATHERINE-ST. APPLICATION. This was made by Mr. Swift, on behalf of Messrs. Greenall and Co., for a full license to be granted to Mr. George Pilling for a hotel proposed to be built in Catherine-st. by Messrs. Greenall and Co. Counsel said the nearest public-house was 900 yards from the site of the new hotel in Catherine-st. In this case it had not occurred to the promoters to be necessary to provide stabling. Should it become necessary to do so, however, they could be easily added. In the meantime, it was Proposed to erect a good hotel suitable to the _present requirements of the district. It would cost £2,800.— Formal evidence was taken. THE APPLICATION OF MRS. Lavrroie, OF THE GROVE. The third application was made by Mr. Segar, barrio- ter, (Liverpool), instructed by Messrs. Percy Davies and Forshaw), and was on behalf of Mrs. Susan Lawton, of the Grove beerhouse, Bewsey-road, for a full ale-house license. Ile pointed out that this was the 13th time the application had been made. The full alehouse license Was once granted by the Bench, but the magistrates at the adjourned meeting declined to confirm. The Grove was a long way from any fully licensed public-house,and the neighbourhood had received the distinction of being " spotted " by Messrs. Greenall and Company, who in their generous anxiety for the morals and convenience of the public had seized upon it as one where their goods eliould be sold. The nearest public-house to the Greve Was 660 yards off, namely, the Three Pigeons. Bewsey- road was the centre of a district containing about , 3,000 persons. The Grove had been licensed for 14 • Years, and Mr. Elijah Lawton, who died in December, --V 18,88, carried on the business for many years. Since his 'death it had been conducted by his widow, to whom no Objection could be made, as she was a person quite suit- able to hold the license asked for. Nearly all the public- houses in the town were situated in batches' but this Was a district remarkably free from licensed premises. 1 That the demand exceeded the present supply was ' • - proved by the face that Messrs. Greenall were so anxious • ba put their licensed house there, and were willing to give up no end ofihouses that paid them admirably for the purpose of supplying this district,which they thought would bring in still more profit. He argued that they thought those other licenses were bad, and that was the reason of their giving up the White Bear, and the Green Dragon, and all the other wild animals. (Laughter.) If they offered to give them up simply because they thought the sale of drink was no advantage to the Public, then their position was inconsistent with the application they had just put forth. The premises of the Grove were well situated for a licensed house, but Messrs. Wagstaffe, the owners, were willing to make any • alterations that might be suggested, and proposed to

r I spend £1,500 to make the house more beautiful still. If a license was to be granted in that neighbourhood at all, it was.clear that the Grove should have it. It was rather coot for great persons who had hundreds of licenses tp try to persuade the Bench to grant them anotherould to waive a license in respect to premises that had been so long off-licensed, and in respect to which applications had so often been made. People-now purchased beer, and drank it in the road way or on the adjacent spare ground, but If they could go oa the premises the public would not be annoyed by that sort of thing.—Mrs. Lawton, in the course of her evidence, said there was stabling near the house and room for a bowling green. She had frequent applications for supplies of spirits. COUNCILLOR BOLTON'S APPLICATION. j

Mr. Segar then applied, on behalf of Mr. William Bolton, for a full alehouse license to off-licensed premises, 112 and 114 Battersby-lane. The applicant was a brewer, he had several public-houses, and he was known to carry on the trade with great care. The nearest beer-house was 480 yards away, and the nearest public-house was 580 yards distant, and the aptilication was made for pre- mises which were situated in the midst of a large popu- lation. This was the fourth time the application had been made. He contended that there was no immorality in drinking intoxicants: people would drink notwith- standing what might be said to the contrary. He did not ask that they should be allowed to get drunk, but that if they wished to have drink they should be able to get it. It seemed to him that prima facie Mr. Bolton had made out a grand case, which the magistrates would do well to nobly and magnanimously listen to. The wants of this neighbourhood also had been" spotted" by Messrs. Gteenall. Mr. Bolton was willing to give up a fully- licensed house if the application was granted, and he proposed to spend £BOO on alterations and improvements. —Mr. Bolton gave evidence in support of the application, and said he had carried on business in Warrington as a brewer for many years. He purchased the property in questiod in the year 1882. It was then a licensed house. It had been licensed since 1874. There was a large popu- lation in the district, and many vacant pieces of land would soon be built upon, and the population would still further increase. He proposed to give up the Royal Exchange in the Market-place, if the present application was granted. He had only acquired that house a few weeks; indeed, he had not yet got absolute possession of it. The Cheshire Lines Wagon works were in the district of Battersby-lane. Mr. Segar : Do people drink more or less when they are on or off the premises? It depends upon the amount of money they have to spend—(laugh- ter)—Given a man who is not d. teetotaller, the amount of drink he will consume will depend upon his wages rather than anything else? The amount of money he has for the purpose of supplying his appetite for drink. —Those gentlemen who are heads of works or majors, and so on, have either wine cellars or teetotal principles (laughter). I think they have no teetotal principles, but they are dogs in the manger (laughter),

div.head: APPLICATION FOR GROCER'S LICENSE.
div.p: APPLICATION FOR GROCER'S LICENSE.

Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, applied, on behalf of Mr. J. Edward Hopkins, of 12, Horsemarket-st., for a grocer's license (six days) to sell winos, spirits, and sweets off the premises.—Mr. Hopkins gave evidence as to the rateable value •ff the premises; and In answer to Mr. Browne, he said he was the manager for the Home and Colonial Company. He was the tenant, and was responsible for the management of the premises: The stock in the shop did not belong to him. If a license was granted, and he was fined £5 for an offence, he would find that amount. —Mr. Browne: Are there sufficient goods on the pre- mises belonging to you personally to make good any fine up to £so,which the magistrates ha.ve power to impose? —Applicant: I should be able to satisfy them.

div.head: MR ALEXANDRA BERARDI:I'SE.
div.p: MR ALEXANDRA BERARDI:I'SE.

Mr. James Taylor, of the Alexandra beerhouse, Scot- land-road, applied for a license entitling him to sell wine on and off the premises.—The Chief Constable said the premises were formerly known as the Gun Inn. They belonged to Messrs. Greenell and Co.—ln answer to Mr. Browne, applicant said this was not an attempt to get in the thin end of the wedge before applying for a full ale- house license. ' THE OPPOSITION. Mr. Browne then addressed the Bench, and asked them to refuse to grant any of the licenses. He said the Bewsey-road applications had been made time after time, but no fresh evidence had been adduced that morning to show that the colleagues of the present Licensing Com- mittee had made a mistake in refusing to grant new licenses. The same remark applied to the Grove, a full license to which had been refused time after time, and the whole bench of magistrates refused to confirm what was granted by the Licensing Committee two years ago. No fresh grounds had been given for granting the applications for licenses to premises in Battersby-lane, while with regard to Mr. Hop- kins' request, he asked the Bench if they intended to graut a license to a man who was neither the owner nor occupier of a shop, and who had no goods about him except what belonged to the company. If they did so it would be establishing a bad precedent, and any per- son could come forward and apply for such a license. Messrs. Milling and Company, Mr. Peter Leg,h, and Mr. Brown, of the Old Coffee House, had similar licenses,and he asked the Bench te say that no fresh one was neces- sary. With regard to Mr. Taylor, he had only been at the Alexandra five weeks, and what, therefore, did he know about the requirements of the case? His object in applying for a wine license was simply to get in the thin edge of the wedge after which he would apply for a full license. Messrs. wedge, and Company seemed to be very generous in offering to give up houses that did not pay.—Mr. Jenkins contended that Mr. Hop- kins was perfectly qualified to hold a license such as that asked for. It was impossible for the company for whom he acted as manager to hold a license. The Bench could not grant it to the company. That was, he thought, a sufficient answer to Mr. Browne's objection. It was the invariable rule to grant a license to the person who managed the business on behalf of the company. THE MAGISTRATES' DECIDE.
4.nor

The magistrates then retired to consider their decision, and on their return, in about six or seven minutes, the Mayor said : I have to state that the wholt of the ap- plications are refused. The annual report of the Chief Constable, which was taken as read, was published in our last issue. • RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

.The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were present the Rev. John Wm. Tanner, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. Taylor, Aaron, Lewis, P. Hall, Grice, Brandreth, J. Hall, H. Linaker (clerk), and H. G. Linaker (deputy clerk).

div.head: COUNTY COUNCIL _HATE,
div.p: THE COUNTY COUNCIL _HATE,

Mr. Brandreth said the Finance Committee had ex- amined the County Council account, which amounted to £2,552 3s. Id., being an increase of £358 16s. 11d. over the corresponding period last year, and £2Bl 3s. id. more than was estimated for. This, however,was better than last half year, when the amount was £2,000 more than was estimated for. The Committee recommended the payment of the amount, as they had a balance of £3,905 15s. 2d. in the treasurer's hands.—Carried. - - - • --

div.head: -UNPAID CA.-PO FARMERS AGAIN.
div.p: -UNPAID CA.-PO FARMERS AGAIN.

Mr. Brandreth said he wished to draw attention to the number of unpaid calls, due on the 6th August. The township of Alvanley had not paid the call of £4B, Bud- worth £49, Weston £236.—Mr. Taylor: Summons them. —Mr. Aaron : Weston has paid. (Laughter.)—Mr. Taylor : It was not at the last meeting.—Mr.Brandreth : Oh, yes, it is paid ; it is entered in the book. Frodsham Lordship had not paid the call of £76, and Halton £45. The assistant overseer of the latter township wrote that many could not pay until they had thrashed. (Laughter.) —The Deputy Clerk: Until they are thrashed. (Renewed laughter).—Mr. Brandreth: The writer goes on to say " Certainly our Guardian is not so situated but that he might, (laughter) so that we might have paid the high- way call at all events. However, we will not give you the trouble of writing again if possible—(laughter) .—A member: Who is the Guardian ?—Mr. Brandreth : Mr. Parr. (Loud laughter).—Mr. Brandreth went on to say that Kingsley had not paid the call of £l2s.—Mr. Grice : Have not you thrashed yet, Mr. Hall ?—(laughter)—Mr. Brandreth; I think they want thrashing. The follow- ing calls are also paid :—Kingswood, £39; Moore, £B7; ' Norley, £88; Preston Brook, £B4 ; Walton Superior, £42; Whitley Inferior, £42.—Mr. Aaron said the whole of the townships were usually behind with their calls and he did not think it right that Runcorn and Weston and a few others should pay the calls when due, and those townships should continually delay payment. At Weston they had an excellent assistant overseer, and he always got the money in ; and at those townships where the money was not got in,it was the assistant overseer's fault. He moved that if the outstanding calls were not paid within 14 days, the overseers concerned be sum- moned.—Mr. Hall said under the circumstance that the farmers had not thrashed yet, and with this kind of weather there was no signs of them thrashing, they might give them a little more time. Farmers were very awkwardly fixed at the present time as regarded getting money in.—Mr. Aaron: It is every year alike.— Mr. Hall: Things are going from bad to worse. (Laugh- ter.)—Mr. Taylor said the calls were not paid more throag,h carelessness than poverty, and he protested against Runcorn and a few other townships paying their money to date, while others did not pay for a month or two afterwards. There were plenty of hardships in Runcorn, and some people felt very strongly on this matter, and he thought they had a grievance. He seconded Mr. Aaron's proposition. He should be glad to make a standing rule that if calls were not paid within 14 days of the date due, summonses be Issued.—The Clerk suggested that the matter be left over for a fortnight.—Mr. Taylor : Suppose none of the townships paid, what would be the posi- tion of the Board, would they have a balance to pay accounts.—The Clerk said they would not.—Mr. Taylor: Why should not ad the other townships act on the same principle as these.—The Clerk : We should of necessity issue summonses.—Mr. Brandreth asked that the subject should be adjourned until next meeting. The I discussion would appear in the newspapers and it would do good.—Mr. Aaron said as Mr. Brandreth was the chairman of the Finance Committee,he would withdraw his motion.—Mr. Tanner said the farmers in his district were not a bit better off than in other places, and they had never been behind in their payments. (Hear, hear.) The assistant overseer . was a very good man—Mr. Aaron : It is the fault of the assistant overseers.—Mr. Taylor: Next time after first fortnight I should move that summonses be issued.

According to dispatches from San Salvador, President Ezeta has signed the protocol of peace with Guate- mala. A Lowestoft lugger on Thursday towed into that port the brigantine Laura, of Southampton, found abandoned off the Dudgeon. Dr. Ross, ot Wetherall, near Carlisle, has died from the effects of injuries received on Tuesday night by being thrown out of a dog cart when returning from visiting a patient near Dalston, Cumberland. A St. Petersburg telegram says the Czar and tho German Emperor have discusted the prospects of European peace exhaustively, with the result of creating a feeling that peace has never been so secure since the Russo-Turkish War as it is to-day.

ADVICE GRATIS.-Mr. Banner, registered and doubly qualified under the Medical and Pharmacy Acts, will have great pleasure in giving his advice to anyone so situated as not wishing to consult their family doctor, and by strictly moderate charges for medicine only, to be of some service to those requiribg the benefit of his great experience, by writ- ing fully to 56, Dealer-SC, Liverpool.—Advf.

EARLESTOWN BAPTISTS CONDEMNED. Sir,—Referring to your report of last week re the above subject, permit me to say that Mr. Aked's strong condemnation of Earlestown Baptists does not include in the least all who attend the Baptist Church, as some have inferred from your report. It is the management and leaders who are spoken to so strongly, which is per- haps justifiable when all facts are taken into considera- tion. Your insertion of the above explanation will oblige, yours truly,
GEO. F. CLARKE. 35, Market-St., Earlestown, 27 Aug., 1890.

WELSH LIBERAL PROGRAMME. Sir,—ln your issue of the 23rd August, you give the Welsh Liberal Programme." Would it be possible to add to it Total Abolition of Tithes? Can you give us, in your next issue, the name and address of the Welsh Liberal Association's Secretary, or put us in the way of pressing forward our view respect- ing this total abolition, and oblige thereby some of your COUNTRY SUBSCRIBERS. We shall be glad to open our columns to a discussion of the tithe question. The Secretary of, the North Wales Liberal Federation is Mr. W. H. Tilston , Wrexham; and the Secretary of the Federation for South Wales is Mr. R. N. Hall, Cardiff.—En. Ex.
REV. C. F. AKED AND THE EARLESTOWN BAPTISTS. _ .

- Sir,—As you thought the St. Helens incident with regard to the Earlestown Baptists of sufficient moment for a lengthened account in your last issue, I feel sure you will accord me room for a reply thereto. The feel. ing of indignation, which was not confined to those alone for whom the rod was meant, has now given place to one of astonishment at the supreme act of folly perpetrated by Mr. Aked. I wonder how many "vast careers" had a foundation of abuse to support them. I should like to know if the " heroic and inspired ancestry of Pembroke Church" were heroes in this John Falstaff fashion, or if they gave evidence of their inspiration by their Billingsgate Invec- tive. If Mr. Aked intends to go about his" great and magnificent work" by flattering all whom he can be- guile, and abuse those who are not sufficiently pliable, methinks he will resemble the man in the fable who rolls the stone towards the top of the hill only to find it repeatedly slipping from him and rolling down to the bottom again. As Mr. Aked undoubtedly is well able to express him- self both neatly and elegantly, there is not the remotest excuse for such an outrage upon the Queen's English, while if it be true that "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh," I for one do not envy the possessor of feelings which needs such words to express

them. As for the justice of condemning a whole company of people; well, we may safely appeal from Mr. Aked, who knows us not in spite of his many opportunities for inter- course, to those whom we individually meet day by day; and our "supposed leaders" whom he has sought to belittle have been in Christian service long enough to enable them to survive any such mud-throwing, or to bear with equanimity any utterance of a spoilt child.—l am, sir, yours CON AMORE.

div.head: SHIP CA.NAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CA.NAL.

ANOTHER BIG CHEQUE. A correspondent writes :—" The cheque drawn by the Great Indian Peninsular Railway on the London and County Bank fur £1,250,000 is a fairly substantial one, but in the offices of the Manchester Ship Canal in Man- chestet, hanging in a frame over the fireplace, is a cheque for £1,750.000, the amount of the purchase money of the undertaking known as the Bridgewater Canal, which is now worked by the Manchester Ship Canal Company, and from which it derives a large in- come."

DREDGING AT LYMM. On Monday morning between one and two hundred men were required at Lymm for manning the new dred- ger in the meadows by which it is proposed to tear out the excavations along the bed of the river where the line of canal and the river coalesce and run together for some distance. Of course a breach will net be made in- the canal until it is ready to receive the water for navi- gation purposes, but the bed will be deepened to the level of the canal, an embankment closing the ends of the workings in the meantime. STRIKE OF STONEMASONS. It is stated that on Tuesday a number of stonemasons, estimated at 100 to 150, employed on No. 5 section of the Manchester Ship Canal, that is. the section from Moore to Latchford, stopped work. Their complaint is that they are insufficiently paid, and they ask for an advance of id. per hour. After carefully considering their application, the authorities of the Ship Canal re- fused, for various reasons, to make the advance general. This has caused some dissatisfaction, but with the object of arriving at a satisfactory settlement of the dispute, the contractors decided to suspend work for a week. THE MEAT TRADE ON THE CANAL. At its meeting next Wednesday, the Manchester City Council will be asked to consider the following report by the Markets Committee, prepared in accordance with a resolution passed by the Council at its May meeting : ." In the opinion of your committee suitable provision ought to be made for dealing with live cattle and dead meat arriving by the Ship Canal, and they have inspected several plots of land which they consider suitable for the purposes in view, and they now request the Council to authorise them to enter into negotiations for the acquisi- tion of such properties as may tbe found desirable and suitable for the above purposes." LANDSLIP NEAR LYMM. On Wednesday night, a watchman ou the Lymm sec- tion of the Ship Canal discovered that a large mass of the embankment near the brickyard had given way, the soil having slipped into the cutting. Alongside this por- tion of the canal the main line between Manchester and Eastham runs, and the earth giving way left the line of rails suspended. Gangs were quickly set to work on Thursday morning to fill up the breach, and a new per- manent way was constructed further away from the canal side. It is supposed that the embankment became undermined by the recent rains. Considerable incon- venience was experienced owing to the difficulty of run- ning the usual train loads of material. COMMERCIAL TRAVELLER FALLS INTO THE

CUTTING. Between six and seven o'clock on Saturday morning a man was found by several workmen lying in the Ship Canal cutting near the locks at Thelwall. Although sensible he had been badly injured, and he was conveyed without delay to the Ship Canal Hospital at Latchford, where it was found that one of his legs had been broken, and his head severely bruised. His name is William Blackman, and he is a commercial traveller hailing from Birmingham. Ha cannot say how he got into the canal, but he remember, having come from Runcorn by train i on the previous night. It s conjectured that the injured moan got out of the train at Thelwall and walked along the metals in the cutting till he got to the locks, where he fell into a hole; at all events, he was found under oae of the culverts, where, he says, he had crawled to shelter from the rain. He is believed to have lain in the canal several hours. He is, of course, still detained in the hospital, but is regaining strength. VISIT OF SUGAR MERCHANTS. On Wednesday a number of sugar refiners and mer- chants visited the Manchester Ship Canal Works, under the guidance of Mr. W. H. Bailey, one of the directors, and Mr. Marshall Stevens, representing the Ship Canal Company. The following firms were represented : Liverpool : Thomas Bate and Co., Crosfield, Barrow, and Co., George Crosfield and Co., Farrie and Co„ Limited, S. M. Freeman and Co., Edward Grey and Co., George Jagar and Son, Jones and Co., James Leitch and Co., Macfie and eon; Meyer, Gustav, and Co., Sankey Sugar ,Refining Company, Shut, Higson, aud Co., Nicholas

div.head: BALLOON ON FIRE.
div.p: A BALLOON ON FIRE.

DEATH OF THE AERONAUT. An Ibraila telegram says that on Tuesday an Italian aeronaut, named Borletti, made an ascent from the public gardens there suspended from a balloon without a para- chute. When at a height of a thousand feet the balloon took fire, and Bortelli fell, and was instantly killed, his body being mutilated.

RAILWAY ACCIDENTS IN SCOTLAND. THIRTY PERSONS INJURED. A serious collision occurred on Thursday morning on the Milngavie branch of the North British Railway, near Glasgow. A passenger train which left Milngavie for Glasgow at twenty minutes past eight, and which was well filled, principally with business men and clerks, collided with a goods train near the junction with the Helensburgh line. The goods train had been shunted on a loop line when the passenger train came up. The driver it is supposed mistook the signal, which was at danger, and dashed in upon the goods train, the two en- gines meeting buffer to buffer. The passengers were much shaken and numbers of them were cut and bzuised although happily no one was dangerously injured. In all about thirty: passengers suffered injury. They were conveyed to their homes. The line, which is a single one, was blocked for some hours. Archibald Moir, driver of the passenger train, was arrested by the police. A later telegram states that the number of injured in the collision at Milngavie Junction has been ascertained to be 31. It is probable that the driver will be liberated on bail. The driver of the goods train, John Campbell, and the stoker, Dalziel Peebles, jumped off their locomo- tive and were saved; while the stoker of the passenger train, when he saw that a collision could not be averted, lay down among the coals and also escaped. Shortly after two o'clock an accident occurred at the Caledonian Company's Central Station, Glasgow, to an express train from Edinburgh. The leading spring of the engine broke, and the tender and several carriages were thrown off the line. Beyond being shaken, none of the passengers suffered injury.

--- SPECIAL SERVICES AT THE WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—OR Sunday the Rev. J. Woods, governor of the Primitive Methodist College, Manchester, preached morning and evening in the Wesleyan Chapel. There were good con- gregations. A collection was made at the close of each service to defray the cost of obtaining special preachers.

PENKETH. YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION. At the weekly meeting of the above association, held at Bethany House, on Friday evening week, there was a fair attendance of members. Mr. J. Randall gave an essay on "Musketry." He gave a description of the Martini-Henry rifle, and explained the uses of the various parts of the firearm ; the distance it would carry a bullet, its velocity, and its advantages over other firearms of a like nature, &c. At the close a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Randall.

CYCLE ACCIDENT. On Thursday, a little girl named Jackson, residing at Heath-road, met with an accident by being knocked down by a bicycle. She was returning home from school, walking along the parapet, and , as a young cyclist named Hayes was paSsing,started to run across the road. Hayes, who was riding near the footpath,saw the danger,but was unable to stop his machine in time to avoid running over the little girl. The collision threw Hayes and his machine to the ground, the bicycle falling on Jackson. She was taken home, and Dr. Murray was immediately called in, and upon examination he found that her should blade was fractured. This has been attended to,and she is now progressing favourably.

div.head: BOATING DISASTER AT DEAL
div.p: BOATING DISASTER AT DEAL

FOUR LIVES LOST. A fatal boat accident occurred at three o'clock on Monday afternoon off Deal. A party of visitors had been for a sail towards the Goodwins in the four-oared service galley, Seaman's Glory, and were sailing in. When near the Bank Buoy, within a mile of shore, a sudden gust of wind caught the sail and the boat capsized and sank. There were seven persons in the boat—two boatmen named Mark Nash and John Nott, Mr. and Mrs. Arney and their daughter, and Mr. and Mrs. Pal- mer, visitors staying at Deal, and as the boat sank all were left in the water. Mr. Arney and his daughter, Mr. Palmer, and John Trott were picked up by a passing steamer, but Mr. Palmer died soon after being landed. Mrs. Arney, Mrs. Palmer, and Nash were drowned. The Seaman's Glory was the best service galley on the Deal beach. An inquest was held at Deal, on Tuesday, on the bodies of Mark Nash, boatman, and Charles Palmer, a visitor, who died from the effects of a boat accident on Monday. Martin Hewlett identified his cousin, Charles Henry Palmer, aged about 40, of Broomwood-rd., Clap- ham Common, manager of a large drapery business. John Trott, boatman, said he and Nash took a party of five for a sail to the Goodwins. On returning Nash was steering, and near the Gull lightship the wind dropped calm. They then hoisted the large sail instead of the storm sail, and took in a reef. When they were about tacking to reach home the wind suddenly shifted, and a squall took them flat and aback, forcing the sail against the mast, and the stern under water. The two ladies went under the sail, and were never seen again. The others floated with the aid of oars until picked up by a steamer's boat. Witness had been accustomed to all kinds ef boats for 26 years, but had never met with such an accident. Mr. Arney said it was the work of an instant, no one having time to scream before they were immersed. He was perfectly satisfied with the conduct of the boatmen.—Evidence having been given to the efforts on shore to restore animation, the Jury returned a verdict of 'Accidentally drowned," directing a letter of thanks to be sent to the captain of the steamer who res- cued the survivors.

VISIT OF 3IR. JOHN WILSON, XP., TO WARRINGTON. COMING LABOUR MEETING It will be seen from an advertisement in another column that Mr. John Wilson, M.P., for Mid-Durham; and Financial Secretary to the Durham Miners' Association, will speak to a meeting of workingmen in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-at., Warrington. on Wednesday evening next. The subject of the ad- dress will be, " Why should working-men be Trades Unionists ?" At the time of Mr. Wilson's election to Parliament in 1885, the " Pall Mall Gazette " said of him: "Mr. John Wilson will personify in the new House the great change which has taken place in the basis and constitution of Parliament. Mr. Wilson, who is a pit- man, was the secretary and moving spirit of the Durham Miners' Franchise Association, under whose auspices a great number of meetings were held before the extension of the franchise was conceded ; and he was one of the speakers who, at a meeting of depute,ions from all parts of the country at the Foreign OfEce in 1884, prayed Mr. Gladstone to at once introduce a Parliamentary Reform Bill. Mr. Wilson, 48 years of age (now 53) was born, the son of a labourer, at Greatham, Durham. At the age of ten years he began work at Stanhope Quarries, and he entered the pit at Ludworth Colliery at the age of thirteen. Ile has just defeated an influential member of the best known coal-owning family in the north country. As a young man, Mr. Wilson spent a few years at sea, working afterwards at Hanwell Colliery • and he after- wards worked for three years and a half in the mines of Pennsylvania and Illinois. He is an earnest teetotaller, as well as a local preacher among the Methodists. Mr. Wilson was appointed treasurer of the Durham Miners' Union in 1882. He is a man of great intellectual power, calm, logical, and shrewd, and is lucid and forcible as a speaker. He enjoys the confidence and admiration of his fellow-Unionists, and he may be depended upon to make an impression upon the House of Commons and the country." In the 1888 election, Mr. Wilson suffered de- feat at the hands of his Conservative opponent, but on the vacancy recently caused in Mid-Durham by the death of Mr. Crawford, he was again returned to Parlia- ment by a very large majority.
The expenses of Mr. John Wilson, the successful Liberal candidate in the recent Mid-Durham election were £785. Those of his Conservative opponent, Mr. Vane Tempest, were £1,129.

On Saturday the annual main of bowls in connec- tion with the Conservative Club, which had been postponed for a week in consequence of the un- favourable weather, was commenced on the club green. There were 78 entries, and ten players are still "left in."

On Saturday evening an accident occurred in Horsemarket-st., which narrow thoroughfare was rather crowded. An old man, named Lawrence

'elsh, 60 years of age, was crossing the street,l whea he was knocked down by a passing trap, ' driven by Mr. H. Brown. The injured man, who was insensible, was picked up and conveyed to the Infirmary by P.C. Jones (29). He is now pro- gressing favourably towards recovery, though at first his injuries were considered critical. TEE NATIONAL GAS-WORKERS' AND LABOURERS'

DIPHTHERIA AT CROFT.
This diseaseT,i;-br—oiren out at Hermitage Green, Croft, two deaths having occurred during the past fortnight.

THE LOCAL VOLIINTHBRS. The annual prize competition in connection with the Ist Volunteer Battalion (Prince of Wales' Volunteers) South Lancashire Regiment, was com- menced on Saturday afternoon, on the Widnes Range, and will be continued each Saturday till October next. The prizes will be distributed shortly , before Christmas.

CROFT SCHOOL BOARD. A meeting of this Board should have taken place at the Board School on the 19th inst., but as only two members were present, they could not form a quorum, and the meeting was postponed until Mon- day evening. Only two members put in an appear- ance at the adjourned meeting, which had, in con- sequence, to be again postponed. BOWLING MAIN AT THE LIBERAL CUB. We understand that the annual bowling main in connection with the Warrington :Liberal Club will take place on Saturday next. Already there is a substantial list of prizes amounting to between £lO and £l5, and there is every reason to believe that the event will be as interesting as it has hither- to always been. The green is in splendid condition, and some capital play may be expected. The sub- Committee for the management of the main consists of Messrs. J. Albinson, J. Garner, W. Gilbert, and Mitchell (steward of the club.)

THR SCHOOL OF ART. As will be seen from an advertisement in another column, the classes will reassemble on Tues- day, September 3rd. The course of instruction in- cludes geometry, machine construction, building construction, second and third grade art, outline drawing from plants, drawing figure from life, and painting and modelling. It may be interesting to note that a class for students engaged in trades con- nected with decorative art will be held every Sat- urday afternoon. It is also satisfactory to learn that the Committee of the School of Art contemplate establishing a number of free scholarships for scholars leaving the elementary schools before May next.

THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WADDINGTON. For the week ending Saturday, August 23rd, 1890. —The mean temperature was 56 Fahrenheit, and therefore 21 degrees colder than the pre- c 3ding week. The maximum temperature, 69 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 18th inst, and the minimum temperature, 41 Fahrenheit, on the 19th inst. The rainfall measured .69 in. The general direction of the wind was S.W. During the week, which was the 34th ot the current year, 40 births and 271 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 28.08 per thousand, against 1812, the average of the previous four weeks, and against 20.49 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 1 from English cholera, 5 from diarrhcea, 2 from premature birth, 2 from old age, 6 from brain disease, 2 from lung disease, 1 from heart disease. Two cases of scarlatina were re- ported under the requirements of the Act of Par- liament.—JonN H. GonrtaLL. Medical Officer of Health. WADDINGTON DISTRICT HIGHWAY BOARD.
