Grounds :(Orford)' with Mr. White (assistant-clerk).—The reports of the Surveyor were read, and from them it appeared that satisfactory progress was being made with repairs and improve- ' ments in various townships. It was also reported that application was being made to the agents of the Ecclesiastical Commissioners for permission to remove certain old cottages and farm buildings at Winwick, for the purposes of making the road more convenient for the traffic, but no decision had been arrived at.—The Assistant-Clerk reported that there was a balance in hand of .£1,050 Ils. 11d., and accounts amounting to a total of .£1,647 12s. 9d. were passed for payment. Several calls were due, it was explained, so that there was no likelihood of the account at the bank being overdrawn. WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.—THE NICETIES OF

div.head: UNION.
div.p: UNION.

On Thursday evening 4a-m—e-eting was held on the fair ground, in furtherance of the object of this I Union. The chair was occupied by Mr. P. Connor, the Manchester district secretary, and there was a fair attendance. The Chairman referred to the ad- vantage of the working-classes combining together, and pointed out that through the efforts of the Union large numbers of men had already obtained an eight hours' working day. Mr. Gardner, of Lon- don, then explained the working of the Union, and the action it takes with regard to disputes between employed and employers, and labour questions gene- rally.
MUSIC IN THB PARE. The bandstand,on Sunday afternoon, was occupied by the band of the Ist Volunteer Battalion (Prince _ .
- of Wales' Volunteers) South Lancashire Regiment. • - •

There was a large attendance, notwithstanding that there were two or three showers, many persons remaining from the opening to the close of the per- formance. The programme included selections from Beethoven, Weber, Gounod,and Rossini. As a mark of respect to the memory of the late Mr. Stirk, the band, at the close of the performance. gave an ex- cellent rendering of the Dead March in "Saul." We understand that an effort will be made to give a performance every Sunday afternoon till the end of , September. •Tke Lymm Church Brass Band will, to- , morrow (Sunday) afternoon, play the following programme : March, "Rough and Ready "; Chorus, " Great and Marvellous "; Trombone solo, Mr. E. Guest, 'Death of Nelson "; Fantasia, "Evening Thoughts "; Chorus, " Hallelujah "; Fantasia. " Le Diva "; overture, " Fair Maid of Perth "; March, "St. Albans." Conductor, T. T. Gregson. On Sunday, on the enclosed ground off Bewsey- st., the above society held their usual meetings. In the afternoon, Mr. J. Leicester was in the chair, and the following gentlemen gave encouraging ad- dresses, viz.:—Messrs. J. Price, W. Higginson, and T. Frain. In the evening the weather was very un- favourable for an outdoor meeting. and it was re- solved to meet under the market shed. Mr. J. Lei- cester presided, and Messrs. J. Caldwell (Manches- ter), J. O'Reilly, J. Price,and J. Yarwood (Runcorn), gave enlightening addresses. Another meeting was held at Bridge-foot, in connection with the society, in the afternoon. Mr. C. H. Mills conducted, and he was supported by Messrs. J. Price,J. O'Reilly, and J. Caldwell, all of whom spoke. Although the weather was very unfavourable,there was a large attendance. Several persons took the pledge.
_ A Bo Y DROWNED AT LATCHFORD.
A boy named Arthur Lee, six years of age, son of Sarah Lee, a widow, living at 282, Knutsford-rd., was drowned in the canal near Black Bear Bridge,

Latchford, on Saturday afternoon. It appears that the deceased was attempting to push a boat upon I which he had been standing into the water, when he slipped and fell into the canal. A boy named Walter Hardman Banks, seeing his companion in danger of being drowned, pushed a plank towards him, but the latter appears to have been unable to reach it and sank. The body was recovered in about five minutes afterwards by a man named George Brailey, but all efforts to restore consciousness were ineffectual. The inquest on the body was held at the Black Bear Inn, Kuntsford-rd., on Monday after- noon, before Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, when a verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. We may mention that the boy had a predilection for playing near the canal, and had twice previously had nar- row escapesof being drowned. AN IRISH LABOURER FOUND DROWNED.

On Tuesday afternoon Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquiry at the Black Horse Inn, Sankey, relative to the death of a man named Wil- liam Banner, 45 years of age, a labourer who had been in the service of Mr. Warburton, of the Collards Farm, Buttonwood. The body of the deceased was found in the St. llelens and Widnes Canal, near Bewsey Locks, on Sunday morning, and was taken out of the water and conveyed by Sergeant Devlin and P.C. Dugdale, of the Lancashire constabulary, to the Black Horse Inn. It was supposed that Banner had been to Warrington on the previous night, and that while on his way home he had acci- dentally fallen into the canal. A brother of the de- ceased, John Banner, met with a fatal accident about twelve months ago in Warrington. After hearing evidence, the jury brought in a verdict to the effect that the deceased was found drowned, and added that there was no evidence to show how he came to get into the canal. WARRINGTON UNITED ANGLERS' ANNUAL COMPETITION.

A match in connection with the United Clubs of Warrington took place at Chester on Saturday, when prizes of the value of ..£lO 19s. 6d., and twelve ether minor prizes, were competed for by the 59 peSons who entered. Fine weather prevailed, and there was some keen competition for the prizes offered, though the takes were not large. The first prize, .£3, was won by Mr. William Hamblett ; the second, .£2, by Mr. James Cook; 3rd, .£1 7s. 6d., by Mr. John Atherton; 4th, .£l, by Mr. James Buckley; sth, by Mr. S. Foulkes, junr. ; and among the other prize winners were Mr. William Bolton, Mr. James Garnett, Mr. John Oultram, Mr. James Green, Mr. T. Drew, Mr. Edward Lawton, Mr. Thomas Turner, Mr. Samuel Foulkes, sen., &c. The lowest prize was a pair of clogs, value is. 6d. The contributors to the prize fund were Sir G. Greenall, Bart, M.P., Mr. Samuel Hartshorne, Mr. James Welsby, Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Company, Mr. James Marson, Mr. John Hewitt, Mr. John Monks, Messrs. G. and J. Greenall, Mr. P. Caldwell, Mr. H. Toft, Mr. Joseph Podmore, Market-place; Messrs. P. Walker and Son, Messrs. J. Crosfield and Sons, Mr. Robert Davies, and Mr. Charles White. PRIMROSB LEAGI7Ii FETE AT WILTON. The third annual fete in connection with the Daresbury Habitation of the Primrose League was, by permission of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., MX., held in the grounds of Walton Hall on Saturday. The proceedings commenced at half-past two, and were continued till after 8 p.m. Quoits, bowls, and croquet were provided, and sports took place, money prizes, amounting altogether to about £lO, being awarded to the successful competitors. The sports, which were under the direction of Mr. Gilbert Greenall. Mr. Cyril Greenall. Mr. Walter Jones, and Mr. J. Whitley, drew together the greater part of the members, and the various races were watched with much interest. The following are the condi- tions of one of the obstacle races: Before he could be allowed to start, each competitor had to drink ' a quantity of lemonade and eat a bun, and it is said the rapid manner in which one or two of the run- ners got through the task was astonishing. Strangers were admitted to the grounds upon payment of a shilling, and it is estimated that from 600 to 700 persons were present. The visitors were allowed to walk through the park, gardens, and conserva- tories. An excellent tea was provided in a large tent, the caterer being Mr. T. 0. Speakman, of the Saracen's Head Hotel, Wilderspool. Sir Giibert and Lady Greenall, Mr. Gilbert Greenall, and the Misses Greenall were in the grounds the greater part of the afternoon. Among others present were the Rev. Dr. Preston (of Runcorn), the Rey. L. J. T. Darwell (vicar of St. John's, Walton), the Rev. T. Whitley (Daresbury), Mr. and Mrs. Charlton Parr, Mrs. Charlton, Mr. and Mrs. Wynne Jones, Miss Townsend, Mr. James Smethurst, Mr. John Weir, Mr. Wright, &c. In the evening a meeting was held. Sir Gilbert Greenall presiding. He remarked that it was not his intention to make a political speech, as they had met more as a united family than for poli- tical purposes. At the same :time they had their own opinions upon political and other matters, and they were determined to maintain in its integrity the constitution of the country. (Applause.) The other speakers were the Rev. Dr. Preston and Mr. J. C. Parr. After the speaking there was dancing.

div.head: LAW.
div.p: THE LAW.

A sitting of the Warrington County Court was held on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes. The cause list comprised one default summons, 123 original plaints, and 73 original judg- ment summonses. A woman named Mary Ellen Hatton, of Napier-st, applied for an administration order under section 122 of the: Bankruptcy Act, 1883. She said, in answer to his Honour, that she kept a butcher's shop, and that maintained her, along with the payment she received for nursing a baby.—His lionour said he was afraid she was not a person who was entitled to ask for an order. If she wished to obtain the protection of the Bank- ruptcy Act she would have to apply to the Court under another part of the Act. He thought he must refuse the order because she was no a person earning wages.—Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for the applicant, submitted that the woman did obtain earnings from the shop.—His Honour: That is income.—Mr. Browne said that the course of filing a petition would be expensive to the applicant.— His Honour said that the granting of administra- tion orders referred to the wage-earning class, and not to persons engaged in trade.—Mr. Browne: She gets three shillings a week wages for nursing. —His Honour: 1 must refuse the order, because you are not a person earning wages. I think this part of the Act is intended for wage-earners. Any- one in trade can onty avail himself of the Act under a different part, which, as Mr. Browne says, will cost you some money. lam sorry for it, but so it is, and I have to deal with the Act as I find it.

FLOWER SHOW AT NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS. IThe fifth annual exhibition of the Newton-le- Willows Horticultural Society was held on Satur- day, in fine weather, and proved a success, especially in the way ot the quality and quantity of the exhibits. Under the circumstances, too, the attendance was better than might have been ex- pected, as, unfortunately. Messrs. McCorquodale's annual excursion was held on the same day, and, as is usual, took a large number of people away from the vicinity. Those who were left, however, were loyal in their adherence to the local attrac- tion, and thus the flower show did not suffer to such an extent as was feared. The exhibition was held in afield adjoining the Newton nurseries, lent by Mr. J. Pardey, and the exhibits were well staged in a large marquee. In another part of the field Mrs. Bond, of the Pied Bull Hotel, Newton, had charge of the refreshment booth, and the Earlestown brass band played selections of music during the afternoon. In the evening they played for dancing. The judges were: Mr. E. Kipps, gardener to Mr. John Crosfield, of Walton Lea; Mr. Lockhart, gardener to Sir Gilbert Greenall, of Walton Hall; Mr. Webster, gardener at Kenyon Hall; Mr. Skeene, Garswood ; and (judges of gardens), Mr. W. MESSRS. MCCORQUODALE AND CO's. ExCITBSIoN. The employs of Messrs. McCorquodale and Co. had their annual excursion on Saturday. Two well filled trains containing the workpeople and their friends left Newton-le-Willows for Blackpool and Liverpool. At the former place splendid weather was experienced, but at Liverpool it was of a squally character, and to some extent marred the enjoyment of the trippers. Many crossed the river to New Brighton, and visited the places of amusement there, returning to the city later in the evening. An enjoyable day was spent by all parties, the arrangements being efficiently carried out. HOPE OF EARLESTOWN LODGE OF GOOD TEMPLAR.%

The usual weekly session of this lodge was held on Monday evening. There was fair attendance of members. Bro. G. E. Warburton presided. After the session was opened in the ordinary form, the report of the district lodge session was given by Bro. G. Clarke, and supplemented by Bro. G. War- burton, and adopted. A paper was afterwards read by Bro. Sergeant T. Mantle, of Orford Be s, Warrington, on "Intemperance in the Army. The paper was a most interesting one, and after :a short discussion upon the various points contained in it, a vote of thanks was accorded to the reader.

THE INFLUENZA AGAIN. The "Dix-Neuvieme Siècle" states that some cases of influenza have lately occurred in Paris.
MORASS OF AUSTRIA. A "Central News" telegram from Paris says the Empress of Austria has gone to Bordeaux, and not to Cologne as reported.
LATEST CRICKET. Kent won by eight wickets. York won by an innings and seventy-eight; Notts all out for eighty-three Lancashire second innings twenty for one wicket.

_ ... I THE CONWAY DISASTER. The body of Robert Evans, son of the Conway harbour master, was recovered yesterday morning, on the Llandudno side of the river, by boatmen. The report as to the finding of the third and last body, Edward Pullin, is unfounded.

div.head: SHOOTING HIS WIFE.
div.p: SHOOTING HIS WIFE.

At Northampton, yesterday, an old decrepit man named Kelpin, who is supposed to be insane was remanded on the charge of attempting to murder his wife. He obtained a revolver' and without any appar- ent cause, tired three shots at her, one inflicting serious injury. CARDINAL NEWMAN AND DR. DOLLINGER.

In an article which Mr. Gladstone has contributed to "The Speaker," he says the late Cardinal Newman and Dr. Dollinger were the two most remarkable men of the contemporary Christian church. Both were great, but diversely great. Dollinger's mind was simple ; Newman's complex.

div.head: FATALITY AT THE ISLE OF MAN.
div.p: FATALITY AT THE ISLE OF MAN.

Early yesterday morning the body of a woman was washed ashore at Blue Point, on the north-west coast of the Isle of Man, and about eight miles from Ramsey. The body has been in the water about two weeks, and was clothed in a bathing dress of dark grey colour, bound with red fluted braid. THE SCOTCH RAILWAY DISASTER.

A Glasgow correspondent telegraphs that there were more persons injured in the Milngavie Junction collision on Thursday than was reported. Frank Junor Garden was lifted from the debris nearly pulseless by his master, but he is now progressing favourably, as also are the rest of the injured, except Mr. M'Laurin, who is in a serious state. There are sufferers in nearly every house at Bearsden, the wealthy residential district near Glasgow.

div.head: STORMY. WEATHER.
div.p: THE STORMY. WEATHER.

Reports continue to be received of serious damage to crops by heavy rains. Lincolnshire and Kent were again deluged on Thursday night. On Thursday night a destructive thunderstorm passed over South Cheshire the lightning being very vivid. At Wrme Hill, near Cheshire, two houses were struck by lightning, and one of them partially destroyed. A man named Webster was badly cut on the head with the falling debris. A little further away two pigs were killed by lightning. The heavy rainfall has laid large quanti- ties of grain. GREAT FIRE IN LONDON.

An extensive conflagration occurred soon after day- break yesterday morning, at the old Sun Wharf, Narrow- at., Rotherhithe. Several thousands of tons of coal stored on the wharf became ignited, and a four-floored building 1201 t. by 60ft. was burning from end to end, illuminating the east and south-east of London for miles round. The outbreak thus attacked from water and land succumbed to the immense body of water thrown upon it, and by seven o'clock it was practically under control. The building, which was used as a coal stores, was then entirely consumed, and the falling walls and floors very nearly caused serious accidents to the firemen. As it was, only a few minor casualties occurred.

div.head: ANOTHER ALPINE _DISASTER.
div.p: ANOTHER ALPINE _DISASTER.

Penn, FRIDAY.-A telegram from Chambery reports another Alpine disaster. M. Sinigaglia, a celebrated Alpine climber, was snowed up for two days on Mount Cervin. One of his guides named Garrel, the most famous in the Alps, died from cold, and another had his hands frozen.

div.head: HARVEST IN MANITOBA.
div.p: THE HARVEST IN MANITOBA.

OTTAWA, Tutrusoax.—The Dominion Minister of Agri- culture, in summing up the complete reports from the most trustworthy sources received from all points in Manitoba and the north-west territories, states that this year's grain crop, most of which is now harvested, is fully up to anticipation, the yield being heavy and the quality excellent.

div.head: HA.YDOCK.
div.p: HA.YDOCK.

OPENING or A NEW Onpm—A new organ which has just been erected in St. Mary's Catholic Church, Black- brook, was opened on Sunday. Mr. A'nscough, organ builder of Preston, has supplied the instrument at a cost of £254. It is gratifying to note that at the opening ceremony there was only the small balance of £64 , owing. The case is of pitch-pine, varnished, with spotted metal front pipes, and it is a welcome addition to the ornamentation of the church. The tone, which is very rich, is of the most suitable kind for the church. In the morning, when there was a good attendance, there was solemn High Mass, the celebrant being the Rev. Joseph Rigby, who was assisted by the Revs. Fr. Henry and Fr. Heifferman as deacon and sub-deacon respectively. The Rev. E. O'Sullivan was master of ceremonies. The Rev. Fr. Basil Moubert of St. Anne's, Sutton, was the preacher, and he delivered an interesting discourse on the introduction of music into church services. The choir which was augmented for the occasion, sang Farmer's Mass. Mr. James Tom- linson, organist to the Corporation of Preston, presided at the organ. In the afternoon there was solemn Bene- diction. The Rev. Fr. Basil Moubert again occupied the pulpit, his subject being " The Sacrifice of the Mass."

HAYDOCK LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting of the Haydock Local Board was held on Monday afternoon. Mr. T. D. Grimke J.P., pre- sided, and-there were also present Messrs. W. Balharry, J. Turton, J. Waine, John Jackson, and J. Matthews (clerk). Fresxces.—Accounts amounting to £153 14). 3d. were examined and cheques signed for payment. THE STONE Corcrescrs.—The Clerk reported that he had communicated With Messrs. Brundrit and Co. in reference to their contract for handbroken Penmaenmaur stone. The firm had written that they could not reduce their contract. On the motion of Mr. Balharry, seconded by Mr. Waine, it was decided to accept Messrs Brundrit's tender. GAS WANTED.—The Clerk said lie had received several complaints about the lamps not being lit—particularly from the TrarnwaysCo.—Mr. John Jackson said it would soon be a full moon.—The Clerk explained that the usual time for lighting the lamps was in September.— Mr. Balharry moved that the lamps be lit after the full moon.—Mr. Turton seconded the motion, which was carried. SEWERAGE Merrerts.—The Clerk stated that last year some alterations were made in a drain near the Wagon and Horses but it did not do its work completely. The water lodged in the road and the pipe could not carry it away.—Mr. Turton drew attention to a similar state of affairs near Penny-lane and Vista-lane,and said that some- thing would require to be done before long. He also observed that some cottages near the Ram's Head were sewered into an open ditch and the smell was something fearful.—On the motion of Mr. Jackson, seconded by Mr. Turton, it was resolved that Messrs. Balharry, Turton, Harrison, and John Jackson be appointed a sub-com- mittee to report upon the sewerage questions. IMPROVEMENTS.—The Clerk reported that Mr. Brad- shaw, who was building some property in Blockbrook- road wished to have a straight line in Old Whynt-road, and would give them a good footpath. It was decided to leave the matter over until the next meeting.—Mr. Turton reported that he had inspected the Clerk's house, and found there were several repairs wanted doing ; and it was decided that the work should be done at once. MEDICAL OFFICERt REPORT.—Dr. T. E. Hayward (medical officer), read his report for the second quarter of the current year, including the months of April, May, and June. The number of births recorded was 31 males and 32 females, total 83 ; deaths : 14 males, 11 females, total 25. The birth rate was equal to an annual one of 3005 per 1,000 of the population, and the death rate 15.98 ; but excluding two deaths from accident, and one of a stranger, the death rate was reduced to 13.79 per 1,000. The causes of death were as follows : scarlatina and measles 1, pulmonary phthisis 3, heart disease:3, cancer 1, bronchitis 1, pneumonia 2, other diseases 12, injuries 2. During the quarter the health of the township had been very good, no epidemic disease having existed. He drew attention to defective privy accommodation for three houses near the Toll Bar, and to seven houses at Blackbrook, which were reported upon in January last as unfit for human habitation. The houses, he said, were still inhabited except in one case. They were extremely dilapidated and had no drainage, and no proper privy accommodation.—The Chairman considered the report a satisfactory one, and moved the adoption of the report, with a vote of thanks to Dr. Hay- ward.—Mr. Balhar.-y seconded the motion, which was adopted.—TheClerk reported upon nuisances caused by the keeping of pigs in close proximity to dwelling-houses, i ' and he was instructed to communicate with the parties concerned with a view of having an abatement of the nuisance. SCARCITY OF WATER.—The Clerk reported that he had received an application from Mr. Forrest, on behalf of Messrs. Evans and Co. for a supply lof water to the Queen Pit. Mr. Forrest had informed him that they had run short of water, and under an agreement the Board were compelled to supply them.—The Clerk was asked to take the necessary steps to give the required supply of water. This was all the business.

• The Shropshire Union Canal Company are reported to be considering the propriety of prosecuting their Bat- men at Ellesmere Port who recentiy went on strike. At present traffic on the canal is almost entirely suspended.

RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT ACT, 1852.- ELECTION OF COMMISSIONRRS. Notice is Hereby Given, that a MRETING of persons entitled to vote at the Election of Commissioners under the above named Act will be held in the Market Hall, Bridge-et., Runcorn, on Thursday, the 4th day of September, 18911, for the Election of Five Commissioners in the place of Mr. Peter Smith, Mr. Samuel Taylor. Mr. William Whittaker, Mr. William Fisher, and Mr. Richard Morris, who then retire from office, but are eligible for re-election. The voting will commence at Nine o'clock in the forenoon, and close at Four o'clock in the afternoon. E. MARSHALL, Secretary to the said Commissioners. Town Hall, Ruwcorn, August 22nd, 1890.

LECTION OF RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, The time having arrived for your electing five members on the Board, we respectfully ask your consideration of our names as candidates. Three of our members have been for many years members of the Board, and we trust have performed its duties so as to have received your confidence and deserved its renewal. Iwo of our number ask your suffrages for the first time—one of whom was for many years a member of a neighbouring Local Board and Chairman of its Finance Committee, and he is pre- pared to bring the knowledge and experience so gained on the interests of his native town. The other has had a wide experience as an engineer in designing and erecting large public works intimately associated with sanitary authorities, and is eminently qualified to serve you on all questions demanding the consideration of a local authority. Both are sons of those who for many years worked faithfully for you as members of the Board. During the term of office of several of us,works have been com- menced which are not yet completed, and agreements entered into bearing on the future, viz.—the improvement of Waterloo Bridge, the foreshore intercepting sewer, the sewerage of Heath-road and Victoria-road districts, the making of Victoria Bridge and road,enlarged dock and wharfage accommodation; which we venture to submit constitute some reason, at least, why we should be re-elected, as our knowledge of the agree- ments and contracts therefor will enable us to materially protect and advance your interests thereunder. The rapid growth of our town, which we believe will continue and increase as the result of the completion of the Ship Canal,must bring to the front the provision of a pleasure or recreation ground, a proposal which has our warmest sympathy,and to which we shall give our earnest attention,as we are confident that a practical scheme of utilizing the common lands for the purpose can be carried out with a minimum of expense to the ratepayers, and be of incalculable benefit to the inhabitants. If you are good enough to place us in the honourable position of members of the Board of Commissioners, we can say that on all questions we shall ever keep in view and work for the health and prosperity of our town, with due regard to efficiency and economy. We are, faithfully yours, WILLIAM FISHER, SAMUEL TAYLOR, WILLIAM WHITTAKER, THOMAS HANDLEY, WALTER TIMMINS,

At Cardiff, '3ll Monday, William Hopkins, ironmoulder, was charged with causing, the 'death of his wife. ELEVEN SOLDIERS KILLED.. St. Petersburg telegram says there were, it appears, several casualties during the progress ef the recent Rus- sian Army manceuvres, at which the Emperor William was present. Ten soldiers were accidentally killed while blowing up a pontoon bridge at Looga., while one dragoon and three horses were drowned. The Czar will be present at the manwuvres to be held in South- Western Russia, which begin on Septeinber sth. MR. 'GLADSTONE AND THE LITE CARDINAL NEWMAN. There seems to Lbea misapprehension as to the relations between the illustrieus Cardinal and myself.. They were marked by uniform :and extraordinary kind- nessupon his part, they were ;principally by letter, and, were rather casual and. slight.
